Below is an evidence-based overview of photodegradation and photocorrosion in two-dimensional (2D) perovskites, including mechanisms, experimental signatures, environmental drivers, and mitigation strategies.

# What “photodegradation” and “photocorrosion” mean for 2D perovskites

In perovskite systems, corrosion can be classified by the role of charge carriers and external circuits: chemical corrosion (no charge transfer), electrochemical corrosion (selective carrier injection drives reactions), photoelectrochemical corrosion (photoexcited minority carriers at interfaces), and photochemical corrosion (both majority and minority carriers contribute under light without an external bias) <cite id="18dd1670-2">Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: chemical, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, and photochemical; the distinction lies in whether injected or photoexcited carriers drive surface reactions and whether an external bias is present</cite>. A recent perspective emphasizes that mechanistic clarity requires careful, quantitative product detection under illumination and combines in situ electrochemical and surface imaging methods to reveal elementary steps; among mitigation strategies, compositional engineering, surface protection, and preparing 2D perovskites are all highlighted as viable routes <cite id="18dd1670-3">General thermodynamic/kinetic aspects and selected perovskite photocatalyst/photoelectrode corrosion examples are synthesized, with in situ/operando methods recommended; mitigation strategies include compositional engineering, surface protection, and the preparation of 2D perovskites, including bifunctional coatings</cite>. While these discussions span perovskite photocatalysts broadly, the same corrosion regimes and mitigation principles apply to 2D photovoltaic/perovskite-electrode stacks.

# Mechanisms of light-induced degradation in 2D perovskites

2D perovskites (e.g., Ruddlesden–Popper A2PbI4, quasi-2D PEA2(MA)2Pb3I10) can decompose under light via halide loss from the surface layers, progressing to lead iodide (PbI2) and ultimately metallic lead (Pb0) as the most detrimental defect. Systematic illumination studies attribute the loss of iodine to light, with subsequent formation of PbI2 and Pb0 in 2D–RP films <cite id="8e2a8d55-1">Light illumination leads to the loss of iodine in 2D–RP perovskites, resulting in PbI2 and eventually metallic Pb0, a detrimental defect</cite>. Operando imaging under blue laser (488 nm, 120 mW cm−2) shows that 2D perovskite converts to PbI2, underscoring that surface undercoordination and the orientation of Pb–I bonds along the c-axis make 2D layers less photostable than 3D despite their bulk stability <cite id="8e2a8d55-3">In situ CLSM studies found that 2D perovskite turns into PbI2 under blue-laser illumination (488 nm, 120 mW cm−2); 2D appears less photostable than 3D due to more surface Pb–I bonds along the c-axis plane that are undercoordinated and less stable under light</cite>.

The pathway is strongly dependent on photon energy and intensity. In quasi-2D PEA2(MA)2Pb3I10 films, red 635 nm illumination at low intensity (~50 mW cm−2) quenches PL without immediate bulk decomposition, whereas higher photon energy (447 nm) or higher intensity accelerates decomposition; in vacuum, both PL quenching and film degradation are suppressed, indicating oxygen/water and surface reactivity contribute to irreversible changes <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">With 635 nm illumination, the film does not decompose in air below ~500 mW cm−2; higher energy (447 nm) or intensity speeds decomposition; in vacuum, both PL quenching and film degradation are significantly suppressed</cite>. Quantitatively, under white light and modest illumination, quasi–2D films can go from bright to dark within ~100 minutes, with PL intensity dropping to zero and not recovering after darkness, consistent with decomposition into PbI2; continuous 447 nm illumination at ~350 mW cm−2 further confirms rapid degradation <cite id="8e2a8d55-4">After 100 min of white light, the film becomes almost completely dark with PL intensity near zero and no recovery after darkness treatment, proving decomposition into PbI2; under 447 nm at ~350 mW cm−2, continuous illumination drives degradation</cite>.

Process windows matter. A systematic study of PEA2PbI4 (a prototypical 2D–RP) shows that only high-energy light (blue laser, AM1.5G, and common fluorescent lamps) significantly degrades films; red laser and UV-filtered fluorescent lamps do not cause photodegradation. Critically, photodegradation is stronger when films are illuminated during annealing than after completion, because the photodegraded PbI2 layer passivates and stabilizes the structure during thermal treatment—explaining morphology discrepancies across labs and guiding fabrication best practices <cite id="8e2a8d55-1,8e2a8d55-4">Only blue laser, AM1.5G, and daily-use fluorescent lamps significantly degrade PEA2PbI4; red laser and UV-filtered FL do not; degradation during annealing is stronger than after film completion, suggesting PbI2 passivation</cite>.

Environmental interactions accelerate or mediate these reactions. In situ/operando work notes that interfacial interactions can drive a 2D-to-PbI2 conversion even at ~55% RH, consistent with a mixed photochemical/electrochemical mechanism at interfaces; IBIC imaging in devices corroborates light-induced degradation pathways under illumination <cite id="2a104753-0">Similar degradation in complete devices was confirmed by in situ laser-beam-induced current imaging; interfacial interactions at ~55% RH can drive 2D perovskite to PbI2 under blue laser; 2D appears less photostable than 3D due to undercoordinated surface Pb–I bonds</cite>.

# Experimental signatures and operando diagnostics

Operando and near-operando diagnostics reveal characteristic signatures of photodegradation. In quasi–2D films, PL quenching shows blue-shifting and broadening spectra with time under illumination, while intensity collapses to zero irreversibly; AFM/SEM show roughening, bumps at grain boundaries, and nanorod morphology changes that can be traced to prior light exposure; XPS confirms halide loss and surface chemical changes <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">PL quenching displays blue-shifting and broadening with time under illumination; films darken and PL recovers to zero with no recovery after darkness, indicating decomposition</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-1">AFM and SEM show rough morphology and bumps at grain boundaries; XPS and PL indicate halide loss and surface structural changes linked to photodegradation</cite>. In situ CLSM and IBIC further confirm that illumination-driven halide loss and PbI2 formation occur at the surface and can be mapped spatially and electrically under light <cite id="2a104753-0">In situ CLSM shows 2D perovskite turning into PbI2 under blue-laser illumination; IBIC imaging confirms the degradation process in devices</cite>.

# How 2D perovskites compare to 3D under light

Counterintuitively, many 2D perovskites are at least as photolabile as some 3D analogues, because their 2D layers expose undercoordinated Pb–I bonds at surfaces and {001} facets that are less stable under illumination. This has been directly observed: blue laser exposure converts 2D films to PbI2, and reviews attribute the lower photostability of 2D to the higher density of surface Pb–I bonds along the c-axis plane; in practice, 2D layers can be used as a “buffer” to limit photocorrosion in photoelectrodes, but they themselves still degrade under light <cite id="8e2a8d55-3">2D perovskite converts to PbI2 under blue-laser illumination; 2D appears less photostable than 3D due to undercoordinated surface Pb–I bonds along the c-axis plane</cite><cite id="18dd1670-3">Compositional engineering, surface protection, and preparing 2D perovskites are viable strategies to stabilize perovskites under illumination</cite>.

# Materials/process factors that govern photodegradation

- Halide stoichiometry and phase composition: In mixed-phase quasi–2D PEA2(MA)2Pb3I10, multiple n phases (n = 1,2,3) collapse together during degradation, beginning with crystalline structure collapse; films tend to decompose toward PbI2 under continuous illumination <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">The multiphase n = 1, 2, 3 in PEA2MA2Pb3I10 decomposes together, with degradation beginning with collapses of crystalline structures</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-4">Quasi–2D perovskites would eventually decompose into PbI2 under continuous illumination</cite>.

- Illumination wavelength/intensity and spectral filtering: Red light at modest intensity can be benign (limited PL quenching), but higher photon energy or higher intensity rapidly triggers irreversible changes; using appropriate longpass filters can prolong film lifetime <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">Higher energy photons (447 nm) or higher intensity accelerate decomposition; using a longpass filter can prolong device lifetime</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-4">At ~50 mW cm−2 red illumination, films remain stable below ~500 mW cm−2 for hours; higher energy accelerates degradation</cite>.

- Fabrication-stage sensitivity and passivation by PbI2: Degradation is stronger during annealing than after film completion; the photogenerated PbI2 layer can passivate and reduce further degradation, explaining rough/“bumpy” morphologies and inconsistent prior results if illumination was uncontrolled <cite id="8e2a8d55-1,8e2a8d55-4">Photodegradation occurs more strongly during annealing than after completion; the photodegraded PbI2 passivation effect is suggested; morphological discrepancies can originate from unintended light exposure</cite>.

- Environment (oxygen/water/humidity): Interfacial reactions at ~55% RH can drive 2D layers to PbI2 under illumination; in vacuum, degradation is suppressed, highlighting the role of surface reactions with adsorbates; device IBIC shows light-induced degradation under low humidity, consistent with interfacial photochemical/electrochemical pathways <cite id="2a104753-0">Interfacial interactions at ~55% RH can drive 2D-to-PbI2 conversion under blue laser; IBIC imaging confirms device-level degradation under illumination</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-2">In vacuum, both PL quenching and film degradation are significantly suppressed</cite>.

- Choice of organic cations and 2D stacking: Quasi–2D perovskites based on phenethylammonium (PEA+) and methylammonium (MA+) exhibit clear photodegradation signatures; blue light and high-energy spectra are particularly damaging, whereas red light can be tolerated at low intensity for hours, indicating that cation choice and bandgap widenings in 2D stacks modulate stability <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">PEA2MA2Pb3I10 films show PL quenching and irreversible darkening under high-energy illumination; red light at low intensity can be tolerated, suggesting composition-dependent photostability</cite>.

# Mitigation strategies for 2D perovskites

Process controls:
- Avoid bright, unfiltered lab light during sensitive steps (e.g., deposition and especially annealing); use dark conditions and appropriate optical filters to reduce photon energy flux; perform annealing under inert, shielded conditions <cite id="8e2a8d55-4">Daily-use fluorescent lamps significantly degrade PEA2PbI4; red laser without UV can be benign; photodegradation is stronger during annealing; dark conditions are highly recommended, especially during annealing</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-2">Using a longpass filter can be useful for prolonging lifetime; higher energy photons accelerate degradation</cite>.

Materials/compositional engineering:
- Incorporate wider bandgap 2D layers to reduce visible absorption and suppress carrier generation; mix halides (Br/I) to widen the bandgap and reduce surface reactivity; select cations with more stable surface coordination (e.g., alkali/alkylammoniums), while monitoring for phase segregation in quasi–2D stacks <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">Quasi–2D films with mixed n-phases degrade via structural collapse; higher photon energy accelerates PbI2 formation</cite>.

Surface protection and coatings:
- Surface passivation with compatible molecules and inorganic/organic overlayers to reduce halide loss; the perspective highlights bifunctional coatings that provide both catalytic stability and protection as a particularly promising direction; in 2D–RP fabrication, an unexpected but effective passivation layer is the photodegraded PbI2 itself, which can cap the surface during annealing <cite id="18dd1670-3">Bifunctional coatings that merge catalytic and protective functions are particularly promising for stabilizing perovskites under light</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-4">Photodegraded PbI2 can passivate and reduce further degradation during annealing</cite>.

Device-level design to suppress photocorrosion:
- Use 2D layers as surface capping layers or buffer layers to limit 3D perovskite exposure to corrosive environments (electrolytes or humid atmospheres) while recognizing that the 2D layer itself will still photo-degrade and must be protected <cite id="18dd1670-3">Compositional engineering and surface protection, including preparation of 2D perovskites, are viable strategies to mitigate photocorrosion</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-3">2D perovskites can be prepared to buffer stability, but they still convert to PbI2 under blue laser and are less photostable than 3D due to surface chemistry</cite>.

# Practical guidance and open questions

Operational cautions are concrete: avoid exposing 2D perovskite films to unfiltered fluorescent lighting and broad solar AM1.5G during annealing; use red/longpass illumination in lab characterization; and perform in-situ/operando diagnostics (IBIC, CLSM, AFM/SEM, XPS, PL) to quantify degradation kinetics and morphology evolution under controlled light and humidity <cite id="8e2a8d55-4">Daily-use fluorescent lamps significantly degrade PEA2PbI4; red/UV-filtered lamps do not; photodegradation during annealing is stronger; dark conditions are recommended</cite><cite id="2a104753-0">IBIC imaging confirms light-induced degradation pathways; interfacial reactions at ~55% RH drive 2D-to-PbI2 conversion under blue laser</cite>. Mechanistically, the dominant pathways appear to be light-driven halide loss from surface Pb–I bonds, followed by PbI2 formation and possible Pb0 generation, with interfacial reactions accelerated by oxygen/water; quantitative thresholds show that high-energy/blue light and high intensity rapidly trigger irreversible changes, whereas red light at low intensity can be tolerated for hours in some quasi–2D systems <cite id="8e2a8d55-1">Light causes iodine loss in 2D–RP perovskites, leading to PbI2 and Pb0</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-2">Blue or high-energy photons at modest intensities accelerate decomposition; red light at ~50 mW cm−2 can avoid immediate decomposition; vacuum suppresses both PL quenching and film degradation</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-4">White light can cause near-zero PL within 100 minutes with no recovery; continuous 447 nm at ~350 mW cm−2 accelerates degradation</cite>.

Open questions include: how to universally stabilize 2D surfaces without sacrificing bandgap and conductivity; whether bifunctional coatings can reliably outperform PbI2-derived passivation in the long term; and the role of facet engineering in suppressing Pb–I bond photoactivity. Continued development of in situ/operando tools and standardized, quantitative protocols is emphasized to disentangle photochemical vs. photoelectrochemical contributions and to benchmark stability across compositions and cations <cite id="18dd1670-3">Careful, quantitative characterization protocols with in situ/operando methods are necessary to understand instability mechanisms and guide design; possible mitigation strategies include composition and surface protection, including 2D perovskites</cite>.

# Summary

Light-induced degradation (photodegradation/photocorrosion) in 2D perovskites is driven by surface halide loss from undercoordinated Pb–I bonds, accelerated by high photon energy/intensity, interfacial reactions with oxygen/water, and process conditions like annealing; it manifests as PL quenching with spectral blue-shifting, structural collapse, and chemical evolution to PbI2/Pb0, and can be mitigated by wavelength filtering, dark/controlled illumination during processing, composition engineering, and surface passivation (including PbI2-derived capping or bifunctional coatings) <cite id="8e2a8d55-1">Light causes halide loss and progression to PbI2 and Pb0 in 2D–RP perovskites</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-2">High-energy/blue light accelerates decomposition in quasi–2D films; red at low intensity can be tolerated; vacuum suppresses degradation</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-3">2D perovskites are less photostable than 3D due to undercoordinated surface Pb–I bonds; blue laser converts 2D films to PbI2</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-4">Avoid daily-use fluorescent lamps during annealing; red/filtered illumination helps; photodegraded PbI2 can passivate surfaces</cite><cite id="2a104753-0">Interfacial interactions at moderate humidity drive 2D-to-PbI2 conversion; device-level IBIC confirms light-induced degradation</cite>.

We can approach the underlying processes from a thermodynamics perspective (i.e., whether it can happen or not); however, the convoluted reaction kinetics (i.e., multiple steps, chemical transitions) must also be considered. Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: (i) chemical, where no net charge transfer occurs at the interface; (ii) electrochemical, where the selectively injected charge carriers induce corrosion; (iii) photoelectrochemical, where the photoexcited minority carriers are predominantly responsible for the corrosion; (iv) photochemical, where both the minority and majority charge carriers can induce chemical changes. In the case of photochemical corrosion there is no external driving force that removes the majority carriers (as opposed to photoelectrochemical corrosion). Therefore, a larger fraction of majority carriers can reach the photocatalyst surface and can induce corrosion processes. 

In this Perspective, we discuss the last three corrosion processes from the above list, highlighting the peculiar features of perovskites. First, we present some general thermodynamic and kinetics aspects of photocorrosion. Selected examples of corrosion processes of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes form the main body of the article, where photo-(electro)catalytic and photo(electro)synthetic examples are both scrutinized. This is followed by a compilation of in situ/ operando methods, which provide mechanistic insights with spatial and temporal resolution. Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies, which also outline future research and development avenues.

Elaborating on the experience gathered from pioneering studies on photocorrosion processes and from stabilizing perovskite layers in PV devices will greatly accelerate the progress of this field. As the first step, careful characterization protocols are necessary for both PC and PEC studies (with quantitative product detection), to understand reasons and processes behind the instability. Furthermore, combined in situ electrochemical measurements will furnish mechanistic insights, with the possibility of revealing the elementary steps of corrosion. For nanoscale studies, in situ electrochemical atomic force microscopy 231−234 and PEC transmission electron microscopy will be useful to visualize morphological changes that occur on the surface of photocatalysts and photoelectrodes. Pinpointing structural weaknesses in these systems (e.g., sensitive facets, morphological features) will guide better design of stable solar energy conversion devices. With setups allowing few femtoseconds (or even sub-femtosecond) resolution, 236 the initial stages of charge carrier generation can be followed, providing new insights for subsequent rational materials design. While single crystal surfaces can be used to identify elementary steps in photocorrosion processes (including identification of stable and active facets), crystal facet engineering will help to translate this knowledge to nanostructured materials of practical importance.

Title: Impact of light illumination on the surface structure of two-dimensional Ruddlesden–Popper perovskite in the fabrication process
Snippet: Zhang et al showed many small bumps at the grain boundaries in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images [28]. In addition, Yang et al observed a rough surface morphology in the atomic force microscopy (AFM) image, which is in contrast to previous results [33]. 

During the fabrication process, 2DRP perovskites were often unintentionally exposed to light, such as a daily-use fluorescent lamp (FL) or sunlight from the window, in the laboratory. In previous works [34,35], they observed that light illumination leads to the loss of iodine in 2DRP perovskites, which results in the generation of lead iodide (PbI 2 ) and eventually, metallic lead (Pb 0 ), which has been reported as the most detrimental defect [36][37][38][39]. In this reason, we assume that above discrepancies may be, at least partially, originated from an unintended light illumination in the fabrication processes. However, it remains unclear how photodegradation occurs, and its impact has not been determined because there are no systematic studies on this topic. 

This study makes a unique contribution to the literature by investigating the effect of light illumination on all sample-fabrication processes. Various light sources, such as blue lasers, red lasers, a laboratory FL without/without an ultraviolet (UV) filter, and air mass (AM) 1.5, will be used to understand the photodegradation process of 2DRP perovskite. A phenethylammonium lead iodide (PEA 2 PbI 4 ) film was selected as the model structure to represent the 2DRP perovskite. We monitored the morphological evolution resulting from photodegradation via AFM and SEM. The degree of degradation and surface chemical structure were examined using PL and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). From this systematic study, we will address (1) which energy (wavelength) of light induces photodegradation, (2) how strongly it impacts the optoelectronic properties of 2DRP perovskite, and (3) which process of the film fabrication is most severely affected.

Title: Impact of light illumination on the surface structure of two-dimensional Ruddlesden–Popper perovskite in the fabrication process
Snippet: Two-dimensional Ruddlesden–Popper (2DRP) perovskites are promising owing to their excellent environmental stability and competitive efficiency. During the fabrication process, 2DRP perovskites were often unintentionally exposed to light in the laboratory. However, the influence of light illumination on the surface structure of 2DRP during fabrication is unclear. Herein, the photodegradation of 2DRP perovskite (phenethylammonium lead iodide, PEA2PbI4) is comprehensively investigated using x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and photoluminescence spectroscopy. We observed that only high-energy light, including that from a blue laser, air mass 1.5G, and notably, the daily used fluorescent lamp (FL) in the laboratory, significantly degraded PEA2PbI4. However, the red laser and ultraviolet-filtered FL, which had low energies, did not cause photodegradation. From this systematic study, we can explain the discrepancies in the surface morphologies previously studied. For instance, randomly oriented nanorod or rough surface of PEA2PbI4 mostly stems from photodegradation. We observed that photodegradation occurred more strongly when the films were illuminated during annealing than when they were illuminated after all fabrication processes were completed. We suggest that this difference stems from the completeness of the structure and the photodegraded PbI2 passivation effect. Our study provides two key guidelines for the fabrication of PEA2PbI4 films. The daily-use FL in the laboratory must be avoided for high-quality samples, and dark conditions are highly recommended, at least during the annealing process.

Below is an evidence-based overview of photodegradation and photocorrosion in two-dimensional (2D) perovskites, including mechanisms, experimental signatures, environmental drivers, and mitigation strategies.

# What “photodegradation” and “photocorrosion” mean for 2D perovskites

In perovskite systems, corrosion can be classified by the role of charge carriers and external circuits: chemical corrosion (no charge transfer), electrochemical corrosion (selective carrier injection drives reactions), photoelectrochemical corrosion (photoexcited minority carriers at interfaces), and photochemical corrosion (both majority and minority carriers contribute under light without an external bias) <cite id="18dd1670-2">Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: chemical, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, and photochemical; the distinction lies in whether injected or photoexcited carriers drive surface reactions and whether an external bias is present</cite>. A recent perspective emphasizes that mechanistic clarity requires careful, quantitative product detection under illumination and combines in situ electrochemical and surface imaging methods to reveal elementary steps; among mitigation strategies, compositional engineering, surface protection, and preparing 2D perovskites are all highlighted as viable routes <cite id="18dd1670-3">General thermodynamic/kinetic aspects and selected perovskite photocatalyst/photoelectrode corrosion examples are synthesized, with in situ/operando methods recommended; mitigation strategies include compositional engineering, surface protection, and the preparation of 2D perovskites, including bifunctional coatings</cite>. While these discussions span perovskite photocatalysts broadly, the same corrosion regimes and mitigation principles apply to 2D photovoltaic/perovskite-electrode stacks.

# Mechanisms of light-induced degradation in 2D perovskites

2D perovskites (e.g., Ruddlesden–Popper A2PbI4, quasi-2D PEA2(MA)2Pb3I10) can decompose under light via halide loss from the surface layers, progressing to lead iodide (PbI2) and ultimately metallic lead (Pb0) as the most detrimental defect. Systematic illumination studies attribute the loss of iodine to light, with subsequent formation of PbI2 and Pb0 in 2D–RP films <cite id="8e2a8d55-1">Light illumination leads to the loss of iodine in 2D–RP perovskites, resulting in PbI2 and eventually metallic Pb0, a detrimental defect</cite>. Operando imaging under blue laser (488 nm, 120 mW cm−2) shows that 2D perovskite converts to PbI2, underscoring that surface undercoordination and the orientation of Pb–I bonds along the c-axis make 2D layers less photostable than 3D despite their bulk stability <cite id="8e2a8d55-3">In situ CLSM studies found that 2D perovskite turns into PbI2 under blue-laser illumination (488 nm, 120 mW cm−2); 2D appears less photostable than 3D due to more surface Pb–I bonds along the c-axis plane that are undercoordinated and less stable under light</cite>.

The pathway is strongly dependent on photon energy and intensity. In quasi-2D PEA2(MA)2Pb3I10 films, red 635 nm illumination at low intensity (~50 mW cm−2) quenches PL without immediate bulk decomposition, whereas higher photon energy (447 nm) or higher intensity accelerates decomposition; in vacuum, both PL quenching and film degradation are suppressed, indicating oxygen/water and surface reactivity contribute to irreversible changes <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">With 635 nm illumination, the film does not decompose in air below ~500 mW cm−2; higher energy (447 nm) or intensity speeds decomposition; in vacuum, both PL quenching and film degradation are significantly suppressed</cite>. Quantitatively, under white light and modest illumination, quasi–2D films can go from bright to dark within ~100 minutes, with PL intensity dropping to zero and not recovering after darkness, consistent with decomposition into PbI2; continuous 447 nm illumination at ~350 mW cm−2 further confirms rapid degradation <cite id="8e2a8d55-4">After 100 min of white light, the film becomes almost completely dark with PL intensity near zero and no recovery after darkness treatment, proving decomposition into PbI2; under 447 nm at ~350 mW cm−2, continuous illumination drives degradation</cite>.

Process windows matter. A systematic study of PEA2PbI4 (a prototypical 2D–RP) shows that only high-energy light (blue laser, AM1.5G, and common fluorescent lamps) significantly degrades films; red laser and UV-filtered fluorescent lamps do not cause photodegradation. Critically, photodegradation is stronger when films are illuminated during annealing than after completion, because the photodegraded PbI2 layer passivates and stabilizes the structure during thermal treatment—explaining morphology discrepancies across labs and guiding fabrication best practices <cite id="8e2a8d55-1,8e2a8d55-4">Only blue laser, AM1.5G, and daily-use fluorescent lamps significantly degrade PEA2PbI4; red laser and UV-filtered FL do not; degradation during annealing is stronger than after film completion, suggesting PbI2 passivation</cite>.

Environmental interactions accelerate or mediate these reactions. In situ/operando work notes that interfacial interactions can drive a 2D-to-PbI2 conversion even at ~55% RH, consistent with a mixed photochemical/electrochemical mechanism at interfaces; IBIC imaging in devices corroborates light-induced degradation pathways under illumination <cite id="2a104753-0">Similar degradation in complete devices was confirmed by in situ laser-beam-induced current imaging; interfacial interactions at ~55% RH can drive 2D perovskite to PbI2 under blue laser; 2D appears less photostable than 3D due to undercoordinated surface Pb–I bonds</cite>.

# Experimental signatures and operando diagnostics

Operando and near-operando diagnostics reveal characteristic signatures of photodegradation. In quasi–2D films, PL quenching shows blue-shifting and broadening spectra with time under illumination, while intensity collapses to zero irreversibly; AFM/SEM show roughening, bumps at grain boundaries, and nanorod morphology changes that can be traced to prior light exposure; XPS confirms halide loss and surface chemical changes <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">PL quenching displays blue-shifting and broadening with time under illumination; films darken and PL recovers to zero with no recovery after darkness, indicating decomposition</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-1">AFM and SEM show rough morphology and bumps at grain boundaries; XPS and PL indicate halide loss and surface structural changes linked to photodegradation</cite>. In situ CLSM and IBIC further confirm that illumination-driven halide loss and PbI2 formation occur at the surface and can be mapped spatially and electrically under light <cite id="2a104753-0">In situ CLSM shows 2D perovskite turning into PbI2 under blue-laser illumination; IBIC imaging confirms the degradation process in devices</cite>.

# How 2D perovskites compare to 3D under light

Counterintuitively, many 2D perovskites are at least as photolabile as some 3D analogues, because their 2D layers expose undercoordinated Pb–I bonds at surfaces and {001} facets that are less stable under illumination. This has been directly observed: blue laser exposure converts 2D films to PbI2, and reviews attribute the lower photostability of 2D to the higher density of surface Pb–I bonds along the c-axis plane; in practice, 2D layers can be used as a “buffer” to limit photocorrosion in photoelectrodes, but they themselves still degrade under light <cite id="8e2a8d55-3">2D perovskite converts to PbI2 under blue-laser illumination; 2D appears less photostable than 3D due to undercoordinated surface Pb–I bonds along the c-axis plane</cite><cite id="18dd1670-3">Compositional engineering, surface protection, and preparing 2D perovskites are viable strategies to stabilize perovskites under illumination</cite>.

# Materials/process factors that govern photodegradation

- Halide stoichiometry and phase composition: In mixed-phase quasi–2D PEA2(MA)2Pb3I10, multiple n phases (n = 1,2,3) collapse together during degradation, beginning with crystalline structure collapse; films tend to decompose toward PbI2 under continuous illumination <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">The multiphase n = 1, 2, 3 in PEA2MA2Pb3I10 decomposes together, with degradation beginning with collapses of crystalline structures</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-4">Quasi–2D perovskites would eventually decompose into PbI2 under continuous illumination</cite>.

- Illumination wavelength/intensity and spectral filtering: Red light at modest intensity can be benign (limited PL quenching), but higher photon energy or higher intensity rapidly triggers irreversible changes; using appropriate longpass filters can prolong film lifetime <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">Higher energy photons (447 nm) or higher intensity accelerate decomposition; using a longpass filter can prolong device lifetime</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-4">At ~50 mW cm−2 red illumination, films remain stable below ~500 mW cm−2 for hours; higher energy accelerates degradation</cite>.

- Fabrication-stage sensitivity and passivation by PbI2: Degradation is stronger during annealing than after film completion; the photogenerated PbI2 layer can passivate and reduce further degradation, explaining rough/“bumpy” morphologies and inconsistent prior results if illumination was uncontrolled <cite id="8e2a8d55-1,8e2a8d55-4">Photodegradation occurs more strongly during annealing than after completion; the photodegraded PbI2 passivation effect is suggested; morphological discrepancies can originate from unintended light exposure</cite>.

- Environment (oxygen/water/humidity): Interfacial reactions at ~55% RH can drive 2D layers to PbI2 under illumination; in vacuum, degradation is suppressed, highlighting the role of surface reactions with adsorbates; device IBIC shows light-induced degradation under low humidity, consistent with interfacial photochemical/electrochemical pathways <cite id="2a104753-0">Interfacial interactions at ~55% RH can drive 2D-to-PbI2 conversion under blue laser; IBIC imaging confirms device-level degradation under illumination</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-2">In vacuum, both PL quenching and film degradation are significantly suppressed</cite>.

- Choice of organic cations and 2D stacking: Quasi–2D perovskites based on phenethylammonium (PEA+) and methylammonium (MA+) exhibit clear photodegradation signatures; blue light and high-energy spectra are particularly damaging, whereas red light can be tolerated at low intensity for hours, indicating that cation choice and bandgap widenings in 2D stacks modulate stability <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">PEA2MA2Pb3I10 films show PL quenching and irreversible darkening under high-energy illumination; red light at low intensity can be tolerated, suggesting composition-dependent photostability</cite>.

# Mitigation strategies for 2D perovskites

Process controls:
- Avoid bright, unfiltered lab light during sensitive steps (e.g., deposition and especially annealing); use dark conditions and appropriate optical filters to reduce photon energy flux; perform annealing under inert, shielded conditions <cite id="8e2a8d55-4">Daily-use fluorescent lamps significantly degrade PEA2PbI4; red laser without UV can be benign; photodegradation is stronger during annealing; dark conditions are highly recommended, especially during annealing</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-2">Using a longpass filter can be useful for prolonging lifetime; higher energy photons accelerate degradation</cite>.

Materials/compositional engineering:
- Incorporate wider bandgap 2D layers to reduce visible absorption and suppress carrier generation; mix halides (Br/I) to widen the bandgap and reduce surface reactivity; select cations with more stable surface coordination (e.g., alkali/alkylammoniums), while monitoring for phase segregation in quasi–2D stacks <cite id="8e2a8d55-2">Quasi–2D films with mixed n-phases degrade via structural collapse; higher photon energy accelerates PbI2 formation</cite>.

Surface protection and coatings:
- Surface passivation with compatible molecules and inorganic/organic overlayers to reduce halide loss; the perspective highlights bifunctional coatings that provide both catalytic stability and protection as a particularly promising direction; in 2D–RP fabrication, an unexpected but effective passivation layer is the photodegraded PbI2 itself, which can cap the surface during annealing <cite id="18dd1670-3">Bifunctional coatings that merge catalytic and protective functions are particularly promising for stabilizing perovskites under light</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-4">Photodegraded PbI2 can passivate and reduce further degradation during annealing</cite>.

Device-level design to suppress photocorrosion:
- Use 2D layers as surface capping layers or buffer layers to limit 3D perovskite exposure to corrosive environments (electrolytes or humid atmospheres) while recognizing that the 2D layer itself will still photo-degrade and must be protected <cite id="18dd1670-3">Compositional engineering and surface protection, including preparation of 2D perovskites, are viable strategies to mitigate photocorrosion</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-3">2D perovskites can be prepared to buffer stability, but they still convert to PbI2 under blue laser and are less photostable than 3D due to surface chemistry</cite>.

# Practical guidance and open questions

Operational cautions are concrete: avoid exposing 2D perovskite films to unfiltered fluorescent lighting and broad solar AM1.5G during annealing; use red/longpass illumination in lab characterization; and perform in-situ/operando diagnostics (IBIC, CLSM, AFM/SEM, XPS, PL) to quantify degradation kinetics and morphology evolution under controlled light and humidity <cite id="8e2a8d55-4">Daily-use fluorescent lamps significantly degrade PEA2PbI4; red/UV-filtered lamps do not; photodegradation during annealing is stronger; dark conditions are recommended</cite><cite id="2a104753-0">IBIC imaging confirms light-induced degradation pathways; interfacial reactions at ~55% RH drive 2D-to-PbI2 conversion under blue laser</cite>. Mechanistically, the dominant pathways appear to be light-driven halide loss from surface Pb–I bonds, followed by PbI2 formation and possible Pb0 generation, with interfacial reactions accelerated by oxygen/water; quantitative thresholds show that high-energy/blue light and high intensity rapidly trigger irreversible changes, whereas red light at low intensity can be tolerated for hours in some quasi–2D systems <cite id="8e2a8d55-1">Light causes iodine loss in 2D–RP perovskites, leading to PbI2 and Pb0</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-2">Blue or high-energy photons at modest intensities accelerate decomposition; red light at ~50 mW cm−2 can avoid immediate decomposition; vacuum suppresses both PL quenching and film degradation</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-4">White light can cause near-zero PL within 100 minutes with no recovery; continuous 447 nm at ~350 mW cm−2 accelerates degradation</cite>.

Open questions include: how to universally stabilize 2D surfaces without sacrificing bandgap and conductivity; whether bifunctional coatings can reliably outperform PbI2-derived passivation in the long term; and the role of facet engineering in suppressing Pb–I bond photoactivity. Continued development of in situ/operando tools and standardized, quantitative protocols is emphasized to disentangle photochemical vs. photoelectrochemical contributions and to benchmark stability across compositions and cations <cite id="18dd1670-3">Careful, quantitative characterization protocols with in situ/operando methods are necessary to understand instability mechanisms and guide design; possible mitigation strategies include composition and surface protection, including 2D perovskites</cite>.

# Summary

Light-induced degradation (photodegradation/photocorrosion) in 2D perovskites is driven by surface halide loss from undercoordinated Pb–I bonds, accelerated by high photon energy/intensity, interfacial reactions with oxygen/water, and process conditions like annealing; it manifests as PL quenching with spectral blue-shifting, structural collapse, and chemical evolution to PbI2/Pb0, and can be mitigated by wavelength filtering, dark/controlled illumination during processing, composition engineering, and surface passivation (including PbI2-derived capping or bifunctional coatings) <cite id="8e2a8d55-1">Light causes halide loss and progression to PbI2 and Pb0 in 2D–RP perovskites</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-2">High-energy/blue light accelerates decomposition in quasi–2D films; red at low intensity can be tolerated; vacuum suppresses degradation</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-3">2D perovskites are less photostable than 3D due to undercoordinated surface Pb–I bonds; blue laser converts 2D films to PbI2</cite><cite id="8e2a8d55-4">Avoid daily-use fluorescent lamps during annealing; red/filtered illumination helps; photodegraded PbI2 can passivate surfaces</cite><cite id="2a104753-0">Interfacial interactions at moderate humidity drive 2D-to-PbI2 conversion; device-level IBIC confirms light-induced degradation</cite>. </answer>

We can approach the underlying processes from a thermodynamics perspective (i.e., whether it can happen or not); however, the convoluted reaction kinetics (i.e., multiple steps, chemical transitions) must also be considered. Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: (i) chemical, where no net charge transfer occurs at the interface; (ii) electrochemical, where the selectively injected charge carriers induce corrosion; (iii) photoelectrochemical, where the photoexcited minority carriers are predominantly responsible for the corrosion; (iv) photochemical, where both the minority and majority charge carriers can induce chemical changes. In the case of photochemical corrosion there is no external driving force that removes the majority carriers (as opposed to photoelectrochemical corrosion). Therefore, a larger fraction of majority carriers can reach the photocatalyst surface and can induce corrosion processes. 

In this Perspective, we discuss the last three corrosion processes from the above list, highlighting the peculiar features of perovskites. First, we present some general thermodynamic and kinetics aspects of photocorrosion. Selected examples of corrosion processes of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes form the main body of the article, where photo-(electro)catalytic and photo(electro)synthetic examples are both scrutinized. This is followed by a compilation of in situ/ operando methods, which provide mechanistic insights with spatial and temporal resolution. Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies, which also outline future research and development avenues.

snippet.text:
uring corrosion, either complete self-decomposition or the formation of active or inactive surface layers can occur. We can approach the underlying processes from a thermodynamics perspective (i.e., whether it can happen or not); however, the convoluted reaction kinetics (i.e., multiple steps, chemical transitions) must also be considered. Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: (i) chemical, where no net charge transfer occurs at the interface; (ii) electrochemical, where the selectively injected charge carriers induce corrosion; (iii) photoelectrochemical, where the photoexcited minority carriers are predominantly responsible for the corrosion; (iv) photochemical, where both the minority and majority charge carriers can induce chemical changes. In the case of photochemical corrosion there is no external driving force that removes the majority carriers (as opposed to photoelectrochemical corrosion). Therefore, a larger fraction of majority carriers can reach the photocatalyst surface and can induce corrosion processes. 

In this Perspective, we discuss the last three corrosion processes from the above list, highlighting the peculiar features of perovskites. First, we present some general thermodynamic and kinetics aspects of photocorrosion. Selected examples of corrosion processes of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes form the main body of the article, where photo-(electro)catalytic and photo(electro)synthetic examples are both scrutinized. This is followed by a compilation of in situ/ operando methods, which provide mechanistic insights with spatial and temporal resolution. Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies, which also outline future research and development avenues.

Title: Light-Induced Photoluminescence Quenching and Degradation in Quasi 2D Perovskites Film of (C6H5C2H4NH3)2 (CH3NH3)2[Pb3I10]
Snippet: Quasi-two-dimensional (2D) perovskites recently came into the focus because of their moisture stability. In addition to ambient air, light illumination could also cause degradation for the film of 2D perovskites; however, few studies have investigated their photostability. Here, we work on light-induced photoluminescence quenching, as well as the degradation of quasi-2D perovskites of PEA2MAn−1PbnI3n+1 (n = 3 nominally, PEA+ = C6H5(CH2)2NH3+, MA+ = CH3NH3+). Light-induced photoluminescence (PL) quenching generally happens with different speeds, depending on the wavelength and intensity of the laser as well as the film’s environment. With red light (635 nm) illumination, the film does not decompose into ambient air with an intensity below ~500 mW/cm2, although in general, a higher laser intensity and/or higher photon energy (447 nm) could render the decomposition process easier and faster. On the other hand, when the film is in a vacuum, both light-induced PL quenching and film degradation are significantly suppressed. Furthermore, we find that the multiphase of n = 1, 2, 3 in the PEA2MA2Pb3I10 film decomposes together and that the degradation processes begin with the collapses of the crystalline structures.

documents.title: Light-Induced Photoluminescence Quenching and Degradation in Quasi 2D Perovskites Film of (C6H5C2H4NH3)2 (CH3NH3)2[Pb3I10]
documents.snippet: Quasi-two-dimensional (2D) perovskites recently came into the focus because of their moisture stability. In addition to ambient air, light illumination could also cause degradation for the film of 2D perovskites; however, few studies have investigated their photostability. Here, we work on light-induced photoluminescence quenching, as well as the degradation of quasi-2D perovskites of PEA2MAn−1PbnI3n+1 (n = 3 nominally, PEA+ = C6H5(CH2)2NH3+, MA+ = CH3NH3+). Light-induced photoluminescence (PL) quenching generally happens with different speeds, depending on the wavelength and intensity of the laser as well as the film’s environment. With red light (635 nm) illumination, the film does not decompose into ambient air with an intensity below ~500 mW/cm2, although in general, a higher laser intensity and/or higher photon energy (447 nm) could render the decomposition process easier and faster. On the other hand, when the film is in a vacuum, both light-induced PL quenching and film degradation are significantly suppressed. Furthermore, we find that the multiphase of n = 1, 2, 3 in the PEA2MA2Pb3I10 film decomposes together and that the degradation processes begin with the collapses of the crystalline structures.

Title: Impact of light illumination on the surface structure of two-dimensional Ruddlesden–Popper perovskite in the fabrication process
Snippet: Two-dimensional Ruddlesden–Popper (2DRP) perovskites are promising owing to their excellent environmental stability and competitive efficiency. During the fabrication process, 2DRP perovskites were often unintentionally exposed to light in the laboratory. However, the influence of light illumination on the surface structure of 2DRP during fabrication is unclear. Herein, the photodegradation of 2DRP perovskite (phenethylammonium lead iodide, PEA2PbI4) is comprehensively investigated using x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and photoluminescence spectroscopy. We observed that only high-energy light, including that from a blue laser, air mass 1.5G, and notably, the daily used fluorescent lamp (FL) in the laboratory, significantly degraded PEA2PbI4. However, the red laser and ultraviolet-filtered FL, which had low energies, did not cause photodegradation. From this systematic study, we can explain the discrepancies in the surface morphologies previously studied. For instance, randomly oriented nanorod or rough surface of PEA2PbI4 mostly stems from photodegradation. We observed that photodegradation occurred more strongly when the films were illuminated during annealing than when they were illuminated after all fabrication processes were completed. We suggest that this difference stems from the completeness of the structure and the photodegraded PbI2 passivation effect. Our study provides two key guidelines for the fabrication of PEA2PbI4 films. The daily-use FL in the laboratory must be avoided for high-quality samples, and dark conditions are highly recommended, at least during the annealing process.

Summary
In the perovskite literature, “photodegradation” generally denotes light‑induced structural and chemical changes within the perovskite lattice (e.g., phase conversion, defect formation, ion migration) that degrade optoelectronic properties, while “photocorrosion” emphasizes light‑accelerated surface and interface breakdown—dissolution/etching and corrosion product formation—often electrochemical or photoelectrochemical in nature. In 2D perovskites, both processes can occur under illumination and in humid/oxidizing environments, but they capture distinct mechanisms: photodegradation is bulk/phase/defect evolution (often to PbI2), whereas photocorrosion is surface/interface loss and product formation (e.g., PbI2, PbI x surface layers) at the material–electrolyte/air interface. Authors sometimes use the terms loosely, but mechanistic and experimental signatures allow them to be distinguished. <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">Under blue light in air, 2D BA2MA n−1 PbnI3n+1 films undergo near‑complete loss of the perovskite (200) XRD peak and emergence of a broad PbI2 signal within hours, indicating rapid light‑induced phase degradation</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-3">with oxygen facilitating fast photodegradation in dry air, whereas in inert (<10 ppm O2) conditions the same films retain color for hours</cite>. <cite id="b3bc27f3-2">Operando imaging shows 2D perovskite converting to PbI2 under blue illumination, consistent with light‑induced structural/phase changes</cite>.

Mechanistic distinctions and definitions
Recent perspectives define photocorrosion at irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces as a thermodynamic/kinetic process that can proceed via chemical, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, or photochemical pathways, producing either complete self‑decomposition or surface layers/corrosion products (e.g., dissolution/etching products at the interface). <cite id="8ea07133-1">Perovskites are sensitive to solvents and electrolytes and are susceptible to photocorrosion, motivating mechanistic studies via in situ/operando electrochemical and surface techniques</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-2">and strategies including surface protection, materials/electrolyte engineering, and preparation of 2D perovskites</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-3">with corrosion events categorized by charge‑transfer and carrier involvement, including formation of surface layers or complete decomposition</cite>. <cite id="28d61341-4">More generally, illumination generates carriers that can decompose semiconductors in contact with water/ electrolytes (photocorrosion), a process controllable by corrosion state concepts</cite>. By contrast, photodegradation is often used to describe light‑induced changes in absorption/PL, phase evolution (e.g., to PbI2), and defect/ion dynamics that reduce performance without necessarily framing the dissolution/etching aspect. <cite id="b3bc27f3-3">Light soaking in air drives rapid photodegradation of layered 2D perovskites to PbI2 within tens of minutes, whereas inert atmospheres suppress the reaction</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">and XRD shows orders‑of‑magnitude loss of perovskite peak intensity and emergence of PbI2</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-2">with undercoordinated surface Pb–I bonds in 2D perovskites contributing to instability and photo‑conversion to PbI2 under illumination</cite>.

Evidence in 2D perovskites
Light‑induced photodegradation in 2D layers. In BA2MA n−1 PbnI3n+1 homologous layered perovskites, blue‑light exposure in air rapidly eliminates the perovskite (200) peak, broadens the PbI2 peak, and collapses PL, indicating structural phase conversion and strong performance decay; oxygen penetration into the layered framework accelerates this transformation relative to denser 3D frameworks. <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">After 5 h in air, the n1 2D sample undergoes almost complete phase degradation with a 4×10−4 fraction of the initial perovskite peak area and a widened PbI2 peak; oxygen dramatically increases the rate</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-3">and under identical illumination, 2D films in dry air degrade within 20 min to a light‑yellow color while 3D MAPI films resist much longer</cite>. <cite id="b3bc27f3-2">Under blue‑laser illumination (488 nm, 120 mW cm−2), 2D perovskite transforms into PbI2</cite>. Oxygen and humidity modulate the mechanism: <cite id="eecf6cd8-0">in air the material undergoes ~20× faster photodegradation than in nonpolar decane, with measurable PbI2 onset after 10 min</cite> <cite id="eecf6cd8-4">and thermal degradation differs (volatilization of MA/BA with PbI2 formation), indicating distinct light‑ vs heat‑induced processes</cite>.

Surface reconstruction and passivation by 2D layers. Light and ligand treatments can drive surface reconstruction where 2D perovskite forms on 3D surfaces, passivating defects and improving optoelectronic properties. <cite id="fb43ab61-1">Chlorinated 4Cl‑BA treatment yields a diffraction peak at 6.18° assigned to a pure 2D perovskite surface layer, with reduced PbI2 peak intensity, suppressed trap states, and enhanced PL; the improved device performance is attributed to 2D perovskite surface reconstruction and built‑in fields at 2D/3D heterojunctions</cite> <cite id="fb43ab61-0">and sequential ligand passivation can fill surface pits and grain‑boundary defects, reduce contact potential difference from ~400 mV to ~150 mV then ~10 mV, and homogenize surface potential via 2D perovskite formation</cite> <cite id="fb43ab61-3">XPS and scattering show BA cation grafting and vertical 2D perovskite orientation that passivates 3D surfaces and creates field‑effect passivation</cite>. <cite id="fb43ab61-4">Light illumination can improve crystallization and lattice expansion of 2D perovskites, enhancing PL by 3.1× and reducing trap‑assisted recombination</cite>.

Answer to the question

- Short answer: They are often used loosely but are mechanistically related and not strictly synonymous. Photodegradation denotes light‑induced structural/phase/defect evolution (e.g., perovskite→PbI2 conversion, PL loss, performance decay), whereas photocorrosion emphasizes light‑accelerated surface/interface breakdown and corrosion product formation at irradiated perovskite–electrolyte/air interfaces. In 2D perovskites, both mechanisms coexist: light can drive rapid photodegradation to PbI2 and surface etching (photocorrosion), or 2D surface reconstruction and passivation that suppresses degradation and enhances properties; thus, authors may treat them as overlapping phenomena in practice. <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">Light in oxygenated air causes near‑complete perovskite→PbI2 conversion in 2D layers within hours</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-3">and minutes in air vs hours in inert conditions</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-3">photocorrosion frameworks classify interface‑driven corrosion products and mechanisms</cite> <cite id="fb43ab61-1">2D reconstruction can suppress nonradiative recombination and improve devices</cite>.
- How to tell them apart in a paper: Look for mechanistic probes. Title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
Snippet: Metal–halide perovskites transformed optoelectronics research and development during the past decade. They have also gained a foothold in photocatalytic and photoelectrochemical processes recently, but their sensitivity to the most commonly applied solvents and electrolytes together with their susceptibility to photocorrosion hinders such applications. Understanding the elementary steps of photocorrosion of these materials can aid the endeavor of realizing stable devices. In this Perspective, we discuss both thermodynamic and kinetic aspects of photocorrosion processes occurring at the interface of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes with different electrolytes. We show how combined in situ and operando electrochemical techniques can reveal the underlying mechanisms. Finally, we also discuss emerging strategies to mitigate photocorrosion (such as surface protection, materials and electrolyte engineering, etc.).
</snippet>

Snippet: PC and PEC scenarios are recent additions to the potential research arenas where the optoelectronic properties of perovskites can be harnessed. Elaborating on the experience gathered from pioneering studies on photocorrosion processes and from stabilizing perovskite layers in PV devices will greatly accelerate the progress of this field. As the first step, careful characterization protocols are necessary for both PC and PEC studies (with quantitative product detection), to understand reasons and processes behind the instability. Furthermore, combined in situ electrochemical measurements will furnish mechanistic insights, with the possibility of revealing the elementary steps of corrosion. For nanoscale studies, in situ electrochemical atomic force microscopy 231−234 and PEC transmission electron microscopy will be useful to visualize morphological changes that occur on the surface of photocatalysts and photoelectrodes. Pinpointing structural weaknesses in these systems (e.g., sensitive facets, morphological features) will guide better design of stable solar energy conversion devices. In a similar fashion, coupled ultrafast techniques can shed light on how corrosion affects the charge carrier dynamics of these complex systems. 158,235 Ultrafast spectroscopic studies under electrochemical control have just been employed for perovskite electrodes recently, and further breakthroughs are expected once the pulse duration is decreased. With setups allowing few femtoseconds (or even sub-femtosecond) resolution, 236 the initial stages of charge carrier generation can be followed, providing new insights for subsequent rational materials design. While single crystal surfaces can be used to identify elementary steps in photocorrosion processes (including identification of stable and active facets), crystal facet engineering will help to translate this knowledge to nanostructured materials of practical importance. 

Once the elementary steps of the photocorrosion process are uncovered, different strategies can be employed to stabilize perovskites. Compositional engineering, various surface protection approaches and the preparation of 2D perovskites are all viable options. As a particularly promising direction, bifunctional coatings can be developed, where the catalytic and protective functions are merged.
</snippet>

We can approach the underlying processes from a thermodynamics perspective (i.e., whether it can happen or not); however, the convoluted reaction kinetics (i.e., multiple steps, chemical transitions) must also be considered. Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: (i) chemical, where no net charge transfer occurs at the interface; (ii) electrochemical, where the selectively injected charge carriers induce corrosion; (iii) photoelectrochemical, where the photoexcited minority carriers are predominantly responsible for the corrosion; (iv) photochemical, where both the minority and majority charge carriers can induce chemical changes. In the case of photochemical corrosion there is no external driving force that removes the majority carriers (as opposed to photoelectrochemical corrosion). Therefore, a larger fraction of majority carriers can reach the photocatalyst surface and can induce corrosion processes. 

In this Perspective, we discuss the last three corrosion processes from the above list, highlighting the peculiar features of perovskites. First, we present some general thermodynamic and kinetics aspects of photocorrosion. Selected examples of corrosion processes of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes form the main body of the article, where photo-(electro)catalytic and photo(electro)synthetic examples are both scrutinized. This is followed by a compilation of in situ/ operando methods, which provide mechanistic insights with spatial and temporal resolution. Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies, which also outline future research and development avenues.
</snippet>

However, in device structures, these effects are partially mitigated by the inclusion of charge-transport layers. Prolonged exposure of PSCs with standard back electrodes (Ag, Au, Cu) to exploitation conditions (temperature 25 -85°C, light intensity ~100 mW/cm 2 ) leads to electrode oxidation, delamination, and a reduction in photoelectric performance [16], [17]. 

Among the others approaches, the use of perovskite heterostructures was considered as an effective strategy to mitigate the corrosion effects at the interfaces of PSCs. The heterostructure of halide perovskites typically consists of a standard microcrystalline absorber film combined with low-dimensional perovskite configurations. Replacing the A-site cation with a large spacer molecule (typically phenyl-ethyl ammonium (PEA) or C4H9NH3 (BA)) induces spatial separation within the 3D perovskite crystal lattice, resulting in alternating layers of 3D perovskite and large organic spacers [18]. The molar ratio between the spacer molecule and the perovskite framework dictated the dimensionality of the resulting phase. This results in the formation of so called quasi-two-dimensional (2D) Ruddlesden-Popper phases coupled with the lattice of the photoactive three-dimensional (3D) perovskite phase. Current literature [19], [20], [21], [22] highlights the effects of surface passivation in perovskite films, including reduced defect concentrations at inter-grain interfaces and improved thermal stability in 2D/3D perovskite heterostructures (PHS). The integration methods of 2D perovskite additives also strongly impacts the crystal structure of perovskite thin-films. A pioneering study by Loi group demonstrated [23] the impact of employing a 2D perovskite template, deposited via a scalable technique, which subsequently undergoes in situ conversion to form a highly crystalline 3D perovskite.

Snippet: Particularly, light illumination has become a useful approach to improving the morphology and optical properties of 3D perovskites. In addition, the properties of the perovskites could be optimized by the photochemical reaction occurred during light exposure [39]. Although widely studied in 3D perovskites, the influence of light illumination on the growth and optoelectronic properties of 2D layered organic-inorganic perovskites still needs detailed understanding, which will lay great importance for fabricating high-quality 2D perovskites for functional devices. 

Herein, we report the enhanced optoelectronic performances of 2D organic-inorganic hybrid perovskite through UV-light illumination. UV-light illumination will lead to an improvement of the crystallization and lattice expansion of the 2D perovskite monocrystalline films. Consequently, the PL emission of the 2D perovskite can be enhanced by 3.1 folds, with the trap-assisted recombination greatly decreased. For functional applications, photoconductive devices is fabricated based on the optimized 2D perovskites and the optoelectronic responses have been enhanced.

Title: Nonmonotonic Photostability of BA2MAn-1PbnI3n+1 Homologous Layered Perovskites.
Snippet: We simultaneously perform two types of stability tests -light-soaking under blue LED (450 nm, 100 mW/cm 2 ) and thermal heating at 100°C (Figure 3a), in order to distinguish light and heat-induced processes in hybrid perovskites. As an analytical signal we use an average intensity of perovskite PL peak, collected from multiple dots, normalized to the initial average PL intensity of each sample at the beginning of the stability experiment. The results of both tests are shown in Figure 3b for light-soaking and 3c for thermal heating. Original PL spectra after averaging are given in Figure S15 (ESI). According to the results of light-soaking, we observe the following photostability trend: n3 > n2 ~ MAPI > n1. Notably, this result does not agree with the previously observed stability trend in decane: MAPI > n3 ~ n2 > n1. The strongest controversy is found for 3D perovskite MAPI appeared to be the most stable in decane, but being one of the least stable material in argon atmosphere (Figure 3b). At the same time, the layered perovskites follow the overall trend of increasing photostability with the growth of the n number (Figure 1c and 3b). In the case of heat-induced degradation, we observe a less pronounced difference in relative distribution of PL intensity with the following stability trend: n1 > n3 > n2 > MAPI. Both photoand thermal stability trends are proved to be reproducible on the basis of two sequentially conducted stability tests in the same conditions (Figure S16, ESI). The resulting XRD patterns for the n2 sample (Figure 3d) confirm the principal difference of hybrid perovskites degradation mechanisms under heating and under light irradiation: thermal degradation is mainly caused by the loss of volatile species (CH3NH2, HI, C4H9NH2) with crystallization of the PbI2 solid phase while photodegradation seems to be driven by the combination of photoelectrochemical reactions, discussed in more details below. The same features in X-ray diffraction patterns are observed for all other samples (Figure S17, ESI).
