Summary
In the perovskite literature, “photodegradation” generally denotes light‑induced structural and chemical changes within the perovskite lattice (e.g., phase conversion, defect formation, ion migration) that degrade optoelectronic properties, while “photocorrosion” emphasizes light‑accelerated surface and interface breakdown—dissolution/etching and corrosion product formation—often electrochemical or photoelectrochemical in nature. In 2D perovskites, both processes can occur under illumination and in humid/oxidizing environments, but they capture distinct mechanisms: photodegradation is bulk/phase/defect evolution (often to PbI2), whereas photocorrosion is surface/interface loss and product formation (e.g., PbI2, PbI x surface layers) at the material–electrolyte/air interface. Authors sometimes use the terms loosely, but mechanistic and experimental signatures allow them to be distinguished. <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">Under blue light in air, 2D BA2MA n−1 PbnI3n+1 films undergo near‑complete loss of the perovskite (200) XRD peak and emergence of a broad PbI2 signal within hours, indicating rapid light‑induced phase degradation</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-3">with oxygen facilitating fast photodegradation in dry air, whereas in inert (<10 ppm O2) conditions the same films retain color for hours</cite>. <cite id="b3bc27f3-2">Operando imaging shows 2D perovskite converting to PbI2 under blue illumination, consistent with light‑induced structural/phase changes</cite>.

Mechanistic distinctions and definitions
Recent perspectives define photocorrosion at irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces as a thermodynamic/kinetic process that can proceed via chemical, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, or photochemical pathways, producing either complete self‑decomposition or surface layers/corrosion products (e.g., dissolution/etching products at the interface). <cite id="8ea07133-1">Perovskites are sensitive to solvents and electrolytes and are susceptible to photocorrosion, motivating mechanistic studies via in situ/operando electrochemical and surface techniques</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-2">and strategies including surface protection, materials/electrolyte engineering, and preparation of 2D perovskites</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-3">with corrosion events categorized by charge‑transfer and carrier involvement, including formation of surface layers or complete decomposition</cite>. <cite id="28d61341-4">More generally, illumination generates carriers that can decompose semiconductors in contact with water/ electrolytes (photocorrosion), a process controllable by corrosion state concepts</cite>. By contrast, photodegradation is often used to describe light‑induced changes in absorption/PL, phase evolution (e.g., to PbI2), and defect/ion dynamics that reduce performance without necessarily framing the dissolution/etching aspect. <cite id="b3bc27f3-3">Light soaking in air drives rapid photodegradation of layered 2D perovskites to PbI2 within tens of minutes, whereas inert atmospheres suppress the reaction</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">and XRD shows orders‑of‑magnitude loss of perovskite peak intensity and emergence of PbI2</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-2">with undercoordinated surface Pb–I bonds in 2D perovskites contributing to instability and photo‑conversion to PbI2 under illumination</cite>.

Evidence in 2D perovskites
Light‑induced photodegradation in 2D layers. In BA2MA n−1 PbnI3n+1 homologous layered perovskites, blue‑light exposure in air rapidly eliminates the perovskite (200) peak, broadens the PbI2 peak, and collapses PL, indicating structural phase conversion and strong performance decay; oxygen penetration into the layered framework accelerates this transformation relative to denser 3D frameworks. <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">After 5 h in air, the n1 2D sample undergoes almost complete phase degradation with a 4×10−4 fraction of the initial perovskite peak area and a widened PbI2 peak; oxygen dramatically increases the rate</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-3">and under identical illumination, 2D films in dry air degrade within 20 min to a light‑yellow color while 3D MAPI films resist much longer</cite>. <cite id="b3bc27f3-2">Under blue‑laser illumination (488 nm, 120 mW cm−2), 2D perovskite transforms into PbI2</cite>. Oxygen and humidity modulate the mechanism: <cite id="eecf6cd8-0">in air the material undergoes ~20× faster photodegradation than in nonpolar decane, with measurable PbI2 onset after 10 min</cite> <cite id="eecf6cd8-4">and thermal degradation differs (volatilization of MA/BA with PbI2 formation), indicating distinct light‑ vs heat‑induced processes</cite>.

Surface reconstruction and passivation by 2D layers. Light and ligand treatments can drive surface reconstruction where 2D perovskite forms on 3D surfaces, passivating defects and improving optoelectronic properties. <cite id="fb43ab61-1">Chlorinated 4Cl‑BA treatment yields a diffraction peak at 6.18° assigned to a pure 2D perovskite surface layer, with reduced PbI2 peak intensity, suppressed trap states, and enhanced PL; the improved device performance is attributed to 2D perovskite surface reconstruction and built‑in fields at 2D/3D heterojunctions</cite> <cite id="fb43ab61-0">and sequential ligand passivation can fill surface pits and grain‑boundary defects, reduce contact potential difference from ~400 mV to ~150 mV then ~10 mV, and homogenize surface potential via 2D perovskite formation</cite> <cite id="fb43ab61-3">XPS and scattering show BA cation grafting and vertical 2D perovskite orientation that passivates 3D surfaces and creates field‑effect passivation</cite>. <cite id="fb43ab61-4">Light illumination can improve crystallization and lattice expansion of 2D perovskites, enhancing PL by 3.1× and reducing trap‑assisted recombination</cite>.

Photocorrosion signatures at interfaces and mitigation by 2D layers. At irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces, photocorrosion produces corrosion products and morphological changes; mitigation strategies include surface protection and using 2D perovskites. <cite id="8ea07133-1">Perspective work on photocorrosion emphasizes that perovskites are susceptible at interfaces and that understanding elementary corrosion steps via in situ/operando electrochemistry is key</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-2">with strategies such as 2D perovskite preparation to stabilize surfaces</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-3">and mechanistic classification by corrosion type and product formation</cite>. <cite id="b3bc27f3-1">Topotactic growth of ultrathin 2D layers on 3D perovskites passivates against environmental degradation; capping layers >10 nm prevent discoloration even after ~20 h at >85% RH</cite>. These 2D layers formed by light/ligand can thus act as anti‑photocorrosion barriers by reducing surface reactivity and water/oxidant ingress, while light‑induced 2D reconstruction can also be a cause of photodegradation if it proceeds via PbI2 formation and surface etching.

When are the terms synonymous or distinct?
- Overlap: Many studies report light‑induced conversion to PbI2 and device decay under illumination in air/humidity, which are mechanistically linked to surface and interfacial reactions. In this regime, “photodegradation” often encompasses the full pathway—light‑driven bond breaking, ion migration, surface conversion to PbI2, and subsequent dissolution/etching—so authors may use the terms interchangeably. <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">The rapid perovskite→PbI2 conversion under light in oxygenated environments</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-3">and pronounced device decay under light</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-2">are classic photodegradation signatures that also produce corrosion‑like surface products</cite>.
- Distinctness: Photocorrosion specifically highlights corrosion product formation, interfacial reactions, and morphology evolution at irradiated surfaces/electrolytes (chemical/electrochemical/photochemical pathways), whereas photodegradation can include bulk defect formation, phase separation, and ion migration that do not necessarily involve surface dissolution unless coupled to moisture/electrolytes. <cite id="8ea07133-3">The mechanistic taxonomy of photocorrosion at interfaces</cite> <cite id="28d61341-4">and illumination‑driven semiconductor self‑decomposition in contact with water</cite> emphasize surface dissolution/etching and product formation, which may only manifest downstream as photodegradation signals (PL loss, phase change) if not directly quantified. In 2D perovskites, light‑driven surface reconstruction can either accelerate degradation (if it proceeds via PbI2 formation and etching) or stabilize (if rigid 2D caps passivate and repassivate surfaces). <cite id="fb43ab61-1">2D surface reconstruction suppresses nonradiative recombination and improves performance</cite> <cite id="fb43ab61-0">while sequential passivation fills surface pits and homogenizes potential</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-2">and 2D layers are explicitly proposed to mitigate photocorrosion</cite>.

Practical usage in literature
- Many device/layered‑perovskite papers discuss “photodegradation” under illumination and oxygen/humidity with XRD/PL evidence of perovskite→PbI2 conversion and performance loss; these sections often implicitly describe photocorrosion at the film–air/electrolyte interface when moisture/oxygen participate. <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">Oxygen accelerates 2D photodegradation to PbI2</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-3">and even minutes of illumination can cause complete discoloration and phase conversion under air</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-2">with undercoordinated surface bonds as a mechanistic driver</cite>.
- Electrochemical/photoelectrochemical works and interfacial studies explicitly frame instability as “photocorrosion,” define its thermodynamic/kinetic classes, and recommend 2D passivation layers as mitigation. <cite id="8ea07133-1">Perovskite susceptibility to photocorrosion at irradiated interfaces</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-3">with product detection and mechanistic mapping</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-2">and 2D perovskites as stabilization strategies</cite>.
- Surface science papers on 2D/3D heterojunctions emphasize light‑/ligand‑induced 2D reconstruction and passivation as property enhancement, underscoring that surface evolution can be beneficial (passivation) or harmful (etching to PbI2) depending on pathway and rigidity. <cite id="fb43ab61-1">2D reconstruction improves PL and device metrics</cite> <cite id="fb43ab61-0">passivation fills pits and reduces surface potential inhomogeneity</cite>.

Answer to the question
Are photodegradation and photocorrosion distinct or synonymous in 2D perovskites?
- Short answer: They are often used loosely but are mechanistically related and not strictly synonymous. Photodegradation denotes light‑induced structural/phase/defect evolution (e.g., perovskite→PbI2 conversion, PL loss, performance decay), whereas photocorrosion emphasizes light‑accelerated surface/interface breakdown and corrosion product formation at irradiated perovskite–electrolyte/air interfaces. In 2D perovskites, both mechanisms coexist: light can drive rapid photodegradation to PbI2 and surface etching (photocorrosion), or 2D surface reconstruction and passivation that suppresses degradation and enhances properties; thus, authors may treat them as overlapping phenomena in practice. <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">Light in oxygenated air causes near‑complete perovskite→PbI2 conversion in 2D layers within hours</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-3">and minutes in air vs hours in inert conditions</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-3">photocorrosion frameworks classify interface‑driven corrosion products and mechanisms</cite> <cite id="fb43ab61-1">2D reconstruction can suppress nonradiative recombination and improve devices</cite>.
- How to tell them apart in a paper: Look for mechanistic probes. Photodegradation papers highlight absorption/PL blueshift, emergence of PbI2 peaks, rapid phase loss, and device performance decay under light; they often attribute changes to undercoordinated surface bonds and oxygen/humidity participation. Photocorrosion papers emphasize in situ/operando electrochemical and surface measurements, corrosion product identification, and interfacial dissolution/etching pathways, frequently recommending 2D passivation layers as mitigation. <cite id="b3bc27f3-2">Operando imaging shows 2D→PbI2 under illumination</cite> <cite id="eecf6cd8-0">oxygen accelerates photodegradation and drives I2/polyiodide release</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-1">electrochemical mechanistic mapping and mitigation via 2D layers</cite>.
- Practical guidance: If a study reports only phase/PL evolution and performance loss under illumination (especially in air/humidity), it is primarily documenting photodegradation that includes surface reactions leading to corrosion products; if it quantifies surface product formation, interfacial etching, or electrochemical signatures under light, it is explicitly describing photocorrosion. In 2D perovskites, surface reconstructions to rigid 2D caps can act as anti‑photocorrosion barriers, while light‑induced PbI2 formation can mark aggressive photodegradation/photocorrosion fronts. <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">Rapid perovskite→PbI2 conversion under light in air</cite> <cite id="b3bc27f3-1">2D caps suppress discoloration and moisture damage</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-3">photocorrosion mechanisms by corrosion type and product formation</cite>.

Bottom line
For 2D perovskites, the terms are frequently used interchangeably in device reports that show light‑induced phase conversion and surface discoloration, but mechanistic and experimental evidence supports treating photodegradation as the broader light‑induced structural/chemical decay (often culminating in PbI2), and photocorrosion as the specific interfacial dissolution/etching and product formation process that can drive or be triggered by photodegradation. Distinguishing them requires looking at interfacial measurements, product identification, and whether surface reconstruction passivates or degrades the material under illumination. <cite id="b3bc27f3-0">Light in air drives rapid perovskite→PbI2 conversion and performance loss in 2D perovskites</cite> <cite id="8ea07133-3">photocorrosion at irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces forms products and involves complex charge‑carrier–driven steps</cite> <cite id="fb43ab61-1">2D surface reconstruction can suppress recombination and enhance performance, illustrating passivation vs degradation pathways</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Nonmonotonic Photostability of BA2MAn-1PbnI3n+1 Homologous Layered Perovskites.
Snippet: In the case of maximal oxygen concentration in the atmosphere (2*10 5 ppm), we observe a pronounced difference in behavior of 2D and 3D perovskites: after 5 h of light-soaking the n1 sample undergoes almost complete phase degradation with the decrease of incident perovskite (200) diffraction peak area by 4 orders of magnitude (A/A0=7*10 -4 ) and also a widened PbI2 peak at 12.6° appears (Figure 2a). In contrast, the MAPI sample reveals only a ~3 times decrease of diffraction intensity and demonstrates negligible signs of the PbI2 phase (PbI2/pvsk = 0.14) (Figure 2b). We suppose that a more rapid photodegradation of the 2D perovskite under oxidizing environment is caused by a much easier penetration of oxygen molecules into the layered structure as compared to a denser, interlinked framework of the 3D perovskite structure (Figure 2c  and d). This result is consistent with the UV-light stability study in air of perovskite solar cells based on MAPI and n3 samples in which 2D-PSCs demonstrate a pronounced decrease of PCE for only 30 min of light-soaking due to a strong Voc decrease while the MAPI-based device shows no sign of degradation (Figure S11). 

A decrease of the O2 amount down to 100 ppm almost completely diminishes the discrepancy between 2D and 3D perovskites on the time scale of 83 h of the photostability test. In both cases, we observe a complete disappearance of diffraction reflexes from perovskite phases and formation of PbI2 as also seen by the samples color change (Figure S12). Interestingly, the widening of the PbI2 (001) reflex monotonically increases with a decrease of the n number (Figure S13). We suppose that this behavior might be caused by the formation of disordered PbI2 ultrathin flakes during the degradation of the layered structures with a low thickness of perovskite slabs (n= 1-3).

The PL emission map for the 2D emission band (500−550 nm) is shown in Figure 5f for the ultrathin 2D layers grown on top of the 3D surface (regime II in Figure 1c). The uniform green emission across the 140 × 140 μm 2 area of the 2D emission map is consistent with spatial homogeneity, admittedly at a coarser scale, of the grown 2D phase on top of the 3D grains. 

2.6. Ultrathin 2D Cap Suffices to Stabilize 3D HaP Layers. The vapor-phase growth of 2D on 3D HaP layers is topotactic as it yields 2D layers with strong chemical and structural correlation to the 3D HaP layers underneath. Also, because the 2D film grows within, and not on top of, the 3D HaP layers, the 2D layers are conformal, as was discussed in Section 2.5. Hence, it can be assumed that even for ultrathin (∼5 nm) 2D layers grown in regime II of the PL intensity vs time profile (Figure 1c), the 3D HaP underneath the 2D cap will be effectively passivated against environmental degradation, especially moisture. 

To evaluate the stability of 2D-coated 3D layers against moisture, we performed degradation tests on pristine 3D and 2D/3D samples by exposing them to high humidity conditions (>85% RH) in a custom-built chamber. The optical images of the corresponding films captured at different representative time intervals are shown in Figure 6. The untreated MAPbI 3 films show a noticeable change in their appearance within a few hours of exposure to humidity; after ∼20 h exposure, the black perovskite phase has almost completely disappeared. However, all 3D films with a 2D capping on top do not show such severe damage (disappearance of the characteristic perovskite black phase). 

For 2D layers on the 3D films that are relatively thick (>10 nm, grown till regime IV, and as deduced from XPS analysis), the MAPbI 3 films do not show discoloration even after 20 h in the high humidity ambient.

Title: Nonmonotonic Photostability of BA2MAn-1PbnI3n+1 Homologous Layered Perovskites.
Snippet: Our results demonstrate that light-soaking effects in dry air (~2*10 5 ppm of O2) and in an inert glove box (<10 ppm of O2) differ drastically. In the case of inert atmosphere, all sets of samples retain their initial color for at least 16 h of the constant blue light irradiation with power density 100 mW/cm 2 (Figure S10). In the case of dry air, we observe a complete degradation of all 2D perovskites regardless of n leading to light-yellow color already after 20 min under the same light-soaking conditions, while MAPI films retain at most initial color with only local yellowing, highlighted in Figure S10 with red circles. To reveal the influence of oxygen concentration on the photodegradation mechanism and to identify a critical O2 concentration, we analyzed phase composition and crystal structure of n1 and MAPI perovskite films by XRD after aging under three types of atmospheres: (1) dry air with ~2*10 5 ppm O2, (2) argon with 99.99% purity (~100 ppm O2), and (3) argon-filled glove box with < 10 ppm O2. The duration of light-soaking was increased from 5 h for (1), to 83 h for (2), and 150 h for (3) in order to diminish the impact of different degradation rate of hybrid perovskites, known to be dependent on the oxygen amount in the case of 3D perovskites. 34 The XRD patterns of n1 and MAPI samples are provided in Figure 2a and 2b, respectively. In the case of maximal oxygen concentration in the atmosphere (2*10 5 ppm), we observe a pronounced difference in behavior of 2D and 3D perovskites: after 5 h of light-soaking the n1 sample undergoes almost complete phase degradation with the decrease of incident perovskite (200) diffraction peak area by 4 orders of magnitude (A/A0=7*10 -4 ) and also a widened PbI2 peak at 12.6° appears (Figure 2a).

Snippet: To better interpret these results, the λ max emission values were extracted and their variation is drawn as a function of aging time in Figure 8d. An emission blue shift is deduced from the decrease of λ max for all the samples aged under ambient atmosphere. This emission blue shift is compatible with the absorption blue shift already detected with UV-visible spectroscopy under air aging conditions. Regarding the expansion of spectral PL intensity, it reaches values two to six times less important for perovskite half-cells aged in ambient atmosphere than for those aged under vacuum, Figure S5, Supporting Information. This, combined with the blue shift observed both in absorption and emission, confirms here the large participation of a competitive degradation mechanism due to additional oxygen/humidity stress. 

In addition to the previously applied characterizations, PL imaging was performed to visualize irradiance levels overall the surface and compare the homogeneity of the different electrodeposited generated films. [61] Figure 8b presents the PL images of the perovskite samples at the initial state and after 500 h aging (all images made during the aging campaign are available in Figure S6, Supporting Information). The drastic increase in irradiance observed on imaging for samples aged in ambient atmosphere, and not observed in a such huge intensity from spectral PL data, indicates the degradation of the perovskite. Indeed, we can clearly detect the presence of PbI 2 in the photographs in Figure 8a (PbCl 2 and PbBr 2 being uncolored). The imaging irradiance level detected in this case and represented with aging time in Figure 8d is not only a response of the perovskite but also a residual part of diffuse reflection of the 520 nm beam on the PbI 2 that does not absorb this wavelength (see PbI 2 PL imaging in Figure S7, Supporting Information). This degradation starts from the borders and gradually propagates to the center (Figure 8b). The PL images also confirm that electrodeposited mixed perovskites are more stable than electrodeposited MAPbI 3 .

In the case of inert atmosphere, all sets of samples retain their initial color for at least 16 h of the constant blue light irradiation with power density 100 mW/cm 2 (Figure S10). In the case of dry air, we observe a complete degradation of all 2D perovskites regardless of n leading to light-yellow color already after 20 min under the same light-soaking conditions, while MAPI films retain at most initial color with only local yellowing, highlighted in Figure S10 with red circles. To reveal the influence of oxygen concentration on the photodegradation mechanism and to identify a critical O2 concentration, we analyzed phase composition and crystal structure of n1 and MAPI perovskite films by XRD after aging under three types of atmospheres: (1) dry air with ~2*10 5 ppm O2, (2) argon with 99.99% purity (~100 ppm O2), and (3) argon-filled glove box with < 10 ppm O2. The duration of light-soaking was increased from 5 h for (1), to 83 h for (2), and 150 h for (3) in order to diminish the impact of different degradation rate of hybrid perovskites, known to be dependent on the oxygen amount in the case of 3D perovskites. 34 The XRD patterns of n1 and MAPI samples are provided in Figure 2a and 2b, respectively. To better interpret these results, the λ max emission values were extracted and their variation is drawn as a function of aging time in Figure 8d. An emission blue shift is deduced from the decrease of λ max for all the samples aged under ambient atmosphere. This emission blue shift is compatible with the absorption blue shift already detected with UV-visible spectroscopy under air aging conditions. Regarding the expansion of spectral PL intensity, it reaches values two to six times less important for perovskite half-cells aged in ambient atmosphere than for those aged under vacuum, Figure S5, Supporting Information. This, combined with the blue shift observed both in absorption and emission, confirms here the large participation of a competitive degradation mechanism due to additional oxygen/humidity stress. 

In addition to the previously applied characterizations, PL imaging was performed to visualize irradiance levels overall the surface and compare the homogeneity of the different electrodeposited generated films. [61] Figure 8b presents the PL images of the perovskite samples at the initial state and after 500 h aging (all images made during the aging campaign are available in Figure S6, Supporting Information). The drastic increase in irradiance observed on imaging for samples aged in ambient atmosphere, and not observed in a such huge intensity from spectral PL data, indicates the degradation of the perovskite. Indeed, we can clearly detect the presence of PbI 2 in the photographs in Figure 8a (PbCl 2 and PbBr 2 being uncolored). The imaging irradiance level detected in this case and represented with aging time in Figure 8d is not only a response of the perovskite but also a residual part of diffuse reflection of the 520 nm beam on the PbI 2 that does not absorb this wavelength (see PbI 2 PL imaging in Figure S7, Supporting Information). This degradation starts from the borders and gradually propagates to the center (Figure 8b). The PL images also confirm that electrodeposited mixed perovskites are more stable than electrodeposited MAPbI 3 .

documents.snippet:
In the case of maximal oxygen concentration in the atmosphere (2*10 5 ppm), we observe a pronounced difference in behavior of 2D and 3D perovskites: after 5 h of light-soaking the n1 sample undergoes almost complete phase degradation with the decrease of incident perovskite (200) diffraction peak area by 4 orders of magnitude (A/A0=7*10 -4 ) and also a widened PbI2 peak at 12.6° appears (Figure 2a). In contrast, the MAPI sample reveals only a ~3 times decrease of diffraction intensity and demonstrates negligible signs of the PbI2 phase (PbI2/pvsk = 0.14) (Figure 2b). We suppose that a more rapid photodegradation of the 2D perovskite under oxidizing environment is caused by a much easier penetration of oxygen molecules into the layered structure as compared to a denser, interlinked framework of the 3D perovskite structure (Figure 2c  and d). This result is consistent with the UV-light stability study in air of perovskite solar cells based on MAPI and n3 samples in which 2D-PSCs demonstrate a pronounced decrease of PCE for only 30 min of light-soaking due to a strong Voc decrease while the MAPI-based device shows no sign of degradation (Figure S11). 

A decrease of the O2 amount down to 100 ppm almost completely diminishes the discrepancy between 2D and 3D perovskites on the time scale of 83 h of the photostability test. In both cases, we observe a complete disappearance of diffraction reflexes from perovskite phases and formation of PbI2 as also seen by the samples color change (Figure S12). Interestingly, the widening of the PbI2 (001) reflex monotonically increases with a decrease of the n number (Figure S13). We suppose that this behavior might be caused by the formation of disordered PbI2 ultrathin flakes during the degradation of the layered structures with a low thickness of perovskite slabs (n= 1-3).

documents.snippet:
However, to get further information about the uniformity of 2D surface coverage on the 3D film, we studied the PL emission of the 2D layer by laser scanning confocal microscopy of the 2D/ 3D layers with 488 nm excitation. The PL emission map for the 2D emission band (500−550 nm) is shown in Figure 5f for the ultrathin 2D layers grown on top of the 3D surface (regime II in Figure 1c). The uniform green emission across the 140 × 140 μm 2 area of the 2D emission map is consistent with spatial homogeneity, admittedly at a coarser scale, of the grown 2D phase on top of the 3D grains. 

2.6. Ultrathin 2D Cap Suffices to Stabilize 3D HaP Layers. The vapor-phase growth of 2D on 3D HaP layers is topotactic as it yields 2D layers with strong chemical and structural correlation to the 3D HaP layers underneath. Also, because the 2D film grows within, and not on top of, the 3D HaP layers, the 2D layers are conformal, as was discussed in Section 2.5. Hence, it can be assumed that even for ultrathin (∼5 nm) 2D layers grown in regime II of the PL intensity vs time profile (Figure 1c), the 3D HaP underneath the 2D cap will be effectively passivated against environmental degradation, especially moisture. 

To evaluate the stability of 2D-coated 3D layers against moisture, we performed degradation tests on pristine 3D and 2D/3D samples by exposing them to high humidity conditions (>85% RH) in a custom-built chamber. The optical images of the corresponding films captured at different representative time intervals are shown in Figure 6. The untreated MAPbI 3 films show a noticeable change in their appearance within a few hours of exposure to humidity; after ∼20 h exposure, the black perovskite phase has almost completely disappeared. However, all 3D films with a 2D capping on top do not show such severe damage (disappearance of the characteristic perovskite black phase). 

For 2D layers on the 3D films that are relatively thick (>10 nm, grown till regime IV, and as deduced from XPS analysis), the MAPbI 3 films do not show discoloration even after 20 h in the high humidity ambient.

Title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
Snippet: Metal–halide perovskites transformed optoelectronics research and development during the past decade. They have also gained a foothold in photocatalytic and photoelectrochemical processes recently, but their sensitivity to the most commonly applied solvents and electrolytes together with their susceptibility to photocorrosion hinders such applications. Understanding the elementary steps of photocorrosion of these materials can aid the endeavor of realizing stable devices. In this Perspective, we discuss both thermodynamic and kinetic aspects of photocorrosion processes occurring at the interface of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes with different electrolytes. We show how combined in situ and operando electrochemical techniques can reveal the underlying mechanisms. Finally, we also discuss emerging strategies to mitigate photocorrosion (such as surface protection, materials and electrolyte engineering, etc.).

Title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
Snippet: PC and PEC scenarios are recent additions to the potential research arenas where the optoelectronic properties of perovskites can be harnessed. Elaborating on the experience gathered from pioneering studies on photocorrosion processes and from stabilizing perovskite layers in PV devices will greatly accelerate the progress of this field. As the first step, careful characterization protocols are necessary for both PC and PEC studies (with quantitative product detection), to understand reasons and processes behind the instability. Furthermore, combined in situ electrochemical measurements will furnish mechanistic insights, with the possibility of revealing the elementary steps of corrosion. For nanoscale studies, in situ electrochemical atomic force microscopy 231−234 and PEC transmission electron microscopy will be useful to visualize morphological changes that occur on the surface of photocatalysts and photoelectrodes. Pinpointing structural weaknesses in these systems (e.g., sensitive facets, morphological features) will guide better design of stable solar energy conversion devices. In a similar fashion, coupled ultrafast techniques can shed light on how corrosion affects the charge carrier dynamics of these complex systems. 158,235 Ultrafast spectroscopic studies under electrochemical control have just been employed for perovskite electrodes recently, and further breakthroughs are expected once the pulse duration is decreased. With setups allowing few femtoseconds (or even sub-femtosecond) resolution, 236 the initial stages of charge carrier generation can be followed, providing new insights for subsequent rational materials design. While single crystal surfaces can be used to identify elementary steps in photocorrosion processes (including identification of stable and active facets), crystal facet engineering will help to translate this knowledge to nanostructured materials of practical importance. 

Once the elementary steps of the photocorrosion process are uncovered, different strategies can be employed to stabilize perovskites. Compositional engineering, various surface protection approaches and the preparation of 2D perovskites are all viable options. As a particularly promising direction, bifunctional coatings can be developed, where the catalytic and protective functions are merged.

Title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
Snippet: uring corrosion, either complete self-decomposition or the formation of active or inactive surface layers can occur. We can approach the underlying processes from a thermodynamics perspective (i.e., whether it can happen or not); however, the convoluted reaction kinetics (i.e., multiple steps, chemical transitions) must also be considered. Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: (i) chemical, where no net charge transfer occurs at the interface; (ii) electrochemical, where the selectively injected charge carriers induce corrosion; (iii) photoelectrochemical, where the photoexcited minority carriers are predominantly responsible for the corrosion; (iv) photochemical, where both the minority and majority charge carriers can induce chemical changes. In the case of photochemical corrosion there is no external driving force that removes the majority carriers (as opposed to photoelectrochemical corrosion). Therefore, a larger fraction of majority carriers can reach the photocatalyst surface and can induce corrosion processes. 

In this Perspective, we discuss the last three corrosion processes from the above list, highlighting the peculiar features of perovskites. First, we present some general thermodynamic and kinetics aspects of photocorrosion. Selected examples of corrosion processes of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes form the main body of the article, where photo-(electro)catalytic and photo(electro)synthetic examples are both scrutinized. This is followed by a compilation of in situ/ operando methods, which provide mechanistic insights with spatial and temporal resolution. Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies, which also outline future research and development avenues.

Title: Stabilization of interfaces for double-cation halide perovskites with AVA2FAPb2I7 additives
Snippet: The migration of the ionic defects also adversely affects metal electrodes. It is well established that the perovskite/metal contact is prone to immediate chemical interactions, resulting in instability [13], [14], [15]. However, in device structures, these effects are partially mitigated by the inclusion of charge-transport layers. Prolonged exposure of PSCs with standard back electrodes (Ag, Au, Cu) to exploitation conditions (temperature 25 -85°C, light intensity ~100 mW/cm 2 ) leads to electrode oxidation, delamination, and a reduction in photoelectric performance [16], [17]. 

Among the others approaches, the use of perovskite heterostructures was considered as an effective strategy to mitigate the corrosion effects at the interfaces of PSCs. The heterostructure of halide perovskites typically consists of a standard microcrystalline absorber film combined with low-dimensional perovskite configurations. Replacing the A-site cation with a large spacer molecule (typically phenyl-ethyl ammonium (PEA) or C4H9NH3 (BA)) induces spatial separation within the 3D perovskite crystal lattice, resulting in alternating layers of 3D perovskite and large organic spacers [18]. The molar ratio between the spacer molecule and the perovskite framework dictated the dimensionality of the resulting phase. This results in the formation of so called quasi-two-dimensional (2D) Ruddlesden-Popper phases coupled with the lattice of the photoactive three-dimensional (3D) perovskite phase. Current literature [19], [20], [21], [22] highlights the effects of surface passivation in perovskite films, including reduced defect concentrations at inter-grain interfaces and improved thermal stability in 2D/3D perovskite heterostructures (PHS). The integration methods of 2D perovskite additives also strongly impacts the crystal structure of perovskite thin-films. A pioneering study by Loi group demonstrated [23] the impact of employing a 2D perovskite template, deposited via a scalable technique, which subsequently undergoes in situ conversion to form a highly crystalline 3D perovskite.

In a similar fashion, coupled ultrafast techniques can shed light on how corrosion affects the charge carrier dynamics of these complex systems. 158,235 Ultrafast spectroscopic studies under electrochemical control have just been employed for perovskite electrodes recently, and further breakthroughs are expected once the pulse duration is decreased. With setups allowing few femtoseconds (or even sub-femtosecond) resolution, 236 the initial stages of charge carrier generation can be followed, providing new insights for subsequent rational materials design. Once the elementary steps of the photocorrosion process are uncovered, different strategies can be employed to stabilize perovskites. documents.title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
documents.snippet:
uring corrosion, either complete self-decomposition or the formation of active or inactive surface layers can occur. We can approach the underlying processes from a thermodynamics perspective (i.e., whether it can happen or not); however, the convoluted reaction kinetics (i.e., multiple steps, chemical transitions) must also be considered. Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: (i) chemical, where no net charge transfer occurs at the interface; (ii) electrochemical, where the selectively injected charge carriers induce corrosion; (iii) photoelectrochemical, where the photoexcited minority carriers are predominantly responsible for the corrosion; (iv) photochemical, where both the minority and majority charge carriers can induce chemical changes. In the case of photochemical corrosion there is no external driving force that removes the majority carriers (as opposed to photoelectrochemical corrosion). Therefore, a larger fraction of majority carriers can reach the photocatalyst surface and can induce corrosion processes. 

In this Perspective, we discuss the last three corrosion processes from the above list, highlighting the peculiar features of perovskites. First, we present some general thermodynamic and kinetics aspects of photocorrosion. Selected examples of corrosion processes of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes form the main body of the article, where photo-(electro)catalytic and photo(electro)synthetic examples are both scrutinized. This is followed by a compilation of in situ/ operando methods, which provide mechanistic insights with spatial and temporal resolution. Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies, which also outline future research and development avenues.

documents.title: Stabilization of interfaces for double-cation halide perovskites with AVA2FAPb2I7 additives
documents.snippet:
The migration of the ionic defects also adversely affects metal electrodes. It is well established that the perovskite/metal contact is prone to immediate chemical interactions, resulting in instability [13], [14], [15]. However, in device structures, these effects are partially mitigated by the inclusion of charge-transport layers. Prolonged exposure of PSCs with standard back electrodes (Ag, Au, Cu) to exploitation conditions (temperature 25 -85°C, light intensity ~100 mW/cm 2 ) leads to electrode oxidation, delamination, and a reduction in photoelectric performance [16], [17]. 

Among the others approaches, the use of perovskite heterostructures was considered as an effective strategy to mitigate the corrosion effects at the interfaces of PSCs. The heterostructure of halide perovskites typically consists of a standard microcrystalline absorber film combined with low-dimensional perovskite configurations. Replacing the A-site cation with a large spacer molecule (typically phenyl-ethyl ammonium (PEA) or C4H9NH3 (BA)) induces spatial separation within the 3D perovskite crystal lattice, resulting in alternating layers of 3D perovskite and large organic spacers [18]. The molar ratio between the spacer molecule and the perovskite framework dictated the dimensionality of the resulting phase. This results in the formation of so called quasi-two-dimensional (2D) Ruddlesden-Popper phases coupled with the lattice of the photoactive three-dimensional (3D) perovskite phase. Current literature [19], [20], [21], [22] highlights the effects of surface passivation in perovskite films, including reduced defect concentrations at inter-grain interfaces and improved thermal stability in 2D/3D perovskite heterostructures (PHS). The integration methods of 2D perovskite additives also strongly impacts the crystal structure of perovskite thin-films. A pioneering study by Loi group demonstrated [23] the impact of employing a 2D perovskite template, deposited via a scalable technique, which subsequently undergoes in situ conversion to form a highly crystalline 3D perovskite.

In the Perovskite/X, the number of black pits decreased significantly, and the average depth reduced to ~40 nm. While for the Perovskite/X/Y, nearly all pits were eliminated, with the average depth further reduced to ~20 nm. These results suggest that the TSS-DL method effectively fills the pits, indicating successful reconstruction of GBs and GSs sequentially. Title: Visualizing Interfacial Energy Offset and Defects in Efficient 2D/3D Heterojunction Perovskite Solar Cells and Modules
Snippet: To improve the photovoltaic performance of PSCs by controlling the energy offset and defect density, a heterojunction of 2D/3D perovskites was introduced. The interlaminar molecules in 2D perovskites can effectively saturate the 3D perovskite surface to reduce surface defects during the fabrication process, leading to the formation of a potential energy offset for field-effect passivation. Figure 2A shows a schematic of the PSC (experimental details are provided in the Experimental Section, see Supporting Information). Two typical types of precursors, namely, BABr and BAI, were used to fabricate uniform 2D perovskite layers with thicknesses of ≈30 nm (Figure S2 and Note S1, Supporting Information). X-ray techniques confirmed the presence of the 2D perovskite layer, and grazing-incidence wide-angle scattering (GI-WAXS) was used to determine its orientation (Figure 2B; Figure S3, Supporting Information). The scattering patterns showed that the crystal orientation of 2D perovskite, by both BABr and BAI post-treatments, was vertical and different from the polycrystal 3D perovskite, which has a random orientation (typical rings located at 0.97 Å −1 ). The cut-lines along the q z axis revealed three additional scattering vectors located at 0.30, 0.43, and 0.62 Å −1 , which were indexed to (020) (n = 2), (020) (n = 1), and (040) (n = 2), respectively (Figure 2C; Figure S3, Supporting Information). Similar results were obtained from the XRD patterns (Figure S4, Supporting Information). Moreover, no 2Drelated signals were observed along the q xy axis, indicating that the 2D perovskite orientation was mainly parallel to the substrate (Figure S3, Supporting Information). In addition, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements demonstrated the effective interaction of the BA cation, indicating chemical grafting of the 2D perovskite (Figure S5 and Note S2, Supporting Information). [7]

Title: Enhanced optoelectronic performance of 2D organic-inorganic hybrid perovskite through light-illumination.
Snippet: Particularly, light illumination has become a useful approach to improving the morphology and optical properties of 3D perovskites. Proper light soaking will promote a superior surface coverage and an enlarged unit cell of the 3D perovskite films, thus resulting in an improvement of the fill factor and open circuit voltage of the perovskite devices [37,38]. In addition, the properties of the perovskites could be optimized by the photochemical reaction occurred during light exposure [39]. Although widely studied in 3D perovskites, the influence of light illumination on the growth and optoelectronic properties of 2D layered organic-inorganic perovskites still needs detailed understanding, which will lay great importance for fabricating high-quality 2D perovskites for functional devices. 

Herein, we report the enhanced optoelectronic performances of 2D organic-inorganic hybrid perovskite through UV-light illumination. UV-light illumination will lead to an improvement of the crystallization and lattice expansion of the 2D perovskite monocrystalline films. Consequently, the PL emission of the 2D perovskite can be enhanced by 3.1 folds, with the trap-assisted recombination greatly decreased. For functional applications, photoconductive devices is fabricated based on the optimized 2D perovskites and the optoelectronic responses have been enhanced.

Proper light soaking will promote a superior surface coverage and an enlarged unit cell of the 3D perovskite films, thus resulting in an improvement of the fill factor and open circuit voltage of the perovskite devices [37,38]. In addition, the properties of the perovskites could be optimized by the photochemical reaction occurred during light exposure [39]. Although widely studied in 3D perovskites, the influence of light illumination on the growth and optoelectronic properties of 2D layered organic-inorganic perovskites still needs detailed understanding, which will lay great importance for fabricating high-quality 2D perovskites for functional devices. 

Herein, we report the enhanced optoelectronic performances of 2D organic-inorganic hybrid perovskite through UV-light illumination. UV-light illumination will lead to an improvement of the crystallization and lattice expansion of the 2D perovskite monocrystalline films. Consequently, the PL emission of the 2D perovskite can be enhanced by 3.1 folds, with the trap-assisted recombination greatly decreased. For functional applications, photoconductive devices is fabricated based on the optimized 2D perovskites and the optoelectronic responses have been enhanced.

Title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
Snippet: uring corrosion, either complete self-decomposition or the formation of active or inactive surface layers can occur. We can approach the underlying processes from a thermodynamics perspective (i.e., whether it can happen or not); however, the convoluted reaction kinetics (i.e., multiple steps, chemical transitions) must also be considered. Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: (i) chemical, where no net charge transfer occurs at the interface; (ii) electrochemical, where the selectively injected charge carriers induce corrosion; (iii) photoelectrochemical, where the photoexcited minority carriers are predominantly responsible for the corrosion; (iv) photochemical, where both the minority and majority charge carriers can induce chemical changes. In the case of photochemical corrosion there is no external driving force that removes the majority carriers (as opposed to photoelectrochemical corrosion). Therefore, a larger fraction of majority carriers can reach the photocatalyst surface and can induce corrosion processes. 

In this Perspective, we discuss the last three corrosion processes from the above list, highlighting the peculiar features of perovskites. First, we present some general thermodynamic and kinetics aspects of photocorrosion. Selected examples of corrosion processes of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes form the main body of the article, where photo-(electro)catalytic and photo(electro)synthetic examples are both scrutinized. This is followed by a compilation of in situ/ operando methods, which provide mechanistic insights with spatial and temporal resolution. Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies, which also outline future research and development avenues.

Title: Corrosion of Semiconductors under Illumination
Snippet: Semiconductor under illumination produces free electrons and positive holes. These photoproduced charge carriers usually have strong reductive or oxidative forces, and sometimes decompose the semiconductor itself by these forces. This kind of decomposition is easy to take place if the semiconductor has contact with water, that is photocorrosion of semiconductor. This article explains this phenomenon using the concept of the corrosion state, and shows how to prevent the corrosion of semiconductors.

Title: Nonmonotonic Photostability of BA2MAn-1PbnI3n+1 Homologous Layered Perovskites.
Snippet: Notably, the polyiodide absorption steeply decreases moving from n1 to n2, and for the n3 sample (MA/BA = 1) no In -absorption is already detected as well as for the MAPI phase (Figure 2b, Figure S4). Based on these observations, we assume that BAI extraction in decane may enhance degradation of layered perovskites immersed in a nonpolar solvent upon light-soaking. This effect is more pronounced for the studied layered perovskites with lower n and also for 2D perovskites based on hydrophobic cations; therefore, in situ photometry of a nonpolar solvent seems to be insufficiently universal and should be applied with cautions for 2D perovskites. 

In addition, we revealed an influence of dissolved oxygen in decane on the rate of lightinduced perovskites degradation. The amount of O2 in 2 ml of decane under standard conditions (25°C, 100 kPa) is about 2*10 -5 mol 32 which is two orders of magnitude higher than the estimated amount of perovskite in the immersed films used in this experiment (2-3*10 -7 mol), leading to the involvement of O2 into perovskite photodegradation rate. 33 We found that degassing of decane before the light-soaking experiment allows to slow down the release of both iodine-containing products (I2 and polyiodide) by three times (Figure 1d). Moreover, we revealed that the mechanism of perovskite light-induced degradation in non-polar solvent differs from the one under the ambient atmosphere. According to absorption spectroscopy of n2 perovskite films before and after lightsoaking in different environment, the material undergoes ~20 times faster photodegradation in ambient air than in decane (Figure S9, ESI). In particular, already after 10 min of light soaking in air, we observe a noticeable growth of absorption edge at 2.36 eV corresponding to PbI2 phase which is not the case for the sample irradiated in decane.

Title: Nonmonotonic Photostability of BA2MAn-1PbnI3n+1 Homologous Layered Perovskites.
Snippet: We simultaneously perform two types of stability tests -light-soaking under blue LED (450 nm, 100 mW/cm 2 ) and thermal heating at 100°C (Figure 3a), in order to distinguish light and heat-induced processes in hybrid perovskites. As an analytical signal we use an average intensity of perovskite PL peak, collected from multiple dots, normalized to the initial average PL intensity of each sample at the beginning of the stability experiment. The results of both tests are shown in Figure 3b for light-soaking and 3c for thermal heating. Original PL spectra after averaging are given in Figure S15 (ESI). According to the results of light-soaking, we observe the following photostability trend: n3 > n2 ~ MAPI > n1. Notably, this result does not agree with the previously observed stability trend in decane: MAPI > n3 ~ n2 > n1. The strongest controversy is found for 3D perovskite MAPI appeared to be the most stable in decane, but being one of the least stable material in argon atmosphere (Figure 3b). At the same time, the layered perovskites follow the overall trend of increasing photostability with the growth of the n number (Figure 1c and 3b). In the case of heat-induced degradation, we observe a less pronounced difference in relative distribution of PL intensity with the following stability trend: n1 > n3 > n2 > MAPI. Both photoand thermal stability trends are proved to be reproducible on the basis of two sequentially conducted stability tests in the same conditions (Figure S16, ESI). The resulting XRD patterns for the n2 sample (Figure 3d) confirm the principal difference of hybrid perovskites degradation mechanisms under heating and under light irradiation: thermal degradation is mainly caused by the loss of volatile species (CH3NH2, HI, C4H9NH2) with crystallization of the PbI2 solid phase while photodegradation seems to be driven by the combination of photoelectrochemical reactions, discussed in more details below. The same features in X-ray diffraction patterns are observed for all other samples (Figure S17, ESI).

At the same time, the layered perovskites follow the overall trend of increasing photostability with the growth of the n number (Figure 1c and 3b). In the case of heat-induced degradation, we observe a less pronounced difference in relative distribution of PL intensity with the following stability trend: n1 > n3 > n2 > MAPI. Both photoand thermal stability trends are proved to be reproducible on the basis of two sequentially conducted stability tests in the same conditions (Figure S16, ESI). Below is a practical framework to determine whether photodegradation or photocorrosion dominates in two-dimensional (2D) perovskites, together with mechanistic markers and environmental levers that tip the balance. We define photodegradation as light‑induced changes to the surface and near-surface structure/chemistry that reduce optoelectronic performance (e.g., halide loss, defect formation, phase segregation, voids), whereas photocorrosion denotes self‑decomposition or surface/interfacial dissolution processes (chemical, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, or photochemical) that convert the perovskite into secondary phases or ions, often accelerated by oxygen/electrolyte/water and charge injection at interfaces. <cite id="4fe09237-1">Photocorrosion can be subdivided into chemical, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, and photochemical modes, with the mode determined by thermodynamics and kinetics at the irradiated interface, including whether charge carrier injection or photoexcitation drives surface reactions and whether minority and majority carriers reach the reactive surface</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-3">Surface reactions at irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces are central, and understanding elementary steps enables stability design</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-4">Mitigation strategies include surface protection, materials/electrolyte engineering, and preparation of 2D perovskites; facet and nanoscale imaging under operando are recommended to reveal corrosion pathways</cite>.

Conceptual distinction and drivers
- Mechanistic categories. <cite id="4fe09237-1">In perovskite photoelectrochemistry, corrosion arises from irradiation-driven surface reactions; in chemical corrosion, no net charge transfer is required, whereas electrochemical and photoelectrochemical corrosion are driven by carrier injection and photoexcited minority carriers, respectively; in photochemical corrosion, both majority and minority carriers contribute because majority carriers are not removed</cite>. <cite id="4fe09237-1">A key difference versus pure photodegradation is whether the light-induced process converts the material into soluble/dissolved species or into passivating surface products without bulk dissolution</cite>.
- Environmental levers. <cite id="4fe09237-3">The presence of electrolytes and oxygen accelerates perovskite corrosion via surface reactions and ion exchange at the interface</cite> <cite id="edc01642-1">Oxygen and moisture generally weaken chemical stability by reacting with protonated organic cations, though controlled oxygen exposure can also passivate defects and brighten perovskites under light</cite>.

Conditions where photodegradation dominates in 2D perovskites
- Light above bandgap and surface halide loss pathways. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Light exposure during fabrication or operation causes iodine loss from 2D Ruddlesden–Popper (2DRP) perovskites, forming PbI2 and eventually metallic Pb0, which is detrimental; this is a prototypical photodegradation sequence at surfaces</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Even everyday light sources (fluorescent lamps, sunlight) can induce these changes; systematic studies show that different wavelengths and processes (grain boundary vs overall film evolution) affect morphology and optoelectronic properties</cite>.
- Wavelength and photon flux dependence, including “low-energy” light. <cite id="545d0ac1-4">Contrary to the common view that high-energy light dominates degradation, low-energy white light can have a stronger effect on perovskite surface degradation than X‑rays; nanoscale measurements link losses of organic cations and iodine to work-function changes, indicating intrinsic photochemical conversion at the surface</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-3">Photochemical degradation of mixed-halide perovskites shows decreased iodine core-level intensity and emergence of surface features consistent with halide loss and surface reconstruction, with further reduction upon simultaneous light+ambient exposure</cite>.
- Surface reconstruction, voiding, and morphology changes without bulk dissolution. <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Operando AFM/KPFM/CLSM on a phenethylammonium lead iodide (PEA2PbI4) 2DRP film show that combined light+electrolyte exposure produces larger and deeper voids spanning the film thickness and sparse grain distributions, indicating photodegradation-driven surface damage and recrystallization; dark-only electrolyte exposure also causes voiding and grain boundary contrast changes, but the combined light/electrolyte effect is more severe</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-2">These voids and domain contrast changes are interpreted in terms of grain etching/Ostwald ripening and recrystallization upon drying, consistent with surface-driven photodegradation rather than uniform bulk etching</cite>.
- Time/temperature and phase segregation. <cite id="545d0ac1-0">Real‑time kinetics of light-induced Pb0 formation depend on light intensity and temperature; defect migration and ion segregation at interfaces feed accumulation of metallic lead, highlighting that prolonged irradiation under elevated temperature promotes photodegradation pathways over simple bleaching</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-3">Photoinduced phase segregation in mixed-halide films leads to halide ion depletion near the surface and formation of PbX2, consistent with surface photodegradation chemistry preceding bulk corrosion</cite>.
- Signatures and diagnostics. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">AFM/SEM morphological roughening at grain boundaries and roughened terraces in 2DRP films can be attributed to prior light exposure; PL and XPS show iodine loss and PbI2 formation as key markers</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Height-profile differences and void depth (≈65–220 nm) across grain boundaries provide operando evidence of light- and/or electrolyte-induced surface damage and recrystallization</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-4">STM/STS/KPFM link organic cation and iodine loss to nanoscale work-function changes, quantifying the photochemical surface conversion</cite>.
- When 2D layers themselves act as passivated films. <cite id="edc01642-0">PEAI passivation can induce 2D perovskite formation on top of 3D films; stability tests under 85 C/85% RH show that unpassivated films develop strong PbI2 peaks within hours and phase degradation, whereas synergistic passivation suppresses PbI2 and preserves perovskite peaks over 100 h, indicating that the 2D passivation layer resists ambient corrosion</cite>. <cite id="edc01642-4">Hybrid 2D/3D films exhibit superior ambient stability to 3D-only films under damp heat, maintaining ~98–91% performance versus ~73–76% for 3D, consistent with 2D layers blocking moisture/oxygen and passivating defects</cite>. <cite id="edc01642-3">2D layers provide hydrophobic barriers that passivate surface defects and block ion migration; carefully chosen 2D compositions and interfaces are key to combining efficiency with stability</cite>.

Conditions where photocorrosion dominates in 2D perovskites
- Presence of oxygen, moisture, and electrolytes at illuminated interfaces. <cite id="4fe09237-3">At irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces, oxygen and moisture catalyze corrosion reactions that convert perovskite into ions or secondary phases; thermodynamic/kinetic control determines whether dissolution is chemical, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, or photochemical</cite> <cite id="edc01642-1">Ambient oxygen and humidity accelerate decomposition of protonated organic cations and perovskite halides, while light plus oxygen can also form passivating superoxide species that transiently brighten perovskites—underscoring the complex interplay between photochemical and electrochemical pathways</cite>.
- Electrode/electrolyte architectures and photoelectrochemical driving. <cite id="4fe09237-1">Photoelectrochemical corrosion is driven by selectively injected carriers at electrodes, promoting surface reactions and dissolution; photochemical corrosion allows majority carriers to reach the surface because there is no external carrier removal, increasing the fraction of surface-approaching electrons and holes that drive chemical changes</cite>.
- 2D films exposed to damp heat and atmospheric moisture. <cite id="edc01642-0">Under 85 C/85% RH, passivated films initially resist PbI2 formation, but over 100 h the unpassivated control shows PbI2 becoming dominant, revealing that sustained moisture/oxygen exposure drives corrosion even in 2D systems unless barriers are effective</cite>. <cite id="edc01642-2">High humidity increases defect density and shifts surface energy levels, reducing PL and lifetime; passivation layers and low‑hygroscopic processing that maintain narrow CPD distributions suppress moisture-perovskite interactions and preserve stability</cite>.
- Evidence of halide salt formation and dissolution. <cite id="545d0ac1-3">During photochemical degradation, halide ion depletion near the surface with concomitant PbX2 formation is observed by XPS; in ambient/dark combined exposure, further reduction of iodine signatures indicates progression toward corrosion products</cite>. <cite id="edc01642-1">Ambient exposure can convert MA/FA-based perovskites into PbI2 and δ-FAPbI3 within hours, consistent with corrosion-driven phase changes</cite>.
- Interface-specific etching and void growth feeding bulk loss. <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Electrolyte in the dark induces defined voids and grain boundary features (~65 nm depth), while light plus electrolyte drives deeper, film‑spanning voids (~220 nm) consistent with irradiation-accelerated surface etching and grain loss at the perovskite/electrolyte interface</cite>.

Switching conditions and decision rules
- Oxygen/humidity vs inert/dry environments. <cite id="edc01642-1">In inert atmospheres (e.g., N2), 2D/3D films degrade slightly over hours, but ambient exposure markedly accelerates chemical degradation via oxygen/moisture; thus, in dry/oxygen‑limited conditions, photodegradation (surface halide loss, segregation) tends to dominate, whereas wet/oxygenated environments favor photocorrosion (electrochemical/chemical dissolution)</cite>.
- Irradiance/wavelength regime. <cite id="545d0ac1-4">Low-energy white light can be more damaging than high-energy X‑rays due to cumulative surface conversion, whereas high-energy photons may be absorbed deeper and less at the surface; in strongly oxidizing electrolytes, photoelectrochemical action of visible photons can dominate over simple photodegradation</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Blue and red laser exposures, fluorescent lamp light, and AM sunlight each trigger different degrees of iodine loss and morphology change in 2DRP films, allowing condition-specific dominance to be inferred from AFM/SEM/PL/XPS</cite>.
- Presence and quality of passivation and 2D layers. <cite id="4fe09237-4">Surface protection, facet engineering, and coatings (including 2D perovskites) are recommended to stabilize irradiated interfaces; bifunctional protective layers can merge catalytic and barrier functions</cite> <cite id="edc01642-0">A robust 2D passivation layer blocks water/oxygen ingress and suppresses corrosion products such as PbI2, shifting failure modes from interfacial corrosion to surface photodegradation if present</cite> <cite id="edc01642-4">Hybrid 2D/3D films retain ~98–91% performance over 200 days (ambient, RH>20%) and show superior thermal stability under 60 C/60–70% RH, indicating that high-quality passivation can prevent moisture-driven corrosion even under prolonged light</cite>.
- Device architecture and contact layers. <cite id="edc01642-3">Some interfacial layers improve efficiency but deteriorate operational stability by creating new interfaces that later fail under damp heat; thus, in inverted or passivated-stack devices, photocorrosion at buried interfaces can dominate if passivation is imperfect</cite>.
- Time and temperature. <cite id="545d0ac1-0">Increasing temperature and prolonged irradiation accelerate defect migration, ion segregation, and Pb0 formation; kinetics and interfaces control whether these degradation products remain at surfaces (photodegradation) or dissolve into electrolytes/moisture (photocorrosion)</cite>.
- Measurable diagnostics to disambiguate. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Iodine loss and PbI2 signatures by XPS, with AFM/SEM grain boundary roughening and terrace loss, indicate photodegradation; conversely, electrolyte-contacted corrosion shows surface etching, void growth, and phase conversion dominated by dissolution and interfacial reactions</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Depth-resolved void growth (≈65–220 nm) and grain sparsening under light+electrolyte versus morphology changes under electrolyte-only help classify the dominant mechanism</cite>.

Putting it together: practical guidance for 2D perovskites
- If your 2D film is isolated from oxygen/moisture and electrolyte (inert glovebox/dark storage), expect photodegradation as the main threat: halide loss, PbI2/Pb0 formation at surfaces, segregation, and surface voiding/roughening under irradiation; mitigate by strong surface passivation, hydrophobic large-cation 2D layers, and low-energy illumination or UV-blocking coatings. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Light exposure drives iodine loss to form PbI2 and Pb0 at 2DRP surfaces</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-4">Low-energy white light can be particularly effective at surface degradation</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-2">AFM/CLSM show surface voiding and grain boundary etching under light</cite>.
- If your 2D film is in contact with electrolytes or aqueous environments under illumination (e.g., photoelectrodes, inverted devices with wet contacts), photocorrosion dominates: oxygen/moisture-accelerated dissolution into ions, formation of PbI2 and soluble halides, and interfacial etching; mitigate with conformal hydrophobic passivation (PEAI, m-XPEAI), 2D sacrificial/passivating layers, ion-segregation suppression, and oxygen/humidity barriers. <cite id="4fe09237-3">At irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces, corrosion reactions proceed via multiple mechanisms and kinetics</cite> <cite id="edc01642-0">Synergistic passivation that forms a dense 2D layer blocks water/oxygen and suppresses PbI2 growth under 85 C/85% RH</cite> <cite id="edc01642-4">Hybrid 2D/3D films maintain ~98% ambient stability over 200 days, with improved thermal stability under damp heat</cite> <cite id="edc01642-1">Ambient oxygen/moisture accelerate chemical degradation; oxygen can also transiently passivate defects under light</cite>.
- Under high photon flux across the bandgap (especially blue/white light) with poor surface passivation, expect photodegradation to dominate via rapid halide surface loss and segregation; under the same light but with wet contacts or oxidizing electrolytes, photocorrosion takes over as surface reactions dissolve halides/organic cations. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Wavelength- and process-specific AFM/SEM/PL/XPS show halide loss, PbI2 formation, and morphology evolution under different lights</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-3">XPS reveals halide depletion and surface halide salt formation during photochemical degradation</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-1">Photochemical and photoelectrochemical corrosion modes differ in how carriers drive interfacial reactions and majority carriers reach the surface</cite>.
- With high humidity/damp-heat and thermally assisted conditions, corrosion processes win: soluble halides and Pb(II) species form at interfaces and diffuse; even 2D layers can fail over 100–600 h unless passivation is robust and hydrophobic. <cite id="edc01642-0">Control films develop dominant PbI2 peaks within hours at 85 C/85% RH, while synergistic passivation preserves perovskite peaks for 100 h</cite> <cite id="edc01642-2">Humidity increases defects and shifts surface potential; low-hygroscopic processing and strong passivation suppress moisture interactions</cite> <cite id="edc01642-4">2D/3D devices retain ~98–91% performance in 20–60 day tests under humid/thermal stress</cite>.
- If you observe nanoscale work-function increases and surface recombination centers without clear electrolyte dissolution products, you are likely in a photodegradation-dominated regime; if you see electrolyte-specific features (PbI2 peaks, surface etching, intergranular void growth) under illumination in contact with solution/air, you are in a photocorrosion-dominated regime. <cite id="545d0ac1-4">KPFM links organic/iodine loss to work-function changes under light</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Light/electrolyte exposure yields film-spanning voids and sparse grains</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-3">XPS halide depletion and PbX2 formation mark photochemical surface degradation</cite>.

Mitigation playbook under specific conditions
- Dry, dark storage or low-light operation: maximize surface passivation with hydrophobic 2D layers (PEAI, m-XPEAI), control humidity spikes, and engineer facet curvature to suppress photogenerated carrier-induced surface reactions. <cite id="edc01642-0">2D passivation forms a barrier that blocks water/oxygen and suppresses PbI2 formation</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-4">Facet engineering and in situ/operando imaging reveal structural weaknesses to guide stable designs</cite>.
- Wet/damp or electrolyte-contacted devices: use conformal, hydrophobic, and chemically stable passivation (m-XPEAI, polymer SAMs), incorporate sacrificial/oxidation-tolerant interlayers, tune halide chemistry (Cl/Br ratios) to reduce dissolution kinetics, and minimize oxygen ingress. <cite id="edc01642-4">Hybrid 2D/3D films show superior ambient/damp-heat stability due to 2D barrier and passivation</cite> <cite id="edc01642-1">Oxygen/moisture accelerate chemical degradation; controlled oxygen can transiently passivate, aiding design of protective atmospheres</cite>.
- High-sunlight exposure: combine UV-blocking or wide-bandgap passivation with anti-reflective/dispersive surface treatments to reduce photon flux at surfaces; add chloride to slow iodide loss. <cite id="edc01642-4">Photostability under 1-sun shows 3D/2D devices retaining 87–98% performance over 1000–200 days via tailored passivation</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-0">Kinetics under light intensity and temperature guide the choice of thermal management and passivation materials</cite>.
- Electrochemical interfaces: decouple photoactivity from redox by using wide-bandgap 2D layers as quasi‑insulating barriers, choosing inert electrolytes, and adding redox‑buffering additives that suppress PbI2/lead‑ion dissolution. <cite id="4fe09237-1">Photoelectrochemical corrosion is driven by carrier injection; inserting 2D barriers and inert electrolytes reduces interfacial reaction rates</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-4">Surface protection and materials/electrolyte engineering are central to mitigating corrosion</cite>.

Summary conditions mapping
- Photodegradation-dominant: isolated 2D films under irradiation with halide loss and surface reconstruction; low-energy white/blue light; dry/dark or inert but light-exposed operation; thin 2D layers without robust passivation; signatures include iodine loss, PbI2 formation, surface segregation, and nanoscale voiding/roughening. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Light causes iodine loss and PbI2/Pb0 formation in 2DRP perovskites</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-4">Low-energy white light strongly degrades surfaces</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Operando AFM/KPFM/CLSM reveal surface voiding and grain boundary etching</cite>.
- Photocorrosion-dominant: illuminated interfaces in oxygenated/wet environments or electrolytes; photoelectrochemical/electrochemical corrosion modes; ambient/damp-heat exposure; signatures include electrolyte-mediated PbI2/soluble halide formation, interfacial etching, and film-spanning voids under light+electrolyte; mitigation via dense hydrophobic 2D layers, inert electrolytes, and oxygen/humidity barriers. <cite id="4fe09237-3">At irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces, oxygen/moisture accelerate corrosion via multiple mechanisms</cite> <cite id="edc01642-0">Synergistic passivation suppresses PbI2 formation under 85 C/85% RH; control films rapidly form PbI2</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Light plus electrolyte yields deeper, film-spanning voids than electrolyte-only</cite>.

In practice, start with an operando differentiation protocol: run identical light/temperature/time exposures with and without electrolyte contact, and in dry vs humid air; use XPS/UPS to track halide/organic cation loss and work-function shifts, AFM/SEM/CLSM to map surface voiding and grain boundary evolution, and XRD to quantify PbI2/phase conversion. Then, based on which products and morphologies grow under which conditions, assign dominance and tailor passivation/2D-layer engineering, halide composition, and interface chemistries accordingly. <cite id="545d0ac1-0">Time-resolved, environment-controlled measurements are essential to deconvolute competing thermodynamic/kinetic factors in degradation</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-4">In situ/operando imaging and spectroscopy reveal elementary corrosion steps and guide facet/interface engineering</cite> <cite id="edc01642-2">Humidity-tolerant passivation and low-hygroscopic processing preserve surface energy levels and PL under ambient conditions</cite>.

We can approach the underlying processes from a thermodynamics perspective (i.e., whether it can happen or not); however, the convoluted reaction kinetics (i.e., multiple steps, chemical transitions) must also be considered. Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: (i) chemical, where no net charge transfer occurs at the interface; (ii) electrochemical, where the selectively injected charge carriers induce corrosion; (iii) photoelectrochemical, where the photoexcited minority carriers are predominantly responsible for the corrosion; (iv) photochemical, where both the minority and majority charge carriers can induce chemical changes. In the case of photochemical corrosion there is no external driving force that removes the majority carriers (as opposed to photoelectrochemical corrosion). Therefore, a larger fraction of majority carriers can reach the photocatalyst surface and can induce corrosion processes. 

In this Perspective, we discuss the last three corrosion processes from the above list, highlighting the peculiar features of perovskites. First, we present some general thermodynamic and kinetics aspects of photocorrosion. Selected examples of corrosion processes of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes form the main body of the article, where photo-(electro)catalytic and photo(electro)synthetic examples are both scrutinized. This is followed by a compilation of in situ/ operando methods, which provide mechanistic insights with spatial and temporal resolution. Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies, which also outline future research and development avenues.
</snippet>

Title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
Snippet: Metal–halide perovskites transformed optoelectronics research and development during the past decade. They have also gained a foothold in photocatalytic and photoelectrochemical processes recently, but their sensitivity to the most commonly applied solvents and electrolytes together with their susceptibility to photocorrosion hinders such applications. Understanding the elementary steps of photocorrosion of these materials can aid the endeavor of realizing stable devices. In this Perspective, we discuss both thermodynamic and kinetic aspects of photocorrosion processes occurring at the interface of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes with different electrolytes. We show how combined in situ and operando electrochemical techniques can reveal the underlying mechanisms. Finally, we also discuss emerging strategies to mitigate photocorrosion (such as surface protection, materials and electrolyte engineering, etc.).
</snippet>
