Snippet: PC and PEC scenarios are recent additions to the potential research arenas where the optoelectronic properties of perovskites can be harnessed. Elaborating on the experience gathered from pioneering studies on photocorrosion processes and from stabilizing perovskite layers in PV devices will greatly accelerate the progress of this field. As the first step, careful characterization protocols are necessary for both PC and PEC studies (with quantitative product detection), to understand reasons and processes behind the instability. Furthermore, combined in situ electrochemical measurements will furnish mechanistic insights, with the possibility of revealing the elementary steps of corrosion. For nanoscale studies, in situ electrochemical atomic force microscopy 231−234 and PEC transmission electron microscopy will be useful to visualize morphological changes that occur on the surface of photocatalysts and photoelectrodes. Pinpointing structural weaknesses in these systems (e.g., sensitive facets, morphological features) will guide better design of stable solar energy conversion devices. In a similar fashion, coupled ultrafast techniques can shed light on how corrosion affects the charge carrier dynamics of these complex systems. 158,235 Ultrafast spectroscopic studies under electrochemical control have just been employed for perovskite electrodes recently, and further breakthroughs are expected once the pulse duration is decreased. With setups allowing few femtoseconds (or even sub-femtosecond) resolution, 236 the initial stages of charge carrier generation can be followed, providing new insights for subsequent rational materials design. While single crystal surfaces can be used to identify elementary steps in photocorrosion processes (including identification of stable and active facets), crystal facet engineering will help to translate this knowledge to nanostructured materials of practical importance. 

Once the elementary steps of the photocorrosion process are uncovered, different strategies can be employed to stabilize perovskites. Compositional engineering, various surface protection approaches and the preparation of 2D perovskites are all viable options. As a particularly promising direction, bifunctional coatings can be developed, where the catalytic and protective functions are merged.

Title: Metallic Lead Formation in Perovskites: Mechanisms, Suppression, and Future Directions
Snippet: Beyond highlighting the critical degradation pathways in halide perovskites, future studies should also aim to answer targeted mechanistic questions using advanced in situ and operando techniques. For instance, what are the real-time kinetics of Pb 0 formation under varying environmental conditions such as light intensity, and temperature? How do defect migration, ion segregation, and surface reconstruction contribute to Pb 0 accumulation at different interfaces? What are the atomistic differences in degradation mechanisms between triple-cation and single-cation systems, and how do they translate to improved long-term stability? Addressing such questions will require time-resolved spectroscopies, environmental TEM/ XPS, and computational modeling to deconvolute competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors. Standardized degradation protocols and comparative studies across compositions and architectures will be essential to translate laboratory-scale findings into durable real-world optoelectronic applications. 

To this end, in Table 1, we categorize the key environmental and synthetic factors contributing to Pb 0 formation and maps them to suppression strategies that range from chemical additives to fabrication optimizations. This serves as both a reference point for researchers and a roadmap for future work aiming to develop truly stable perovskite systems. 

Finally, it is important to highlight the reliability of using techniques such as XPS, XRD, and TEM to identify Pb 0 formation, given that these methods themselves may induce degradation. While it is well recognized that halide perovskites are sensitive to X-ray and electron beams, several studies have demonstrated that with careful experimental design and proper controls, these tools can still provide reliable insights into the presence and distribution of Pb 0 . In the case of X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), beam-induced damage can be minimized by employing low-power settings and short acquisition times. To distinguish probe-induced Pb 0 from photoinduced degradation, comparative measurements between pristine and light-exposed samples are conducted under identical XPS acquisition conditions. If Pb 0 signals appear only after illumination, this provides compelling evidence of lightinduced degradation rather than XPS-induced artifacts. Similarly, XRD can be susceptible to beam-induced effects if scans are conducted at high exposure or over extended durations.
</snippet>

Title: Impact of light illumination on the surface structure of two-dimensional Ruddlesden–Popper perovskite in the fabrication process
Snippet: Zhang et al showed many small bumps at the grain boundaries in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images [28]. In addition, Yang et al observed a rough surface morphology in the atomic force microscopy (AFM) image, which is in contrast to previous results [33]. 

During the fabrication process, 2DRP perovskites were often unintentionally exposed to light, such as a daily-use fluorescent lamp (FL) or sunlight from the window, in the laboratory. In previous works [34,35], they observed that light illumination leads to the loss of iodine in 2DRP perovskites, which results in the generation of lead iodide (PbI 2 ) and eventually, metallic lead (Pb 0 ), which has been reported as the most detrimental defect [36][37][38][39]. In this reason, we assume that above discrepancies may be, at least partially, originated from an unintended light illumination in the fabrication processes. However, it remains unclear how photodegradation occurs, and its impact has not been determined because there are no systematic studies on this topic. 

This study makes a unique contribution to the literature by investigating the effect of light illumination on all sample-fabrication processes. Various light sources, such as blue lasers, red lasers, a laboratory FL without/without an ultraviolet (UV) filter, and air mass (AM) 1.5, will be used to understand the photodegradation process of 2DRP perovskite. A phenethylammonium lead iodide (PEA 2 PbI 4 ) film was selected as the model structure to represent the 2DRP perovskite. We monitored the morphological evolution resulting from photodegradation via AFM and SEM. The degree of degradation and surface chemical structure were examined using PL and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). From this systematic study, we will address (1) which energy (wavelength) of light induces photodegradation, (2) how strongly it impacts the optoelectronic properties of 2DRP perovskite, and (3) which process of the film fabrication is most severely affected.
</snippet>

Title: Understanding and decoupling the role of wavelength and defects in light-induced degradation of metal-halide perovskites
Snippet: Solution-processed metal halide perovskite solar cells are currently under the spotlight due to their high power conversion efficiencies (PCE reaching up to 25.8%), 1,2 coupled with relatively simple and low-cost fabrication methods.So far, commercialization has been impeded by deleterious drawbacks such as rapid device degradation and J-V hysteresis. 31][22][23][24] However, up to now, a detailed model at the nanoscale of the light-induced chemical conversion/degradation of the perovskite is still lacking.Such a model could uncover unforeseen chemical processes, responsible for the intrinsic light degradation of the perovskite material and infer worthwhile strategies to mitigate them, which is exactly what we tackled in the present study.

In this work, we used state-of-the-art perovskite absorbers (FAPbI 3 ) 0.97 (MAPbBr 3 ) 0.03 that have been successfully employed in photovoltaic devices with a champion PCE reaching 22% (Fig. S1, ESI †).By combining various high-resolution surfacesensitive techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS), Kelvin probe force (KPFM) and atomic force (AFM) microscopies, electron microscopy (EM), secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), we systematically investigated the effect of light, X-rays, and temperature on the intrinsic stability of the metal-halide perovskite surface.

In contrast to what is usually admitted, [25][26][27][28] we demonstrate that low-energy white light has a stronger effect on perovskite degradation as compared to high-energy light (X-rays).Importantly, we show that cooling down the sample helps reducing the formation of metallic lead (Pb(0)) and prevents the release of the organic cation and diiodide during sample analysis.Kelvin probe force microscopy measurements at the nanoscale were employed to link the losses of the organic cations and iodine to changes in the work function.

Below is a practical framework to determine whether photodegradation or photocorrosion dominates in two-dimensional (2D) perovskites, together with mechanistic markers and environmental levers that tip the balance. We define photodegradation as light‑induced changes to the surface and near-surface structure/chemistry that reduce optoelectronic performance (e.g., halide loss, defect formation, phase segregation, voids), whereas photocorrosion denotes self‑decomposition or surface/interfacial dissolution processes (chemical, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, or photochemical) that convert the perovskite into secondary phases or ions, often accelerated by oxygen/electrolyte/water and charge injection at interfaces. <cite id="4fe09237-1">Photocorrosion can be subdivided into chemical, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, and photochemical modes, with the mode determined by thermodynamics and kinetics at the irradiated interface, including whether charge carrier injection or photoexcitation drives surface reactions and whether minority and majority carriers reach the reactive surface</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-3">Surface reactions at irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces are central, and understanding elementary steps enables stability design</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-4">Mitigation strategies include surface protection, materials/electrolyte engineering, and preparation of 2D perovskites; facet and nanoscale imaging under operando are recommended to reveal corrosion pathways</cite>.

Conceptual distinction and drivers
- Mechanistic categories. <cite id="4fe09237-1">In perovskite photoelectrochemistry, corrosion arises from irradiation-driven surface reactions; in chemical corrosion, no net charge transfer is required, whereas electrochemical and photoelectrochemical corrosion are driven by carrier injection and photoexcited minority carriers, respectively; in photochemical corrosion, both majority and minority carriers contribute because majority carriers are not removed</cite>. <cite id="4fe09237-1">A key difference versus pure photodegradation is whether the light-induced process converts the material into soluble/dissolved species or into passivating surface products without bulk dissolution</cite>.
- Environmental levers. <cite id="4fe09237-3">The presence of electrolytes and oxygen accelerates perovskite corrosion via surface reactions and ion exchange at the interface</cite> <cite id="edc01642-1">Oxygen and moisture generally weaken chemical stability by reacting with protonated organic cations, though controlled oxygen exposure can also passivate defects and brighten perovskites under light</cite>.

Conditions where photodegradation dominates in 2D perovskites
- Light above bandgap and surface halide loss pathways. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Light exposure during fabrication or operation causes iodine loss from 2D Ruddlesden–Popper (2DRP) perovskites, forming PbI2 and eventually metallic Pb0, which is detrimental; this is a prototypical photodegradation sequence at surfaces</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Even everyday light sources (fluorescent lamps, sunlight) can induce these changes; systematic studies show that different wavelengths and processes (grain boundary vs overall film evolution) affect morphology and optoelectronic properties</cite>.
- Wavelength and photon flux dependence, including “low-energy” light. <cite id="545d0ac1-4">Contrary to the common view that high-energy light dominates degradation, low-energy white light can have a stronger effect on perovskite surface degradation than X‑rays; nanoscale measurements link losses of organic cations and iodine to work-function changes, indicating intrinsic photochemical conversion at the surface</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-3">Photochemical degradation of mixed-halide perovskites shows decreased iodine core-level intensity and emergence of surface features consistent with halide loss and surface reconstruction, with further reduction upon simultaneous light+ambient exposure</cite>.
- Surface reconstruction, voiding, and morphology changes without bulk dissolution. <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Operando AFM/KPFM/CLSM on a phenethylammonium lead iodide (PEA2PbI4) 2DRP film show that combined light+electrolyte exposure produces larger and deeper voids spanning the film thickness and sparse grain distributions, indicating photodegradation-driven surface damage and recrystallization; dark-only electrolyte exposure also causes voiding and grain boundary contrast changes, but the combined light/electrolyte effect is more severe</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-2">These voids and domain contrast changes are interpreted in terms of grain etching/Ostwald ripening and recrystallization upon drying, consistent with surface-driven photodegradation rather than uniform bulk etching</cite>.
- Time/temperature and phase segregation. <cite id="545d0ac1-0">Real‑time kinetics of light-induced Pb0 formation depend on light intensity and temperature; defect migration and ion segregation at interfaces feed accumulation of metallic lead, highlighting that prolonged irradiation under elevated temperature promotes photodegradation pathways over simple bleaching</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-3">Photoinduced phase segregation in mixed-halide films leads to halide ion depletion near the surface and formation of PbX2, consistent with surface photodegradation chemistry preceding bulk corrosion</cite>.
- Signatures and diagnostics. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">AFM/SEM morphological roughening at grain boundaries and roughened terraces in 2DRP films can be attributed to prior light exposure; PL and XPS show iodine loss and PbI2 formation as key markers</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Height-profile differences and void depth (≈65–220 nm) across grain boundaries provide operando evidence of light- and/or electrolyte-induced surface damage and recrystallization</cite>. <cite id="545d0ac1-4">STM/STS/KPFM link organic cation and iodine loss to nanoscale work-function changes, quantifying the photochemical surface conversion</cite>.
- When 2D layers themselves act as passivated films. <cite id="edc01642-0">PEAI passivation can induce 2D perovskite formation on top of 3D films; stability tests under 85 C/85% RH show that unpassivated films develop strong PbI2 peaks within hours and phase degradation, whereas synergistic passivation suppresses PbI2 and preserves perovskite peaks over 100 h, indicating that the 2D passivation layer resists ambient corrosion</cite>. <cite id="edc01642-4">Hybrid 2D/3D films exhibit superior ambient stability to 3D-only films under damp heat, maintaining ~98–91% performance versus ~73–76% for 3D, consistent with 2D layers blocking moisture/oxygen and passivating defects</cite>. <cite id="edc01642-3">2D layers provide hydrophobic barriers that passivate surface defects and block ion migration; carefully chosen 2D compositions and interfaces are key to combining efficiency with stability</cite>.

Conditions where photocorrosion dominates in 2D perovskites
- Presence of oxygen, moisture, and electrolytes at illuminated interfaces. <cite id="4fe09237-3">At irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces, oxygen and moisture catalyze corrosion reactions that convert perovskite into ions or secondary phases; thermodynamic/kinetic control determines whether dissolution is chemical, electrochemical, photoelectrochemical, or photochemical</cite> <cite id="edc01642-1">Ambient oxygen and humidity accelerate decomposition of protonated organic cations and perovskite halides, while light plus oxygen can also form passivating superoxide species that transiently brighten perovskites—underscoring the complex interplay between photochemical and electrochemical pathways</cite>.
- Electrode/electrolyte architectures and photoelectrochemical driving. <cite id="4fe09237-1">Photoelectrochemical corrosion is driven by selectively injected carriers at electrodes, promoting surface reactions and dissolution; photochemical corrosion allows majority carriers to reach the surface because there is no external carrier removal, increasing the fraction of surface-approaching electrons and holes that drive chemical changes</cite>.
- 2D films exposed to damp heat and atmospheric moisture. <cite id="edc01642-0">Under 85 C/85% RH, passivated films initially resist PbI2 formation, but over 100 h the unpassivated control shows PbI2 becoming dominant, revealing that sustained moisture/oxygen exposure drives corrosion even in 2D systems unless barriers are effective</cite>. <cite id="edc01642-2">High humidity increases defect density and shifts surface energy levels, reducing PL and lifetime; passivation layers and low‑hygroscopic processing that maintain narrow CPD distributions suppress moisture-perovskite interactions and preserve stability</cite>.
- Evidence of halide salt formation and dissolution. <cite id="545d0ac1-3">During photochemical degradation, halide ion depletion near the surface with concomitant PbX2 formation is observed by XPS; in ambient/dark combined exposure, further reduction of iodine signatures indicates progression toward corrosion products</cite>. <cite id="edc01642-1">Ambient exposure can convert MA/FA-based perovskites into PbI2 and δ-FAPbI3 within hours, consistent with corrosion-driven phase changes</cite>.
- Interface-specific etching and void growth feeding bulk loss. <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Electrolyte in the dark induces defined voids and grain boundary features (~65 nm depth), while light plus electrolyte drives deeper, film‑spanning voids (~220 nm) consistent with irradiation-accelerated surface etching and grain loss at the perovskite/electrolyte interface</cite>.

Switching conditions and decision rules
- Oxygen/humidity vs inert/dry environments. <cite id="edc01642-1">In inert atmospheres (e.g., N2), 2D/3D films degrade slightly over hours, but ambient exposure markedly accelerates chemical degradation via oxygen/moisture; thus, in dry/oxygen‑limited conditions, photodegradation (surface halide loss, segregation) tends to dominate, whereas wet/oxygenated environments favor photocorrosion (electrochemical/chemical dissolution)</cite>.
- Irradiance/wavelength regime. <cite id="545d0ac1-4">Low-energy white light can be more damaging than high-energy X‑rays due to cumulative surface conversion, whereas high-energy photons may be absorbed deeper and less at the surface; in strongly oxidizing electrolytes, photoelectrochemical action of visible photons can dominate over simple photodegradation</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Blue and red laser exposures, fluorescent lamp light, and AM sunlight each trigger different degrees of iodine loss and morphology change in 2DRP films, allowing condition-specific dominance to be inferred from AFM/SEM/PL/XPS</cite>.
- Presence and quality of passivation and 2D layers. <cite id="4fe09237-4">Surface protection, facet engineering, and coatings (including 2D perovskites) are recommended to stabilize irradiated interfaces; bifunctional protective layers can merge catalytic and barrier functions</cite> <cite id="edc01642-0">A robust 2D passivation layer blocks water/oxygen ingress and suppresses corrosion products such as PbI2, shifting failure modes from interfacial corrosion to surface photodegradation if present</cite> <cite id="edc01642-4">Hybrid 2D/3D films retain ~98–91% performance over 200 days (ambient, RH>20%) and show superior thermal stability under 60 C/60–70% RH, indicating that high-quality passivation can prevent moisture-driven corrosion even under prolonged light</cite>.
- Device architecture and contact layers. <cite id="edc01642-3">Some interfacial layers improve efficiency but deteriorate operational stability by creating new interfaces that later fail under damp heat; thus, in inverted or passivated-stack devices, photocorrosion at buried interfaces can dominate if passivation is imperfect</cite>.
- Time and temperature. <cite id="545d0ac1-0">Increasing temperature and prolonged irradiation accelerate defect migration, ion segregation, and Pb0 formation; kinetics and interfaces control whether these degradation products remain at surfaces (photodegradation) or dissolve into electrolytes/moisture (photocorrosion)</cite>.
- Measurable diagnostics to disambiguate. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Iodine loss and PbI2 signatures by XPS, with AFM/SEM grain boundary roughening and terrace loss, indicate photodegradation; conversely, electrolyte-contacted corrosion shows surface etching, void growth, and phase conversion dominated by dissolution and interfacial reactions</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Depth-resolved void growth (≈65–220 nm) and grain sparsening under light+electrolyte versus morphology changes under electrolyte-only help classify the dominant mechanism</cite>.

Putting it together: practical guidance for 2D perovskites
- If your 2D film is isolated from oxygen/moisture and electrolyte (inert glovebox/dark storage), expect photodegradation as the main threat: halide loss, PbI2/Pb0 formation at surfaces, segregation, and surface voiding/roughening under irradiation; mitigate by strong surface passivation, hydrophobic large-cation 2D layers, and low-energy illumination or UV-blocking coatings. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Light exposure drives iodine loss to form PbI2 and Pb0 at 2DRP surfaces</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-4">Low-energy white light can be particularly effective at surface degradation</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-2">AFM/CLSM show surface voiding and grain boundary etching under light</cite>.
- If your 2D film is in contact with electrolytes or aqueous environments under illumination (e.g., photoelectrodes, inverted devices with wet contacts), photocorrosion dominates: oxygen/moisture-accelerated dissolution into ions, formation of PbI2 and soluble halides, and interfacial etching; mitigate with conformal hydrophobic passivation (PEAI, m-XPEAI), 2D sacrificial/passivating layers, ion-segregation suppression, and oxygen/humidity barriers. <cite id="4fe09237-3">At irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces, corrosion reactions proceed via multiple mechanisms and kinetics</cite> <cite id="edc01642-0">Synergistic passivation that forms a dense 2D layer blocks water/oxygen and suppresses PbI2 growth under 85 C/85% RH</cite> <cite id="edc01642-4">Hybrid 2D/3D films maintain ~98% ambient stability over 200 days, with improved thermal stability under damp heat</cite> <cite id="edc01642-1">Ambient oxygen/moisture accelerate chemical degradation; oxygen can also transiently passivate defects under light</cite>.
- Under high photon flux across the bandgap (especially blue/white light) with poor surface passivation, expect photodegradation to dominate via rapid halide surface loss and segregation; under the same light but with wet contacts or oxidizing electrolytes, photocorrosion takes over as surface reactions dissolve halides/organic cations. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Wavelength- and process-specific AFM/SEM/PL/XPS show halide loss, PbI2 formation, and morphology evolution under different lights</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-3">XPS reveals halide depletion and surface halide salt formation during photochemical degradation</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-1">Photochemical and photoelectrochemical corrosion modes differ in how carriers drive interfacial reactions and majority carriers reach the surface</cite>.
- With high humidity/damp-heat and thermally assisted conditions, corrosion processes win: soluble halides and Pb(II) species form at interfaces and diffuse; even 2D layers can fail over 100–600 h unless passivation is robust and hydrophobic. <cite id="edc01642-0">Control films develop dominant PbI2 peaks within hours at 85 C/85% RH, while synergistic passivation preserves perovskite peaks for 100 h</cite> <cite id="edc01642-2">Humidity increases defects and shifts surface potential; low-hygroscopic processing and strong passivation suppress moisture interactions</cite> <cite id="edc01642-4">2D/3D devices retain ~98–91% performance in 20–60 day tests under humid/thermal stress</cite>.
- If you observe nanoscale work-function increases and surface recombination centers without clear electrolyte dissolution products, you are likely in a photodegradation-dominated regime; if you see electrolyte-specific features (PbI2 peaks, surface etching, intergranular void growth) under illumination in contact with solution/air, you are in a photocorrosion-dominated regime. <cite id="545d0ac1-4">KPFM links organic/iodine loss to work-function changes under light</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Light/electrolyte exposure yields film-spanning voids and sparse grains</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-3">XPS halide depletion and PbX2 formation mark photochemical surface degradation</cite>.

Mitigation playbook under specific conditions
- Dry, dark storage or low-light operation: maximize surface passivation with hydrophobic 2D layers (PEAI, m-XPEAI), control humidity spikes, and engineer facet curvature to suppress photogenerated carrier-induced surface reactions. <cite id="edc01642-0">2D passivation forms a barrier that blocks water/oxygen and suppresses PbI2 formation</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-4">Facet engineering and in situ/operando imaging reveal structural weaknesses to guide stable designs</cite>.
- Wet/damp or electrolyte-contacted devices: use conformal, hydrophobic, and chemically stable passivation (m-XPEAI, polymer SAMs), incorporate sacrificial/oxidation-tolerant interlayers, tune halide chemistry (Cl/Br ratios) to reduce dissolution kinetics, and minimize oxygen ingress. <cite id="edc01642-4">Hybrid 2D/3D films show superior ambient/damp-heat stability due to 2D barrier and passivation</cite> <cite id="edc01642-1">Oxygen/moisture accelerate chemical degradation; controlled oxygen can transiently passivate, aiding design of protective atmospheres</cite>.
- High-sunlight exposure: combine UV-blocking or wide-bandgap passivation with anti-reflective/dispersive surface treatments to reduce photon flux at surfaces; add chloride to slow iodide loss. <cite id="edc01642-4">Photostability under 1-sun shows 3D/2D devices retaining 87–98% performance over 1000–200 days via tailored passivation</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-0">Kinetics under light intensity and temperature guide the choice of thermal management and passivation materials</cite>.
- Electrochemical interfaces: decouple photoactivity from redox by using wide-bandgap 2D layers as quasi‑insulating barriers, choosing inert electrolytes, and adding redox‑buffering additives that suppress PbI2/lead‑ion dissolution. <cite id="4fe09237-1">Photoelectrochemical corrosion is driven by carrier injection; inserting 2D barriers and inert electrolytes reduces interfacial reaction rates</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-4">Surface protection and materials/electrolyte engineering are central to mitigating corrosion</cite>.

Summary conditions mapping
- Photodegradation-dominant: isolated 2D films under irradiation with halide loss and surface reconstruction; low-energy white/blue light; dry/dark or inert but light-exposed operation; thin 2D layers without robust passivation; signatures include iodine loss, PbI2 formation, surface segregation, and nanoscale voiding/roughening. <cite id="545d0ac1-1">Light causes iodine loss and PbI2/Pb0 formation in 2DRP perovskites</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-4">Low-energy white light strongly degrades surfaces</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Operando AFM/KPFM/CLSM reveal surface voiding and grain boundary etching</cite>.
- Photocorrosion-dominant: illuminated interfaces in oxygenated/wet environments or electrolytes; photoelectrochemical/electrochemical corrosion modes; ambient/damp-heat exposure; signatures include electrolyte-mediated PbI2/soluble halide formation, interfacial etching, and film-spanning voids under light+electrolyte; mitigation via dense hydrophobic 2D layers, inert electrolytes, and oxygen/humidity barriers. <cite id="4fe09237-3">At irradiated perovskite/electrolyte interfaces, oxygen/moisture accelerate corrosion via multiple mechanisms</cite> <cite id="edc01642-0">Synergistic passivation suppresses PbI2 formation under 85 C/85% RH; control films rapidly form PbI2</cite> <cite id="545d0ac1-2">Light plus electrolyte yields deeper, film-spanning voids than electrolyte-only</cite>.

In practice, start with an operando differentiation protocol: run identical light/temperature/time exposures with and without electrolyte contact, and in dry vs humid air; use XPS/UPS to track halide/organic cation loss and work-function shifts, AFM/SEM/CLSM to map surface voiding and grain boundary evolution, and XRD to quantify PbI2/phase conversion. Then, based on which products and morphologies grow under which conditions, assign dominance and tailor passivation/2D-layer engineering, halide composition, and interface chemistries accordingly. <cite id="545d0ac1-0">Time-resolved, environment-controlled measurements are essential to deconvolute competing thermodynamic/kinetic factors in degradation</cite> <cite id="4fe09237-4">In situ/operando imaging and spectroscopy reveal elementary corrosion steps and guide facet/interface engineering</cite> <cite id="edc01642-2">Humidity-tolerant passivation and low-hygroscopic processing preserve surface energy levels and PL under ambient conditions</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
Snippet: uring corrosion, either complete self-decomposition or the formation of active or inactive surface layers can occur. We can approach the underlying processes from a thermodynamics perspective (i.e., whether it can happen or not); however, the convoluted reaction kinetics (i.e., multiple steps, chemical transitions) must also be considered. Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: (i) chemical, where no net charge transfer occurs at the interface; (ii) electrochemical, where the selectively injected charge carriers induce corrosion; (iii) photoelectrochemical, where the photoexcited minority carriers are predominantly responsible for the corrosion; (iv) photochemical, where both the minority and majority charge carriers can induce chemical changes. In the case of photochemical corrosion there is no external driving force that removes the majority carriers (as opposed to photoelectrochemical corrosion). Therefore, a larger fraction of majority carriers can reach the photocatalyst surface and can induce corrosion processes. 

In this Perspective, we discuss the last three corrosion processes from the above list, highlighting the peculiar features of perovskites. First, we present some general thermodynamic and kinetics aspects of photocorrosion. Selected examples of corrosion processes of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes form the main body of the article, where photo-(electro)catalytic and photo(electro)synthetic examples are both scrutinized. This is followed by a compilation of in situ/ operando methods, which provide mechanistic insights with spatial and temporal resolution. Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies, which also outline future research and development avenues.

Title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
Snippet: Metal–halide perovskites transformed optoelectronics research and development during the past decade. They have also gained a foothold in photocatalytic and photoelectrochemical processes recently, but their sensitivity to the most commonly applied solvents and electrolytes together with their susceptibility to photocorrosion hinders such applications. Understanding the elementary steps of photocorrosion of these materials can aid the endeavor of realizing stable devices. In this Perspective, we discuss both thermodynamic and kinetic aspects of photocorrosion processes occurring at the interface of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes with different electrolytes. We show how combined in situ and operando electrochemical techniques can reveal the underlying mechanisms. Finally, we also discuss emerging strategies to mitigate photocorrosion (such as surface protection, materials and electrolyte engineering, etc.).

Title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
Snippet: PC and PEC scenarios are recent additions to the potential research arenas where the optoelectronic properties of perovskites can be harnessed. Elaborating on the experience gathered from pioneering studies on photocorrosion processes and from stabilizing perovskite layers in PV devices will greatly accelerate the progress of this field. As the first step, careful characterization protocols are necessary for both PC and PEC studies (with quantitative product detection), to understand reasons and processes behind the instability. Furthermore, combined in situ electrochemical measurements will furnish mechanistic insights, with the possibility of revealing the elementary steps of corrosion. For nanoscale studies, in situ electrochemical atomic force microscopy 231−234 and PEC transmission electron microscopy will be useful to visualize morphological changes that occur on the surface of photocatalysts and photoelectrodes. Pinpointing structural weaknesses in these systems (e.g., sensitive facets, morphological features) will guide better design of stable solar energy conversion devices. In a similar fashion, coupled ultrafast techniques can shed light on how corrosion affects the charge carrier dynamics of these complex systems. 158,235 Ultrafast spectroscopic studies under electrochemical control have just been employed for perovskite electrodes recently, and further breakthroughs are expected once the pulse duration is decreased. With setups allowing few femtoseconds (or even sub-femtosecond) resolution, 236 the initial stages of charge carrier generation can be followed, providing new insights for subsequent rational materials design. While single crystal surfaces can be used to identify elementary steps in photocorrosion processes (including identification of stable and active facets), crystal facet engineering will help to translate this knowledge to nanostructured materials of practical importance. 

Once the elementary steps of the photocorrosion process are uncovered, different strategies can be employed to stabilize perovskites. Compositional engineering, various surface protection approaches and the preparation of 2D perovskites are all viable options. As a particularly promising direction, bifunctional coatings can be developed, where the catalytic and protective functions are merged.

uring corrosion, either complete self-decomposition or the formation of active or inactive surface layers can occur. We can approach the underlying processes from a thermodynamics perspective (i.e., whether it can happen or not); however, the convoluted reaction kinetics (i.e., multiple steps, chemical transitions) must also be considered. Corrosion events can be divided into four categories: (i) chemical, where no net charge transfer occurs at the interface; (ii) electrochemical, where the selectively injected charge carriers induce corrosion; (iii) photoelectrochemical, where the photoexcited minority carriers are predominantly responsible for the corrosion; (iv) photochemical, where both the minority and majority charge carriers can induce chemical changes. In the case of photochemical corrosion there is no external driving force that removes the majority carriers (as opposed to photoelectrochemical corrosion). Therefore, a larger fraction of majority carriers can reach the photocatalyst surface and can induce corrosion processes. 

In this Perspective, we discuss the last three corrosion processes from the above list, highlighting the peculiar features of perovskites. First, we present some general thermodynamic and kinetics aspects of photocorrosion. Selected examples of corrosion processes of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes form the main body of the article, where photo-(electro)catalytic and photo(electro)synthetic examples are both scrutinized. This is followed by a compilation of in situ/ operando methods, which provide mechanistic insights with spatial and temporal resolution. Finally, we discuss possible mitigation strategies, which also outline future research and development avenues.

Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
documents.snippet: Metal–halide perovskites transformed optoelectronics research and development during the past decade. They have also gained a foothold in photocatalytic and photoelectrochemical processes recently, but their sensitivity to the most commonly applied solvents and electrolytes together with their susceptibility to photocorrosion hinders such applications. Understanding the elementary steps of photocorrosion of these materials can aid the endeavor of realizing stable devices. In this Perspective, we discuss both thermodynamic and kinetic aspects of photocorrosion processes occurring at the interface of perovskite photocatalysts and photoelectrodes with different electrolytes. We show how combined in situ and operando electrochemical techniques can reveal the underlying mechanisms. Finally, we also discuss emerging strategies to mitigate photocorrosion (such as surface protection, materials and electrolyte engineering, etc.).

documents.title: Photocorrosion at Irradiated Perovskite/Electrolyte Interfaces
documents.snippet:
PC and PEC scenarios are recent additions to the potential research arenas where the optoelectronic properties of perovskites can be harnessed. Elaborating on the experience gathered from pioneering studies on photocorrosion processes and from stabilizing perovskite layers in PV devices will greatly accelerate the progress of this field. As the first step, careful characterization protocols are necessary for both PC and PEC studies (with quantitative product detection), to understand reasons and processes behind the instability. Furthermore, combined in situ electrochemical measurements will furnish mechanistic insights, with the possibility of revealing the elementary steps of corrosion. For nanoscale studies, in situ electrochemical atomic force microscopy 231−234 and PEC transmission electron microscopy will be useful to visualize morphological changes that occur on the surface of photocatalysts and photoelectrodes. Pinpointing structural weaknesses in these systems (e.g., sensitive facets, morphological features) will guide better design of stable solar energy conversion devices. In a similar fashion, coupled ultrafast techniques can shed light on how corrosion affects the charge carrier dynamics of these complex systems. 158,235 Ultrafast spectroscopic studies under electrochemical control have just been employed for perovskite electrodes recently, and further breakthroughs are expected once the pulse duration is decreased. With setups allowing few femtoseconds (or even sub-femtosecond) resolution, 236 the initial stages of charge carrier generation can be followed, providing new insights for subsequent rational materials design. While single crystal surfaces can be used to identify elementary steps in photocorrosion processes (including identification of stable and active facets), crystal facet engineering will help to translate this knowledge to nanostructured materials of practical importance. 

Once the elementary steps of the photocorrosion process are uncovered, different strategies can be employed to stabilize perovskites. Compositional engineering, various surface protection approaches and the preparation of 2D perovskites are all viable options. As a particularly promising direction, bifunctional coatings can be developed, where the catalytic and protective functions are merged.

Title: Metallic Lead Formation in Perovskites: Mechanisms, Suppression, and Future Directions
Snippet: Beyond highlighting the critical degradation pathways in halide perovskites, future studies should also aim to answer targeted mechanistic questions using advanced in situ and operando techniques. For instance, what are the real-time kinetics of Pb 0 formation under varying environmental conditions such as light intensity, and temperature? How do defect migration, ion segregation, and surface reconstruction contribute to Pb 0 accumulation at different interfaces? What are the atomistic differences in degradation mechanisms between triple-cation and single-cation systems, and how do they translate to improved long-term stability? Addressing such questions will require time-resolved spectroscopies, environmental TEM/ XPS, and computational modeling to deconvolute competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors. Standardized degradation protocols and comparative studies across compositions and architectures will be essential to translate laboratory-scale findings into durable real-world optoelectronic applications. 

To this end, in Table 1, we categorize the key environmental and synthetic factors contributing to Pb 0 formation and maps them to suppression strategies that range from chemical additives to fabrication optimizations. This serves as both a reference point for researchers and a roadmap for future work aiming to develop truly stable perovskite systems. 

Finally, it is important to highlight the reliability of using techniques such as XPS, XRD, and TEM to identify Pb 0 formation, given that these methods themselves may induce degradation. While it is well recognized that halide perovskites are sensitive to X-ray and electron beams, several studies have demonstrated that with careful experimental design and proper controls, these tools can still provide reliable insights into the presence and distribution of Pb 0 . In the case of X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), beam-induced damage can be minimized by employing low-power settings and short acquisition times. To distinguish probe-induced Pb 0 from photoinduced degradation, comparative measurements between pristine and light-exposed samples are conducted under identical XPS acquisition conditions. If Pb 0 signals appear only after illumination, this provides compelling evidence of lightinduced degradation rather than XPS-induced artifacts. Similarly, XRD can be susceptible to beam-induced effects if scans are conducted at high exposure or over extended durations.

Title: Impact of light illumination on the surface structure of two-dimensional Ruddlesden–Popper perovskite in the fabrication process
Snippet: Zhang et al showed many small bumps at the grain boundaries in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images [28]. In addition, Yang et al observed a rough surface morphology in the atomic force microscopy (AFM) image, which is in contrast to previous results [33]. 

During the fabrication process, 2DRP perovskites were often unintentionally exposed to light, such as a daily-use fluorescent lamp (FL) or sunlight from the window, in the laboratory. In previous works [34,35], they observed that light illumination leads to the loss of iodine in 2DRP perovskites, which results in the generation of lead iodide (PbI 2 ) and eventually, metallic lead (Pb 0 ), which has been reported as the most detrimental defect [36][37][38][39]. In this reason, we assume that above discrepancies may be, at least partially, originated from an unintended light illumination in the fabrication processes. However, it remains unclear how photodegradation occurs, and its impact has not been determined because there are no systematic studies on this topic. 

This study makes a unique contribution to the literature by investigating the effect of light illumination on all sample-fabrication processes. Various light sources, such as blue lasers, red lasers, a laboratory FL without/without an ultraviolet (UV) filter, and air mass (AM) 1.5, will be used to understand the photodegradation process of 2DRP perovskite. A phenethylammonium lead iodide (PEA 2 PbI 4 ) film was selected as the model structure to represent the 2DRP perovskite. We monitored the morphological evolution resulting from photodegradation via AFM and SEM. The degree of degradation and surface chemical structure were examined using PL and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). From this systematic study, we will address (1) which energy (wavelength) of light induces photodegradation, (2) how strongly it impacts the optoelectronic properties of 2DRP perovskite, and (3) which process of the film fabrication is most severely affected.

Title: Photodegradation of 2D Ruddlesden‐Popper Perovskites: Consequences and Design Principles for Photoelectrochemical Applications
Snippet: To further understand the degradation processes observed in the GIWAXS analysis, we utilized constant amplitude noncontact mode atomic force microscopy (AFM) combined with frequency modulation (FM) sideband Kelvin-probe force microscopy (KPFM) and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) to analyze the post-exposure samples. This approach allowed us to investigate the morphological changes in thin films subjected to different experimental conditions, providing deeper insights into the morphological changes upon immersion in the electrolyte. 

Figure 3a shows the histogram of the AFM profile of the three conditions. The pristine sample (Figure 3b) exhibits a flat morphological profile with barely visible grain boundaries. Significant changes are observed in the morphological profile after exposure of the sample to the electrolyte in the dark. As shown in Figure 3c, the interaction of the sample with the aqueous electrolyte results in modifications of the microstructure, with more defined grain boundaries and accompanied with the appearance of voids. These voids have a depth of ≈65 nm, which do not exceed the thickness of the 2D thin film. The grain domains become more evident with increased contrast in morphological profile depth, suggesting an Ostwald ripening effect. [47] or grain etching. [48] The appearance of small structures on top of the grain boundaries are attributed to 2D perovskite recrystallized after drying the sample. 

When exposing the sample to the combined effect of electrolyte and light (Figure 3d), the sample morphology changes significantly: grains become sparser with larger dark areas indicating voids. As a result, differences in the height profile become significantly more prominent. The height difference between the surface and dark voids is on the order of 220 nm, indicating that voids extend through the entire thickness of the 2D perovskite film. The distribution of these voids over the sample surface reflects another clear sign of photodegradation. 

To address the impact of the change in morphology on the optoelectronic properties of the material, we measured confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) as shown in Figure 3e-h.

Snippet: For the reliability of the results, the XPS experiments were conducted on two different perovskite samples (fabricated in different batches) for fresh and photochemical degraded films, and no significant difference was observed. The decrease in halide ions during photochemical degradation of mixed halide perovskites suggests the formation of PbX 2 on the surface. 18,19 gures 3(a at 286.3 eV. 28 Contamination during transfer of samples can be excluded because all fresh films were transferred from the N 2 -filled glovebox to the XPS chamber without any exposure to the ambient atmosphere. It is found that the intensity of the component at 284.8 eV for film 100 increased in comparison with that for the fresh film. The peak positions of N 1s in samples 00 and 100 are at 401.9 and 402.7 eV, respectively. 29,30 o significant shift in the N 1s peak position is observed for the pure halide films under any of the different degradation conditions. However, photoinduced degradation leads to a reduction in the N 1s peak intensity of the degraded films (Fig. S8).

Title: Understanding and decoupling the role of wavelength and defects in light-induced degradation of metal-halide perovskites
Snippet: Solution-processed metal halide perovskite solar cells are currently under the spotlight due to their high power conversion efficiencies (PCE reaching up to 25.8%), 1,2 coupled with relatively simple and low-cost fabrication methods.So far, commercialization has been impeded by deleterious drawbacks such as rapid device degradation and J-V hysteresis. 31][22][23][24] However, up to now, a detailed model at the nanoscale of the light-induced chemical conversion/degradation of the perovskite is still lacking.Such a model could uncover unforeseen chemical processes, responsible for the intrinsic light degradation of the perovskite material and infer worthwhile strategies to mitigate them, which is exactly what we tackled in the present study.

In this work, we used state-of-the-art perovskite absorbers (FAPbI 3 ) 0.97 (MAPbBr 3 ) 0.03 that have been successfully employed in photovoltaic devices with a champion PCE reaching 22% (Fig. S1, ESI †).By combining various high-resolution surfacesensitive techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS), Kelvin probe force (KPFM) and atomic force (AFM) microscopies, electron microscopy (EM), secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), we systematically investigated the effect of light, X-rays, and temperature on the intrinsic stability of the metal-halide perovskite surface.

In contrast to what is usually admitted, [25][26][27][28] we demonstrate that low-energy white light has a stronger effect on perovskite degradation as compared to high-energy light (X-rays).Importantly, we show that cooling down the sample helps reducing the formation of metallic lead (Pb(0)) and prevents the release of the organic cation and diiodide during sample analysis.Kelvin probe force microscopy measurements at the nanoscale were employed to link the losses of the organic cations and iodine to changes in the work function.

snippet.text:
Solution-processed metal halide perovskite solar cells are currently under the spotlight due to their high power conversion efficiencies (PCE reaching up to 25.8%), 1,2 coupled with relatively simple and low-cost fabrication methods.So far, commercialization has been impeded by deleterious drawbacks such as rapid device degradation and J-V hysteresis. 31][22][23][24] However, up to now, a detailed model at the nanoscale of the light-induced chemical conversion/degradation of the perovskite is still lacking.Such a model could uncover unforeseen chemical processes, responsible for the intrinsic light degradation of the perovskite material and infer worthwhile strategies to mitigate them, which is exactly what we tackled in the present study.

In this work, we used state-of-the-art perovskite absorbers (FAPbI 3 ) 0.97 (MAPbBr 3 ) 0.03 that have been successfully employed in photovoltaic devices with a champion PCE reaching 22% (Fig. S1, ESI †).By combining various high-resolution surfacesensitive techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and spectroscopy (STS), Kelvin probe force (KPFM) and atomic force (AFM) microscopies, electron microscopy (EM), secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), we systematically investigated the effect of light, X-rays, and temperature on the intrinsic stability of the metal-halide perovskite surface.

In contrast to what is usually admitted, [25][26][27][28] we demonstrate that low-energy white light has a stronger effect on perovskite degradation as compared to high-energy light (X-rays).Importantly, we show that cooling down the sample helps reducing the formation of metallic lead (Pb(0)) and prevents the release of the organic cation and diiodide during sample analysis.Kelvin probe force microscopy measurements at the nanoscale were employed to link the losses of the organic cations and iodine to changes in the work function.

documents.title: Metallic Lead Formation in Perovskites: Mechanisms, Suppression, and Future Directions
documents.snippet:
Beyond highlighting the critical degradation pathways in halide perovskites, future studies should also aim to answer targeted mechanistic questions using advanced in situ and operando techniques. For instance, what are the real-time kinetics of Pb 0 formation under varying environmental conditions such as light intensity, and temperature? How do defect migration, ion segregation, and surface reconstruction contribute to Pb 0 accumulation at different interfaces? What are the atomistic differences in degradation mechanisms between triple-cation and single-cation systems, and how do they translate to improved long-term stability? Addressing such questions will require time-resolved spectroscopies, environmental TEM/ XPS, and computational modeling to deconvolute competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors. Standardized degradation protocols and comparative studies across compositions and architectures will be essential to translate laboratory-scale findings into durable real-world optoelectronic applications. 

To this end, in Table 1, we categorize the key environmental and synthetic factors contributing to Pb 0 formation and maps them to suppression strategies that range from chemical additives to fabrication optimizations. This serves as both a reference point for researchers and a roadmap for future work aiming to develop truly stable perovskite systems. 

Finally, it is important to highlight the reliability of using techniques such as XPS, XRD, and TEM to identify Pb 0 formation, given that these methods themselves may induce degradation. While it is well recognized that halide perovskites are sensitive to X-ray and electron beams, several studies have demonstrated that with careful experimental design and proper controls, these tools can still provide reliable insights into the presence and distribution of Pb 0 . In the case of X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), beam-induced damage can be minimized by employing low-power settings and short acquisition times. To distinguish probe-induced Pb 0 from photoinduced degradation, comparative measurements between pristine and light-exposed samples are conducted under identical XPS acquisition conditions. If Pb 0 signals appear only after illumination, this provides compelling evidence of lightinduced degradation rather than XPS-induced artifacts. Similarly, XRD can be susceptible to beam-induced effects if scans are conducted at high exposure or over extended durations.

documents.title: Impact of light illumination on the surface structure of two-dimensional Ruddlesden–Popper perovskite in the fabrication process
documents.snippet:
Zhang et al showed many small bumps at the grain boundaries in scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images [28]. In addition, Yang et al observed a rough surface morphology in the atomic force microscopy (AFM) image, which is in contrast to previous results [33]. 

During the fabrication process, 2DRP perovskites were often unintentionally exposed to light, such as a daily-use fluorescent lamp (FL) or sunlight from the window, in the laboratory. In previous works [34,35], they observed that light illumination leads to the loss of iodine in 2DRP perovskites, which results in the generation of lead iodide (PbI 2 ) and eventually, metallic lead (Pb 0 ), which has been reported as the most detrimental defect [36][37][38][39]. In this reason, we assume that above discrepancies may be, at least partially, originated from an unintended light illumination in the fabrication processes. However, it remains unclear how photodegradation occurs, and its impact has not been determined because there are no systematic studies on this topic. 

This study makes a unique contribution to the literature by investigating the effect of light illumination on all sample-fabrication processes. Various light sources, such as blue lasers, red lasers, a laboratory FL without/without an ultraviolet (UV) filter, and air mass (AM) 1.5, will be used to understand the photodegradation process of 2DRP perovskite. A phenethylammonium lead iodide (PEA 2 PbI 4 ) film was selected as the model structure to represent the 2DRP perovskite. We monitored the morphological evolution resulting from photodegradation via AFM and SEM. The degree of degradation and surface chemical structure were examined using PL and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). From this systematic study, we will address (1) which energy (wavelength) of light induces photodegradation, (2) how strongly it impacts the optoelectronic properties of 2DRP perovskite, and (3) which process of the film fabrication is most severely affected.

To further understand the degradation processes observed in the GIWAXS analysis, we utilized constant amplitude noncontact mode atomic force microscopy (AFM) combined with frequency modulation (FM) sideband Kelvin-probe force microscopy (KPFM) and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) to analyze the post-exposure samples. This approach allowed us to investigate the morphological changes in thin films subjected to different experimental conditions, providing deeper insights into the morphological changes upon immersion in the electrolyte. 

Figure 3a shows the histogram of the AFM profile of the three conditions. The pristine sample (Figure 3b) exhibits a flat morphological profile with barely visible grain boundaries. Significant changes are observed in the morphological profile after exposure of the sample to the electrolyte in the dark. As shown in Figure 3c, the interaction of the sample with the aqueous electrolyte results in modifications of the microstructure, with more defined grain boundaries and accompanied with the appearance of voids. These voids have a depth of ≈65 nm, which do not exceed the thickness of the 2D thin film. The grain domains become more evident with increased contrast in morphological profile depth, suggesting an Ostwald ripening effect. [47] or grain etching. [48] The appearance of small structures on top of the grain boundaries are attributed to 2D perovskite recrystallized after drying the sample. 

When exposing the sample to the combined effect of electrolyte and light (Figure 3d), the sample morphology changes significantly: grains become sparser with larger dark areas indicating voids. As a result, differences in the height profile become significantly more prominent. The height difference between the surface and dark voids is on the order of 220 nm, indicating that voids extend through the entire thickness of the 2D perovskite film. The distribution of these voids over the sample surface reflects another clear sign of photodegradation. 

To address the impact of the change in morphology on the optoelectronic properties of the material, we measured confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) as shown in Figure 3e-h.

Snippet: Next, the XRD measurements were used to check the crystal properties of the perovskite films. After PEAI passivation with the concentration of 1 mg mL À1 , no 2D perovskite peaks was detected in the XRD patterns. When we varied the concentration of PEAI solution from 0.5 to 10 mg mL À1 , the 2D perovskite peaks appeared around 5.4 at the concentration of 2 mg mL À1 (Figure 4b). We deduced that the 2D perovskite was formed on the surface in the PEAI passivation sample and the synergistic passivation sample, but it was difficult to be detected by the XRD measurement at a low concentration. Title: Achievements, challenges, and future prospects for industrialization of perovskite solar cells
Snippet: The device employing a hybrid 2D/3D structure exhibited significantly greater stability in comparison to its pure 3D counterpart. Following a 76-hour exposure to ambient air, the pure 3D perovskite device experienced a complete failure. Conversely, the 2D/3D composite device demonstrated remarkable resistance by preserving an impressive 59% of its initial PCE. Further XRD measurements were performed on perovskite samples stored in nitrogen atmosphere and ambient air. The 3D and 2D/3D samples decomposed slightly after 6 hours in an inert atmosphere. Notably, the 3D sample exhibited much quicker chemical degradation than the 2D/3D sample when exposed to ambient conditions. This enhanced ambient stability of the 2D/3D-based device was likely attributed to heightened resistance ability to oxygen and moisture, stemming from improved crystallinity and higher perovskite film hydrophobicity 100 . While the presence of oxygen can substantially weaken the chemical stability of perovskite materials due to reactions with protonated organic cations like MA + and FA + , it's important to highlight that leveraging oxygen for defect passivation has also arisen as a potent and convenient strategy in suppressing nonradiative recombination processes and bolstering the photovoltaic performance of PSCs by strongly interacted with halide vacancies located on the perovskite surface 101 . The mechanism of photo brightening is given in Fig. 7b. After being treated by light, O 2 , and humidity, the density of the shallow state below the conduction band will decrease, leading to the increase of the radiative bimolecular recombination (k R ) and decrease of non-radiative bimolecular component (k n ), which significantly enhance the photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY). The detailed passivation mechanism is as follows: Initially, an untreated MAPbI 3 sample with surface states (Fig. 7cii) was subjected to illumination in the presence of O 2 . This illumination-induced process made a reduction to the density of surface states as well as triggered photo brightening, as depicted in Fig. 7cii). The mechanism behind this phenomenon involved the formation of passivating superoxide species. Importantly, the transformation was reversible and occurred in several hours when subsequently shielded from light.

Snippet: However, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) shows that PEAIperovskite interactions are nearly disappear in the control films but still preserved in the target films under high humidity (Supplementary Fig. 21). Grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) further reveals that the corresponding PEAI-induced 2D diffraction features are significantly weakened in the control films but remain clear in the target films (Supplementary Fig. 22), indicating that the introduction of n-octane has little effect on the crystallinity of the passivation layer while improving its humidity tolerance. Consistently, both the photoluminescence (PL) intensity and carrier lifetime decreases significantly as the relative humidity increases due to moisture-induced defects (Fig. 3a, b). In contrast, target films maintain much stronger PL emission and show only a minor reduction in lifetime. The result was also confirmed by the space-charge-limited current (SCLC) measurements (Supplementary Figs. 23, 24). As shown in Fig. 3c, for control samples, the defect density increased sharply with rising humidity, whereas only minor variation was observed for the low-hygroscopic solvent systems. 

We also employed Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) to examine the surface potential of perovskite films with different posttreatments under various humidity conditions (Fig. 3d, e). For control films, the potential shifts from −194 mV at 0% RH to −331 mV at 80% RH, accompanied by a broadened distribution. This gradual shift toward a more negative contact potential difference (CPD) indicates an increase in the surface work function of the control films, in agreement with the humidity-induced surface energy level shifts observed by ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) (Supplementary Fig. 25), which impedes surface electron transport and charge extraction 41,42 . In contrast, target films exhibit only a minor shift while maintaining a narrow distribution, demonstrating suppressed moisture-perovskite interactions and uniform surface passivation, as also supported by UPS results (Supplementary Fig. 26).

Also, the 2D perovskite can passivate surface defects and block ion migration, contributing to one of the best efficiencies (24.3%) and passing the standard industrial dampheat test 6 . Snippet: Contact angles of the reference and meta-halogenated salttreated perovskite films with water are also measured, as shown in Figure 5a. 3D/2D films exhibit more hydrophobic surfaces than the control 3D perovskite film due to the nature of the m-XPEAI salts, which are oriented so that the organic part of the molecule points away from the surface (Figure 4). An ambient air stability test was performed for all nine salt-treated and reference devices. Non-encapsulated devices were kept in a dry box with relative humidity (RH) of over 20% for 200 days at 20-25 °C (Figure 5b; Figure S16, Supporting Information). The m-XPEAItreated 3D/2D devices (Figure 5b) showed superior ambient stability (average 98% of their original performances) compared to the control device (73% of its original performance). For the thermal stability test, non-encapsulated m-XPEAI-treated devices were kept in a glove box with a RH of 60-70% for 60 min at 60 °C (Figure 5c). All 3D/2D devices, containing only m-XPEAI salts (Figure 5c) demonstrated greater thermal stability (average 91% of their original performances) compared to the control device (76% of its original performance). In order to get more reliable data, the photostability test under continuous 1-sun illumination was also conducted based on the overall best-performing PEAIbased salt (m-ClPEAI) among x-XPEAI family and the reference device (Figure 5d). Both PSC devices were maintained in a nitrogen atmosphere under a constant illumination of 100 mW cm −2 . The current density-voltage (J-V) curves were recorded every 2 h. After 1000 hours of continuous illumination, the MPO (maximum power output) of the m-ClPEAI-treated device exhibited enhanced long-term stability (87% of its original performance) compared to the reference device (36% of its original performance). These results provide a clear perspective of the substantial benefit of our passivation materials, and pave the way toward molecular design of functional passivation materials.

snippet.text: Contact angles of the reference and meta-halogenated salttreated perovskite films with water are also measured, as shown in Figure 5a. 3D/2D films exhibit more hydrophobic surfaces than the control 3D perovskite film due to the nature of the m-XPEAI salts, which are oriented so that the organic part of the molecule points away from the surface (Figure 4). An ambient air stability test was performed for all nine salt-treated and reference devices. Non-encapsulated devices were kept in a dry box with relative humidity (RH) of over 20% for 200 days at 20-25 °C (Figure 5b; Figure S16, Supporting Information). The m-XPEAItreated 3D/2D devices (Figure 5b) showed superior ambient stability (average 98% of their original performances) compared to the control device (73% of its original performance). Both PSC devices were maintained in a nitrogen atmosphere under a constant illumination of 100 mW cm −2 . The current density-voltage (J-V) curves were recorded every 2 h. documents.snippet: The device employing a hybrid 2D/3D structure exhibited significantly greater stability in comparison to its pure 3D counterpart. Following a 76-hour exposure to ambient air, the pure 3D perovskite device experienced a complete failure. Conversely, the 2D/3D composite device demonstrated remarkable resistance by preserving an impressive 59% of its initial PCE. Further XRD measurements were performed on perovskite samples stored in nitrogen atmosphere and ambient air. The 3D and 2D/3D samples decomposed slightly after 6 hours in an inert atmosphere. Notably, the 3D sample exhibited much quicker chemical degradation than the 2D/3D sample when exposed to ambient conditions. This enhanced ambient stability of the 2D/3D-based device was likely attributed to heightened resistance ability to oxygen and moisture, stemming from improved crystallinity and higher perovskite film hydrophobicity 100 . While the presence of oxygen can substantially weaken the chemical stability of perovskite materials due to reactions with protonated organic cations like MA + and FA + , it's important to highlight that leveraging oxygen for defect passivation has also arisen as a potent and convenient strategy in suppressing nonradiative recombination processes and bolstering the photovoltaic performance of PSCs by strongly interacted with halide vacancies located on the perovskite surface 101 . The mechanism of photo brightening is given in Fig. 7b. After being treated by light, O 2 , and humidity, the density of the shallow state below the conduction band will decrease, leading to the increase of the radiative bimolecular recombination (k R ) and decrease of non-radiative bimolecular component (k n ), which significantly enhance the photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY). The detailed passivation mechanism is as follows: Initially, an untreated MAPbI 3 sample with surface states (Fig. 7cii) was subjected to illumination in the presence of O 2 . This illumination-induced process made a reduction to the density of surface states as well as triggered photo brightening, as depicted in Fig. 7cii). The mechanism behind this phenomenon involved the formation of passivating superoxide species. Importantly, the transformation was reversible and occurred in several hours when subsequently shielded from light.

However, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) shows that PEAIperovskite interactions are nearly disappear in the control films but still preserved in the target films under high humidity (Supplementary Fig. 21). Grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) further reveals that the corresponding PEAI-induced 2D diffraction features are significantly weakened in the control films but remain clear in the target films (Supplementary Fig. 22), indicating that the introduction of n-octane has little effect on the crystallinity of the passivation layer while improving its humidity tolerance. Consistently, both the photoluminescence (PL) intensity and carrier lifetime decreases significantly as the relative humidity increases due to moisture-induced defects (Fig. 3a, b). In contrast, target films maintain much stronger PL emission and show only a minor reduction in lifetime. The result was also confirmed by the space-charge-limited current (SCLC) measurements (Supplementary Figs. 23, 24). As shown in Fig. 3c, for control samples, the defect density increased sharply with rising humidity, whereas only minor variation was observed for the low-hygroscopic solvent systems. 

We also employed Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) to examine the surface potential of perovskite films with different posttreatments under various humidity conditions (Fig. 3d, e). For control films, the potential shifts from −194 mV at 0% RH to −331 mV at 80% RH, accompanied by a broadened distribution. This gradual shift toward a more negative contact potential difference (CPD) indicates an increase in the surface work function of the control films, in agreement with the humidity-induced surface energy level shifts observed by ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) (Supplementary Fig. 25), which impedes surface electron transport and charge extraction 41,42 . In contrast, target films exhibit only a minor shift while maintaining a narrow distribution, demonstrating suppressed moisture-perovskite interactions and uniform surface passivation, as also supported by UPS results (Supplementary Fig. 26).

Summary
In 2D lead‑halide perovskites exposed to ambient light and humidity, the dominant early-time degradation bottleneck is a surface/edge oxygen‑reduction electron‑transfer step coupled to adsorbed water, rather than bulk ion diffusion alone. Under simultaneous illumination, oxygen and water accelerate a photo‑oxidation pathway that converts the perovskite into lead oxide/iodide phases, with the rate‑limiting elementary step being proton abstraction by photogenerated superoxide at the interface; water facilitates rapid proton donation and lowers the effective barrier, making the interfacial reaction kinetics the controlling step under ambient conditions. Halide phase segregation and ion migration are suppressed in strictly 2D structures relative to 3D, but they can still occur—especially at heterointerfaces or in quasi‑2D/mixed‑halide systems—and often proceed slower than overall photo‑oxidation unless conditions or defects favor rapid redistribution. <cite id="83c84d56-3">In MAPbI3, dry photooxidation and water‑accelerated photooxidation dominate ambient degradation kinetics, with the rate‑determining step identified as proton abstraction by photogenerated superoxide radicals and water acting via rapid proton donation</cite> <cite id="f3d971e0-0">Mechanistic kinetics show two predominant modes—oxygen‑electron interaction (Ea ≈ 0.47 eV) and humidity‑accelerated photooxidation (Ea ≈ 0.08 eV)—with explicit rate orders and a catalytic role of moisture</cite> <cite id="f3d971e0-2">In (PEA)2PbI4 nanoflakes, light‑induced degradation to PbI2 initiates at crystal edges and surfaces and is suppressed by encapsulation, indicating surface/edge reactions control the process</cite> <cite id="83c84d56-4">Moisture and oxygen penetrate edges, grain boundaries, and defects in 2D heterostructures, weakening organic–inorganic interactions, promoting halide redistribution, defect formation, and structural distortion</cite>.

Mechanisms and Rate-Limiting Steps Under Ambient Light and Humidity
- Light, oxygen, and water cooperate to drive surface oxidation and chemical conversion. In MAPbI3, dry photooxidation (oxygen + photoexcited electrons) proceeds with a rate of 2 × 10^−9 mol m^−2 s^−1 at 25 °C and an effective activation energy of 0.62 eV, while humidity‑accelerated photooxidation at 50% RH reaches 1 × 10^−7 mol m^−2 s^−1 with an activation energy of 0.07 eV; humidity‑only, blue‑light‑only, and thermal pathways are respectively 100×, 1000×, and >1000× slower than photooxidation in ambient conditions. The observed kinetics imply a rate‑limiting proton‑abstraction step by superoxide radicals, with adsorbed water supplying protons rapidly and thus accelerating the RDS; in dry air the rate depends sigmoidally on oxygen and electron density, whereas in humid air it follows first order in water vapor pressure with sigmoidal dependence on oxygen and electron density. <cite id="83c84d56-3">Photooxidation dominates ambient MAPbI3 degradation, with rates and activation energies quantified and the RDS as proton abstraction by superoxide, accelerated by adsorbed water via rapid proton donation</cite> <cite id="f3d971e0-0">Rate orders and activation energies for photooxidation and humidity‑accelerated photooxidation establish a mechanism where oxygen and moisture jointly control degradation through a catalytic pathway</cite>.
- In strictly 2D layered perovskites such as (PEA)2PbI4, illumination converts the material to PbI2 starting from edges and surfaces, quenching PL via surface traps; encapsulation with h‑BN/polycarbonate suppresses this light‑induced degradation, directly evidencing that surface/edge oxidation and trap formation are the initial and rate‑limiting bottlenecks. <cite id="f3d971e0-2">Under resonant excitation, (PEA)2PbI4 degrades to PbI2 initiated at edges/surfaces, with encapsulation by h‑BN/polycarbonate suppressing degradation</cite>.
- In 2D/quasi‑2D RP crystals and thin films, moisture triggers conversion pathways that consume the higher‑n phases and yield n = 1 phases plus MAI and PbI2, indicating a moisture‑driven surface/chemical transformation that is morphology‑independent and faster than halide‑domain evolution; this suggests surface reaction kinetics limit moisture degradation. <cite id="f3d971e0-4">Moisture degrades 2D/quasi‑2D (PEA)2(MA)n−1PbnI3n+1 into n = 1 phase and MAI + PbI2 and is independent of boundaries/morphology</cite>.

Role of Halide Redistribution and Dimensionality
- Halide phase segregation occurs under illumination in mixed‑halide perovskites and is governed by light‑induced carrier gradients, ion migration, and oxidation; in 2D structures, mobility is reduced and segregation is largely inhibited (n = 1), whereas quasi‑2D (n = 2) shows intermediate behavior and can exhibit photo‑de‑mixing into I‑rich/B‑rich phases; dark remixing can occur at higher temperature, underscoring thermodynamic‑kinetic coupling. <cite id="1172824f-2">2D structures show reduced halide mobility and largely inhibited photo‑induced halide segregation; quasi‑2D phases (n = 2) show no suppression and peculiar absence of dark redistribution unless temperature increases</cite> <cite id="1172824f-1">Halide segregation rate shows a temperature/light‑intensity‑dependent reversal arising from entropic remixing and ion migration; high illumination can transiently remix via photothermal heating, after which segregation re‑establishes</cite> <cite id="1172824f-3">Halide segregation is driven by defects, carrier gradients, oxidation, ion migration; under illumination, holes displace iodide to form iodine vacancies and different mobilities drive phase segregation; I2 loss can render changes irreversible</cite>.
- Dimensionality reduces, but does not eliminate, sensitivity to environmental stimuli: in 2D heterostructures, moisture and oxygen still penetrate defects/edges and heterointerfaces to promote halide redistribution and structural distortion, with oxygen accelerating light‑induced degradation upon atmospheric exposure. <cite id="83c84d56-4">Moisture penetrates edges, grain boundaries, and defects, weakening organic–inorganic interactions and promoting halide redistribution; oxygen accelerates illumination‑induced degradation in 2D perovskites</cite>.
- Compared to 3D, 2D films show smaller segregation efficiencies for mixed‑halide systems and limited PL redshift under illumination, consistent with reduced mobility; however, photo‑de‑mixing can occur in Dion‑Jacobson 2D mixed‑halide perovskites under constant illumination, remaining largely stable in the dark at room temperature. <cite id="1172824f-0">Halide segregation efficiency decreases with reduced dimensionality (≈20% for n = 10 to <1% for n = 1), and 2D films show limited PL change under illumination, indicating restricted compositional change</cite> <cite id="1172824f-4">Photo‑induced phase segregation into I‑rich and Br‑rich phases occurs in 2D Dion‑Jacobson mixed‑halide perovskites, maintained in the dark at room temperature but reversible at higher temperatures</cite>.

Synthesis: What Is Rate-Limiting and When It Switches
