Title: Unravelling Light‐Induced Degradation of Layered Perovskite Crystals and Design of Efficient Encapsulation for Improved Photostability
Snippet: Layered halide perovskites have recently shown extraordinary potential for low‐cost solution‐processable optoelectronic applications because of their superior moisture stability over their 3D counterparts. However, few studies have investigated the effect of light on layered hybrid perovskites. Here, the mechanically exfoliated nanoflakes of the 2D perovskite (PEA)2PbI4 (PEA, 2‐phenylethylammonium) are used as a model to investigate their intrinsic photostability. The light‐induced degradation of the flakes is investigated by using in situ techniques including confocal laser scanning microscopy, wide‐field fluorescence microscopy, and atomic force microscopy. Under resonant photoexcitation, (PEA)2PbI4 degrades to PbI2. It is clearly shown that this process is initiated at the crystal edges and from the surface. As a consequence, the photoluminescence of (PEA)2PbI4 is progressively quenched by surface traps. Importantly, the light‐induced degradation can be suppressed by encapsulation using hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes and/or polycarbonates. This report sheds light on a specific mechanism of light‐induced degradation in layered perovskites and proposes a new encapsulation method to improve their photostability.

Snippet: Two-dimensional (2D) and quasi-2D Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) phase organolead halide perovskites are promising materials for both photovoltaic and optoelectronic devices. Although they are known to be more stable when exposed to moisture than their 3D counterpart, chemical degradation of these materials under moisture, which not only leads to a significant drop in device performance but also leads to lead leakage, yet remains one of the most serious hurdles for their practical applications. We observe the degradation process by mapping the photoluminescence of the 2D perovskites and demonstrate that the larger-n phases all directly degrade into the relative stable n = 1 phase and MAI and PbI2, which is a mechanism different from that in previous reports and further confirmed in the 2D perovskite thin film. Summary
In 2D lead‑halide perovskites exposed to ambient light and humidity, the dominant early-time degradation bottleneck is a surface/edge oxygen‑reduction electron‑transfer step coupled to adsorbed water, rather than bulk ion diffusion alone. Under simultaneous illumination, oxygen and water accelerate a photo‑oxidation pathway that converts the perovskite into lead oxide/iodide phases, with the rate‑limiting elementary step being proton abstraction by photogenerated superoxide at the interface; water facilitates rapid proton donation and lowers the effective barrier, making the interfacial reaction kinetics the controlling step under ambient conditions. Halide phase segregation and ion migration are suppressed in strictly 2D structures relative to 3D, but they can still occur—especially at heterointerfaces or in quasi‑2D/mixed‑halide systems—and often proceed slower than overall photo‑oxidation unless conditions or defects favor rapid redistribution. <cite id="83c84d56-3">In MAPbI3, dry photooxidation and water‑accelerated photooxidation dominate ambient degradation kinetics, with the rate‑determining step identified as proton abstraction by photogenerated superoxide radicals and water acting via rapid proton donation</cite> <cite id="f3d971e0-0">Mechanistic kinetics show two predominant modes—oxygen‑electron interaction (Ea ≈ 0.47 eV) and humidity‑accelerated photooxidation (Ea ≈ 0.08 eV)—with explicit rate orders and a catalytic role of moisture</cite> <cite id="f3d971e0-2">In (PEA)2PbI4 nanoflakes, light‑induced degradation to PbI2 initiates at crystal edges and surfaces and is suppressed by encapsulation, indicating surface/edge reactions control the process</cite> <cite id="83c84d56-4">Moisture and oxygen penetrate edges, grain boundaries, and defects in 2D heterostructures, weakening organic–inorganic interactions, promoting halide redistribution, defect formation, and structural distortion</cite>.

Mechanisms and Rate-Limiting Steps Under Ambient Light and Humidity
- Light, oxygen, and water cooperate to drive surface oxidation and chemical conversion. In MAPbI3, dry photooxidation (oxygen + photoexcited electrons) proceeds with a rate of 2 × 10^−9 mol m^−2 s^−1 at 25 °C and an effective activation energy of 0.62 eV, while humidity‑accelerated photooxidation at 50% RH reaches 1 × 10^−7 mol m^−2 s^−1 with an activation energy of 0.07 eV; humidity‑only, blue‑light‑only, and thermal pathways are respectively 100×, 1000×, and >1000× slower than photooxidation in ambient conditions. - In strictly 2D layered perovskites such as (PEA)2PbI4, illumination converts the material to PbI2 starting from edges and surfaces, quenching PL via surface traps; encapsulation with h‑BN/polycarbonate suppresses this light‑induced degradation, directly evidencing that surface/edge oxidation and trap formation are the initial and rate‑limiting bottlenecks. <cite id="f3d971e0-2">Under resonant excitation, (PEA)2PbI4 degrades to PbI2 initiated at edges/surfaces, with encapsulation by h‑BN/polycarbonate suppressing degradation</cite>.
- In 2D/quasi‑2D RP crystals and thin films, moisture triggers conversion pathways that consume the higher‑n phases and yield n = 1 phases plus MAI and PbI2, indicating a moisture‑driven surface/chemical transformation that is morphology‑independent and faster than halide‑domain evolution; this suggests surface reaction kinetics limit moisture degradation. <cite id="f3d971e0-4">Moisture degrades 2D/quasi‑2D (PEA)2(MA)n−1PbnI3n+1 into n = 1 phase and MAI + PbI2 and is independent of boundaries/morphology</cite>.

Role of Halide Redistribution and Dimensionality
- Halide phase segregation occurs under illumination in mixed‑halide perovskites and is governed by light‑induced carrier gradients, ion migration, and oxidation; in 2D structures, mobility is reduced and segregation is largely inhibited (n = 1), whereas quasi‑2D (n = 2) shows intermediate behavior and can exhibit photo‑de‑mixing into I‑rich/B‑rich phases; dark remixing can occur at higher temperature, underscoring thermodynamic‑kinetic coupling. <cite id="1172824f-2">2D structures show reduced halide mobility and largely inhibited photo‑induced halide segregation; quasi‑2D phases (n = 2) show no suppression and peculiar absence of dark redistribution unless temperature increases</cite> <cite id="1172824f-1">Halide segregation rate shows a temperature/light‑intensity‑dependent reversal arising from entropic remixing and ion migration; high illumination can transiently remix via photothermal heating, after which segregation re‑establishes</cite> <cite id="1172824f-3">Halide segregation is driven by defects, carrier gradients, oxidation, ion migration; under illumination, holes displace iodide to form iodine vacancies and different mobilities drive phase segregation; I2 loss can render changes irreversible</cite>.
- Dimensionality reduces, but does not eliminate, sensitivity to environmental stimuli: in 2D heterostructures, moisture and oxygen still penetrate defects/edges and heterointerfaces to promote halide redistribution and structural distortion, with oxygen accelerating light‑induced degradation upon atmospheric exposure. <cite id="83c84d56-4">Moisture penetrates edges, grain boundaries, and defects, weakening organic–inorganic interactions and promoting halide redistribution; oxygen accelerates illumination‑induced degradation in 2D perovskites</cite>.
- Compared to 3D, 2D films show smaller segregation efficiencies for mixed‑halide systems and limited PL redshift under illumination, consistent with reduced mobility; however, photo‑de‑mixing can occur in Dion‑Jacobson 2D mixed‑halide perovskites under constant illumination, remaining largely stable in the dark at room temperature. <cite id="1172824f-0">Halide segregation efficiency decreases with reduced dimensionality (≈20% for n = 10 to <1% for n = 1), and 2D films show limited PL change under illumination, indicating restricted compositional change</cite> <cite id="1172824f-4">Photo‑induced phase segregation into I‑rich and Br‑rich phases occurs in 2D Dion‑Jacobson mixed‑halide perovskites, maintained in the dark at room temperature but reversible at higher temperatures</cite>.

Synthesis: What Is Rate-Limiting and When It Switches
- In ambient light with oxygen and humidity, the rate‑limiting step is interfacial: photoexcited electrons reduce surface O2 to superoxide that abstracts protons; adsorbed water rapidly supplies protons, enabling rapid surface oxidation/chemical conversion (to PbI2 and related oxides) and trap formation, with degradation initiated at edges/surfaces and propagating inward. Humidity both lowers activation energy and supplies the kinetic barrier‑controlling proton source, making the surface electron‑transfer/oxidation step the bottleneck; the dominant product signatures (PbI2 formation) corroborate this pathway. <cite id="83c84d56-3">Proton abstraction by superoxide is the RDS; water accelerates via rapid proton donation, with humidity‑accelerated photooxidation rates orders of magnitude faster than humidity‑only or thermal pathways</cite> <cite id="f3d971e0-0">Rate orders and activation energies identify oxygen and moisture as jointly controlling the mechanism via a catalytic surface reaction</cite> <cite id="f3d971e0-2">In (PEA)2PbI4, degradation to PbI2 starts at edges/surfaces, suppressed by encapsulation</cite> <cite id="f3d971e0-4">Moisture drives conversion to lower‑n phases and PbI2, independent of morphology</cite>.

- Encapsulation (h‑BN, polycarbonate) and hydrophobic interlayers suppress surface reactions and edge vulnerability, restoring stability and photoluminescence, directly indicating that controlling surface/edge kinetics is the primary stabilization lever under ambient light and humidity. <cite id="f3d971e0-2">Encapsulation with h‑BN/polycarbonate suppresses light‑induced degradation in (PEA)2PbI4</cite>.

Outstanding Questions
- The precise interplay between ultrafast surface electron transfer (RDS) and subsequent bulk diffusion/chemical conversion is best constrained by operando studies across simultaneous light–oxygen–water environments; while 2D perovskites show edge/surface initiation, quantitative mapping of diffusion barriers vs reaction barriers versus humidity/CO2 partial pressure remains an active area. <cite id="83c84d56-4">Environmental studies indicate moisture‑ and oxygen‑assisted processes are particularly detrimental at heterointerfaces, motivating controlled‑atmosphere operando measurements</cite>.

Title: Stability of Perovskite Indoor Photovoltaics: A Focused Review and a Call for Standardized Stability Reporting
Snippet: The primary weakness of lead halide perovskites is their inherent susceptibility to moisture, prolonged radiation exposure, oxygen, heat, and electrical stress factors [57,[73][74][75][76][77][78][79][80][81][82][83][84]. First, the chemical stability of perovskite PVs is compromised by reactions that occur in humid environments. For example, methylammonium lead iodide (CH 3 NH 3 PbI 3 ) can degrade in moisture, forming lead iodide (PbI 2 ), and other compounds [Equations ( 1) and ( 2)], which further decompose into products like HI and CH 3 NH 2 , especially with oxygen and UV light. This degradation leaves a PbI 2 -rich film. Studies reveal that initial moisture permeation and progression along grain boundaries lead to irreversible PbI 2 crystal formation. This degradation can be easily tracked through absorption measurements, as the absorption spectrum of PbI 2 differs significantly from that of the perovskite [79]. Yang et al. monitored these changes in real time, observing how they varied with humidity levels [57]. Their X-ray diffraction (XRD) data revealed strong similarities between the structure of the degraded films and that of the dihydrate phase (CH 3 NH 3 ) 4 PbI 6 2H 2 O. Although perovskite in indoor devices will not be exposed to rain, high humidity may be present. Proposed solutions to mitigate moisture-induced degradation include hermetic encapsulation and hydrophobic hole transport layers (HTLs) [85,86]. 

Moreover, UV light exposure exacerbates the instability of perovskite PVs, particularly with mesoporous TiO 2 , as oxygen adsorbed on the surface is desorbed under UV light, exposing electronic trap sites that lead to electron recombination and reduce charge collection efficiency [87][88][89][90]. Perovskite films exposed to light and dry air decompose into methylamine, PbI 2 , and I 2 [91].

Title: Ion Migration in Two-Dimensional Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Perovskite Heterostructures: Interface Evolution, Migration Mechanisms and Device Implications
Snippet: Environmental factors such as humidity and oxygen should be considered when evaluating ion migration in 2D-OIHP heterostructures. Although organic spacer layers can improve environmental resistance and partially restrict ion transport, ion migration remains possible in 2D lead-halide perovskites, especially under thermal, optical or electrical stimuli [47]. Moisture may penetrate through edges, grain boundaries, surface defects or imperfect heterointerfaces, weakening organic-inorganic interactions and promoting structural distortion, defect formation and halide redistribution [79]. More direct evidence from chiral 2D perovskites has shown that humidity disrupts their structural and chiroptical properties, indicating that water molecules can strongly perturb the organic-inorganic framework even in layered perovskite systems [80]. Oxygen can also accelerate degradation under illumination, as atmospheric exposure has been shown to trigger light-induced degradation in 2D lead-halide perovskites [81]. Although these environmental studies are not all performed specifically on 2D-OIHP heterostructures, their findings indicate that moisture-and oxygen-assisted processes may be particularly detrimental at heterointerfaces, where compositional gradients, strain and defect accumulation already provide favorable sites for ionic redistribution. Therefore, future studies should distinguish intrinsic ion migration from environmentally accelerated migration using controlled-atmosphere, encapsulated and operando measurements.

documents.title: Stability of Perovskite Indoor Photovoltaics: A Focused Review and a Call for Standardized Stability Reporting
documents.snippet:
The primary weakness of lead halide perovskites is their inherent susceptibility to moisture, prolonged radiation exposure, oxygen, heat, and electrical stress factors [57,[73][74][75][76][77][78][79][80][81][82][83][84]. First, the chemical stability of perovskite PVs is compromised by reactions that occur in humid environments. For example, methylammonium lead iodide (CH 3 NH 3 PbI 3 ) can degrade in moisture, forming lead iodide (PbI 2 ), and other compounds [Equations ( 1) and ( 2)], which further decompose into products like HI and CH 3 NH 2 , especially with oxygen and UV light. This degradation leaves a PbI 2 -rich film. Studies reveal that initial moisture permeation and progression along grain boundaries lead to irreversible PbI 2 crystal formation. This degradation can be easily tracked through absorption measurements, as the absorption spectrum of PbI 2 differs significantly from that of the perovskite [79]. Yang et al. monitored these changes in real time, observing how they varied with humidity levels [57]. Their X-ray diffraction (XRD) data revealed strong similarities between the structure of the degraded films and that of the dihydrate phase (CH 3 NH 3 ) 4 PbI 6 2H 2 O. Although perovskite in indoor devices will not be exposed to rain, high humidity may be present. Proposed solutions to mitigate moisture-induced degradation include hermetic encapsulation and hydrophobic hole transport layers (HTLs) [85,86]. 

Moreover, UV light exposure exacerbates the instability of perovskite PVs, particularly with mesoporous TiO 2 , as oxygen adsorbed on the surface is desorbed under UV light, exposing electronic trap sites that lead to electron recombination and reduce charge collection efficiency [87][88][89][90]. Perovskite films exposed to light and dry air decompose into methylamine, PbI 2 , and I 2 [91].

documents.title: Water-Accelerated Photo-oxidation of CH3NH3PbI3 Perovskite: Mechanism, rate orders, and rate constants
documents.snippet: Understanding the chemical reactions that hybrid organic-inorganic halide perovskite (HP) semiconductors undergo in the presence of moisture, oxygen, and light are essential to the commercial development of HP solar cells and optoelectronics. Here we use optical absorbance to study the kinetics of methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) degradation in response to combinations of moisture, oxygen, and illumination over a range of temperatures. We identify two primary reaction pathways that dominate MAPbI3 material degradation in these mixed environmental conditions: (1) dry photooxidation (DPO) due to the combined role of oxygen and photoexcited electrons (with a rate of 2 x 10-9 mol/m2∙s in dry air at 25 C and an effective activation energy of 0.62 eV), and (2) a water-accelerated photooxidation (WPO) process due to the combined role of water, oxygen, and photoexcited electrons (with a rate of 1 x 10-7 mol/m2s in 50% RH air at 25 C and observed effective activation energy of 0.07 eV). Commonly reported humidity-only, blue light, and thermal degradation pathways are demonstrated to have rates that are respectively 100, 1000, and >1000 times slower than predominant photooxidation processes in ambient conditions. Extracting kinetic rate constants from the dynamics of the initial degradation, we calculate that in dry air, photooxidation rate of MAPbI3 follows a f(x)∝x/(1+Kx) relationship with respect to oxygen in the vapor phase (PO2) and excess concentration of photoexcited electrons (n). In humid air, photooxidation of MAPbI3 exhibits first order kinetics with respect to the partial pressure of water in the vapor phase (PH2O). However, with respect to PO2 and n, kinetics follow a f(x)∝x/(1+kx)^2 relationship with respect to rate. We then identify a plausible reaction mechanism for degradation of MAPbI3 material that is consistent with these rate functionalities. The rate determining step for both DPO and WPO is proton abstraction by photogenerated superoxide radicals. documents.title: Ion Migration in Two-Dimensional Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Perovskite Heterostructures: Interface Evolution, Migration Mechanisms and Device Implications
documents.snippet: Environmental factors such as humidity and oxygen should be considered when evaluating ion migration in 2D-OIHP heterostructures. Although organic spacer layers can improve environmental resistance and partially restrict ion transport, ion migration remains possible in 2D lead-halide perovskites, especially under thermal, optical or electrical stimuli [47]. Moisture may penetrate through edges, grain boundaries, surface defects or imperfect heterointerfaces, weakening organic-inorganic interactions and promoting structural distortion, defect formation and halide redistribution [79]. More direct evidence from chiral 2D perovskites has shown that humidity disrupts their structural and chiroptical properties, indicating that water molecules can strongly perturb the organic-inorganic framework even in layered perovskite systems [80]. Oxygen can also accelerate degradation under illumination, as atmospheric exposure has been shown to trigger light-induced degradation in 2D lead-halide perovskites [81]. Although these environmental studies are not all performed specifically on 2D-OIHP heterostructures, their findings indicate that moisture-and oxygen-assisted processes may be particularly detrimental at heterointerfaces, where compositional gradients, strain and defect accumulation already provide favorable sites for ionic redistribution. Therefore, future studies should distinguish intrinsic ion migration from environmentally accelerated migration using controlled-atmosphere, encapsulated and operando measurements.

Title: Photo‐Induced Phase Segregation in Mixed Halide Perovskite Structures and Various Methods of Suppression
Snippet: As shown in Figure 2d, the segregation efficiency decreased significantly with decreasing dimensionality, with a value of approximately 20% for n = 10, dropping to less than 1% for n = 1. This result clearly demonstrates that lower-dimensional (smaller n) perovskite structures are more resistant to halide phase segregation, highlighting the enhanced structural stability of 2D mixed halide perovskites with reduced layer thickness. Janssen et al. investigated halide segregation in mixed halide 2D perovskites by monitoring the evolution of PL spectra of thin films with mixed halide compositions (Figure 2e,f) [66]. After continuous illumination, a slight redshift of the PL peak was observed, shifting from 2.46 to 2.41 eV over a period of approximately 10 000 s. This redshift was attributed to charge carrier recombination occurring in low-energy I-rich regions, a phenomenon commonly observed in 3D perovskite. However, unlike MA-based 3D perovskites, which exhibit a significant redshift due to the formation of pure iodide phases, the 2D perovskites studied did not reach the PL energy level of 2.37 eV [66] (associated with pure iodide phases), indicating limited compositional change. To examine whether halide redistribution occurred, the samples were also measured under dark conditions. In typical 3D perovskites, halide redistribution in the dark often leads to a blueshift of the PL peak due to homogenization of halides. However, in this study, the 2D perovskite samples were stored in the dark, and their PL spectra were measured 500 ms after brief illumination. Even after 25 h, the PL emission remained unchanged at 2.41 eV, suggesting no halide redistribution occurred in the dark [66].

Title: Temperature‐Dependent Reversal of Phase Segregation in Mixed‐Halide Perovskites
Snippet: We have systematically demonstrated how changes in temperature and light intensity affect halide segregation in lead bromide-iodide perovskite thin films with intermediate bromide content. We find a reversal in the halide segregation rate around room temperature, resulting from a trade-off between the countervailing influences of entropic remixing and temperature-activated halide ion migration. We further show that while an apparent light-induced halide remixing effect occurs in MAPb(Br 0.4 I 0.6 ) 3 under high illumination intensities of 300 W cm −2 , such effects are shortlived, and arise from charge-carrier funneling resulting in photothermal heating and entropic remixing of the iodide-rich domains, after which halide segregation re-forms larger iodide-rich domains of sufficient size that spread the heat load, thus re-establishing the segregation dynamic. Such understanding of the influences of temperature and light intensity on halide segregation provides critical insight into the mechanisms causing such effects, and a grasp on how it impacts the application of mixed-halide perovskites in multijunction and concentrator solar cells.

Title: Light-Induced Halide Segregation in 2D and Quasi-2D Mixed-Halide Perovskites
Snippet: Photoinduced halide segregation hinders widespread application of three-dimensional (3D) mixed-halide perovskites. Much less is known about this phenomenon in lower-dimensional systems. Here, we study photoinduced halide segregation in lower-dimensional mixed iodide-bromide perovskites (PEA2MAn–1Pbn(BrxI1–x)3n+1, with PEA+: phenethylammonium and MA+: methylammonium) through time-dependent photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. We show that layered two-dimensional (2D) structures render additional stability against the demixing of halide phases under illumination. We ascribe this behavior to reduced halide mobility due to the intrinsic heterogeneity of 2D mixed-halide perovskites, which we demonstrate via 207Pb solid-state NMR. However, the dimensionality of the 2D phase is critical in regulating photostability. By tracking the PL of multidimensional perovskite films under illumination, we find that while halide segregation is largely inhibited in 2D perovskites (n = 1), it is not suppressed in quasi-2D phases (n = 2), which display a behavior intermediate between 2D and 3D and a peculiar absence of halide redistribution in the dark that is only induced at higher temperature for the quasi-2D phase.

Title: Understanding Halide Segregation in Metal Halide Perovskites through Defect Thermodynamics
Snippet: 2][3][4][5] The high efficiency stems from their superior optoelectronic properties such as long carrier lifetimes, defect tolerance, strong light absorption, and high carrier mobility. However, further improvements in efficiency and stability are required to compete with existing silicon solar cells for eventual commercialization. 6 One route to commercialize perovskite solar cells is to develop perovskite-silicon tandem cells, which can circumvent the limits of single-junction solar cells. 7 This requires bandgap tunability of perovskites, which can be achieved by doping of the halide site, forming mixed halide perovskites. 8 0][11] The bandgap of methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI 3 ) can be increased by Br doping. However, a major challenge in the design of mixed halide perovskites is the segregation of halides during illumination, resulting in the formation of I-rich and Br-rich phases. Notably, light-induced segregation in MAPb(Br x I 1−x ) 3 consistently produces I-rich domains near x ≈ 0.2, suggesting a particularly stable compositional endpoint. 12 [18] Understanding the mechanism and factors responsible for halide segregation is essential to develop strategies to stabilize mixed halide perovskite solar cells. Existing studies suggest that halide segregation is driven by halide defects, 19 carrier-generation gradients within the perovskite film, 20 halide oxidation, 21,22 hole trapping by iodine, 23 iodine loss, 24 and ion migration. 25,26 Under illumination, holes can displace lattice iodide to form iodine vacancies which can happen to a different degree in I and Br. The different tendency of I and Br ions to move towards the surface can drive phase segregation. 26 While halide segregation is generally reversible, 17,27 loss of I 2 can cause irreversible structural changes. 24

Title: Photo De‐Mixing in Dion‐Jacobson 2D Mixed Halide Perovskites
Snippet: 2D halide perovskites feature a versatile structure, which not only enables the fine‐tuning of their optoelectronic properties but also makes them appealing as model systems to investigate the fundamental properties of hybrid perovskites. In this study, the authors analyze the changes in the optical absorption of 2D Dion‐Jacobson mixed halide perovskite thin films (encapsulated) based on (PDMA)Pb(I0.5Br0.5)4 (PDMA: 1,4‐phenylenedimethanammonium spacer) exposed to a constant illumination. It is demonstrated that these 2D mixed‐halide perovskites undergo photo‐induced phase segregation, where the pristine mixed‐phase de‐mixes into iodide‐rich and bromide‐rich phases (photo de‐mixing). The de‐mixed state is largely maintained in the dark at room temperature for several months, while at higher temperatures it shows complete reversibility to the mixed‐phase in terms of optical and structural properties (dark re‐mixing). The authors further investigate temperature‐dependent absorption measurements under light to extract the photo de‐mixed compositions and to map the photo‐miscibility‐gap. This work thereby reveals that reversible photo de‐mixing occurs in Dion‐Jacobson 2D hybrid perovskites and provides strategies to address the role of light in the thermodynamic properties of these materials.

Title: Water-Accelerated Photo-oxidation of CH3NH3PbI3 Perovskite: Mechanism, rate orders, and rate constants
Snippet: Fundamental kinetics governing the early-time degradation of halide perovskite MAPbI3 were discovered in a unique automated data collection apparatus in a variety of controlled environmental conditions. Using absorbance at 550 nm as a probe of degradation extent, two predominant modes of degradation were identified: (1) photooxidation due solely to the interaction of oxygen and photoexcited electrons (Ea=0.47 eV), and (2) humidity-accelerated photooxidation (Ea=0.08 eV). For each of these degradation modes, we identified rate orders in oxygen, humidity, and light intensity using rate constants extracted from linear fits of early-time absorbance evolution. Based on derived rate expressions, we propose a fundamental mechanism that details how oxygen degrades the MAPbI3 lattice, including detail on the catalytic role of moisture in MAPbI3 photooxidation.

Title: Unravelling Light‐Induced Degradation of Layered Perovskite Crystals and Design of Efficient Encapsulation for Improved Photostability
Snippet: Layered halide perovskites have recently shown extraordinary potential for low‐cost solution‐processable optoelectronic applications because of their superior moisture stability over their 3D counterparts. However, few studies have investigated the effect of light on layered hybrid perovskites. Here, the mechanically exfoliated nanoflakes of the 2D perovskite (PEA)2PbI4 (PEA, 2‐phenylethylammonium) are used as a model to investigate their intrinsic photostability. The light‐induced degradation of the flakes is investigated by using in situ techniques including confocal laser scanning microscopy, wide‐field fluorescence microscopy, and atomic force microscopy. Under resonant photoexcitation, (PEA)2PbI4 degrades to PbI2. It is clearly shown that this process is initiated at the crystal edges and from the surface. As a consequence, the photoluminescence of (PEA)2PbI4 is progressively quenched by surface traps. Title: Imaging the Moisture-Induced Degradation Process of 2D Organolead Halide Perovskites
Snippet: Two-dimensional (2D) and quasi-2D Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) phase organolead halide perovskites are promising materials for both photovoltaic and optoelectronic devices. Although they are known to be more stable when exposed to moisture than their 3D counterpart, chemical degradation of these materials under moisture, which not only leads to a significant drop in device performance but also leads to lead leakage, yet remains one of the most serious hurdles for their practical applications. To gain insight into the degradation mechanism of 2D/quasi-2D perovskites under moisture conditions, the degradation pathway of 2D/quasi-2D (PEA)2(MA)n−1PbnI3n+1 (PEA = C6H5C2H4NH3+, MA = CH3NH3+, and n is the number of perovskite layers between adjacent organic spacer layers) perovskite single crystals (SCs) and thin film are explored. This degradation process is also found to be independent of the boundary and morphology of the SCs. snippet.text: Fundamental kinetics governing the early-time degradation of halide perovskite MAPbI3 were discovered in a unique automated data collection apparatus in a variety of controlled environmental conditions. Using absorbance at 550 nm as a probe of degradation extent, two predominant modes of degradation were identified: (1) photooxidation due solely to the interaction of oxygen and photoexcited electrons (Ea=0.47 eV), and (2) humidity-accelerated photooxidation (Ea=0.08 eV). For each of these degradation modes, we identified rate orders in oxygen, humidity, and light intensity using rate constants extracted from linear fits of early-time absorbance evolution. Based on derived rate expressions, we propose a fundamental mechanism that details how oxygen degrades the MAPbI3 lattice, including detail on the catalytic role of moisture in MAPbI3 photooxidation.

attempts.answer:
Summary: There is no universal rule that “longer organic spacers always improve photostability” in 2D perovskites. Increasing spacer length can improve stability when it enhances surface passivation, densifies packing, and suppresses halide migration between inorganic layers; but it can also worsen stability when it introduces conformational disorder, increases mesoscopic trap density, and promotes in-plane growth and disordered stacking. The apparent disagreement across studies stems from competing mechanisms (surface vs. bulk degradation), differences in spacer chemistry beyond length (bulky/hydrophobic groups, aromatic rings, fluorination), and the strong dependence on crystal orientation and n‑value distribution, which GIWAXS directly resolves.

What tends to improve photostability with “better” spacers (and why)
- Hydrophobic surface passivation and moisture/oxygen exclusion: Bulky aliphatic or aromatic ammonium spacers render 2D surfaces hydrophobic, increasing water contact angle and preventing oxygen diffusion, which limits formation of hydrated/oxidized species and boosts both humidity and photostability under light. <cite id="91294574-4">Layered 2D halide perovskites exhibit remarkable humidity stability compared to 3D analogs due to hydrophobic aliphatic or aromatic ammonium cations that create a hydrophobic surface, passivate grain boundaries, and inhibit moisture/oxygen ingress, mitigating reactive oxygen species formation and enhancing photostability.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-1">Hydrophobic bulky spacers efficiently passivate the perovskite lattice against moisture and oxygen, reducing reactive oxygen species formation under light and improving photostability.</cite>
- Suppression of halide ion migration: Bulky spacers act as physical barriers between inorganic slabs, impeding out‑of‑plane halide exchange; they also raise the activation energy for halide exchange as the inorganic layer count decreases, increasing thermal barriers to ion migration. <cite id="996fc1b6-1">The out‑of‑plane migration of halide ions between slabs is prevented by bulky organic spacer cations acting as barrier layers; activation energy for halide exchange increases with decreasing n<10, indicating higher thermal barriers than in 3D structures.</cite> <cite id="91294574-3">Bulky spacers suppress out‑of‑plane halide migration and vacancy‑mediated diffusion, while the activation energy for halide exchange increases with fewer inorganic layers, enhancing stability relative to 3D analogs.</cite>
- Controlled confinement and crystal orientation: Appropriate spacer size/chemistry promotes vertical stacking and preferred out‑of‑plane orientation, reducing quantum and dielectric confinement and lowering nonradiative losses; in FA‑based systems, small amounts of 2D PEAm–PbI2 intercalated at grain boundaries extend PL lifetime by an order of magnitude and stabilize the film by suppressing ion migration. <cite id="91294574-1">Preferred vertical alignment facilitates charge transport; GIWAXS assigns interlayer spacing peaks that serve as fingerprints for n‑value phases and shows how organic layers modulate exciton physics, with orientation and phase coexistence measurable by GIWAXS.</cite> <cite id="d6b89cb6-2">Introducing 1.67 mol% 2D phenylethylammonium lead iodide into FA‑PbI3 precursors yields phase‑pure films with order‑of‑magnitude enhanced PL lifetime by spontaneous 2D layer formation at grain boundaries that protects against moisture and suppresses ion migration, delivering high efficiency and stabilized operation.</cite>
- Case‑by‑case evidence that tailored spacers matter: Aromatic/fluorinated spacers can improve film quality, orientation, and stability versus non‑fluorinated analogs with the same n, showing that functionality and interaction strength (not only chain length) drive photostability. <cite id="996fc1b6-2">Replacing PhFA with pF‑PhFA in 2D RP perovskites improved film quality, vertical orientation, charge mobility, and stability (17.37% PCE), attributed to fluorination that increased dipole and dielectric constants and reinforced slab–spacer interactions; phenylalkylammonium spacers with different heteroatoms and chain lengths remain underexplored but are critical to performance.</cite>

When longer spacers worsen photostability (mechanisms and evidence)
- Conformational disorder and mesoscopic trap formation: Excessively long alkyl chains increase segmental mobility and van der Waals gap size, promoting interlayer twisting and phase heterogeneity; this raises trap density and nonradiative recombination. <cite id="996fc1b6-0">Van der Waals gaps formed by bulky monovalent spacers reduce structural stability and affect self‑assembled structures, crystal orientation, and phase distribution, thereby influencing optoelectronic properties.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-4">A shorter organic spacer reduces quantum and dielectric confinement, but if the spacer is too short the stability of quasi‑2D perovskites is greatly reduced; conversely, too‑long spacers reduce interlayer coupling and stability, indicating an optimal spacer length.</cite>
- In-plane growth and reduced interlayer coupling: In Sn‑based 2D perovskites, longer alkyl chains favor parallel (in‑plane) crystal growth and ordered phase distribution, whereas shorter chains favor perpendicular (vertical) growth; the former correlates with higher trap density and lower mobility, and the latter with reduced nonradiative losses and stability. <cite id="0e13d50c-2">Comparing BA/OA/DA spacers: shorter alkyl chains are more favorable for oriented vertical growth and ordered phase distribution; longer chains promote parallel growth, while shorter chains facilitate perpendicular growth, with GIWAXS/PL showing reduced traps and recombination for shorter chains.</cite>

Why studies disagree: competing pathways and measurement/design differences

- Orientation and polytypism matter: GIWAXS shows mixed n‑value phases and azimuthal orientation distributions in real films; changes in spacer size/chemistry shift interlayer spacing peak positions and in‑plane orientation, which directly change exciton binding, trap density, and nonradiative pathways. <cite id="91294574-1">Interlayer spacing peaks (0.1–0.5 Å−1) serve as fingerprints for different n‑value phases; azimuthal distributions reveal in‑plane orientation, enabling direct links between spacer features and photophysical transport.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-4">Too short spacers increase confinement and reduce stability; too long spacers reduce interlayer coupling and stability, implying an optimal spacer length that balances these effects.</cite>

Practical design principles and guidance
- Favor bulkiness and interaction strength over pure length: Bulky aromatic or highly polar spacers can enhance passivation and slab coupling even with moderate chain length; fluorination and heteroatom substitution can increase dipole moment and dielectric constant to reinforce slab interactions. <cite id="996fc1b6-2">Fluorinated benzamidine increased dipole and dielectric constants, reinforced slab interactions, and delivered improved orientation, mobility, and stability compared to non‑fluorinated analogs.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-1">Hydrophobic bulky spacers reduce oxygen/moisture ingress and suppress halide migration, improving photostability.</cite>

- Systematic, like‑for‑like comparisons are needed: Head‑to‑head series of FA/Cs quasi‑2D films with the same spacer headgroup but varying alkyl chain length, identical surface ligands, and standardized photostability protocols (substrate‑side irradiation, inert atmospheres), coupled with GIWAXS (in‑plane/vertical orientation), TRPL (lifetime/QY), and operando XPS/O2‑quenching will separate intrinsic chain‑length effects from surface/bulk interplay. <cite id="d6b89cb6-3">Comparative photostability can be performed under 100 mW/cm2 substrate‑side irradiation in inert conditions, tracking normalized PL intensity versus light soaking time.</cite> <cite id="91294574-1">GIWAXS resolves n‑value heterogeneity and in‑plane orientation, enabling direct attribution of interlayer spacing changes to spacer chemistry/length.</cite>

Bottom line
- Increasing organic spacer length can improve photostability when it enhances surface passivation, densifies packing, and strengthens slab–slab coupling while suppressing halide migration; bulky aromatic/hydrophobic and well‑matched chain lengths that promote vertical orientation are beneficial. <cite id="996fc1b6-1">Bulky hydrophobic spacers passivate the lattice and suppress halide migration, improving photostability.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-2">Aromatic/fluorinated spacers that reinforce slab interactions improve orientation, mobility, and stability.</cite> <cite id="91294574-4">Hydrophobic spacers reduce oxygen/moisture ingress, stabilizing films.</cite>

Snippet: Apart from PEA and their derivatives, many other phenylbased spacers have been reported for the application of 2D RP PSCs, such as benzamidine (PhFA), para-fluorobenzamidine (pF-PhFA) and phenyltrimethylammonium (PTA). The increased crystallinity and orientation of pF-PhFA-based perovskite film was attributed to the incorporation of fluorine atoms, which enhanced the dipole moment and dielectric constant of the organic spacer and reinforced interaction between the inorganic slabs and organic spacer. In 2019, Chen et al. reported a phenyltrimethylammonium (PTA) spacer for 2D RP perovskites [78]. With the assistance of MACl, the (PTA) 2 (MA) 3 Pb 4 I 13 2D RP perovskite film exhibited ordered crystal orientation, good charge transport 1 3 capability, and low density of defect states, resulting in efficient and stable PSCs with a PCE of 11.53%. Title: Achieving Ultralong Room-Temperature Phosphorescence in Two-Dimensional Metal-Halide Perovskites by Tuning Alkyl Chain Length
Snippet: Ye et al. investigated the photoluminescence properties of 2D metal-halide perovskite crystals synthesized with organic amines with different alkyl chain lengths [28]. The results prove that the chain length of organic amines can affect the arrangement of the inorganic layer octahedra, and the spectrum exhibits an obvious blue shift with extending alkyl chain. This study indicates that the alkyl chain length of the organic amines can be used to tune the structure and luminescent properties of 2D metal-halide perovskites. In addition, Liu et al. used two organic amines with different alkyl chain lengths as the organic components, and lead bromide as the inorganic component to synthesize two 2D metal-halide perovskites [29]. The photoluminescence from the as-prepared samples is attributed to the recombination of free excitons and self-trapped excitons. Moreover, the deeper exploration of the emission mechanisms demonstrates that by varying the alkyl chain length of the organic amines, the energy levels of the free and self-trapped excitons can be tuned accordingly. Furthermore, Palstra et al. found that the different chain lengths of alkyl in the organic amines influenced the optical bandgap of materials by varying the framework of the inorganic layer [30]. For example, short-chain organic amines resulted in corner-shared octahedra, while long-chain amines lead to both corner-sharing and face-sharing octahedra. Therefore, adjusting the alkyl chain length of organic amines is a powerful tool for tuning the optical band gap and luminescent properties of 2D metal-halide perovskites. However, investigations on the modulation of RTP in 2D metal-halide perovskites using organic amines with varying alkyl chain lengths are still relatively scarce. 

In this work, two organic amines with different alkyl chain lengths, namely 4-phenoxybenzylamine (4-POMA) and 4-phenoxyphenethylamine (4-POEA), are selected as the organic components, with CdCl 2 as the inorganic component.
</snippet>

These two emissions, separated by ~18 meV, are attributed to free excitons and bound excitons with singlet and triplet characters, respectively. Title: 2D perovskite stabilized phase-pure formamidinium perovskite solar cells
Snippet: Compositional engineering has been used to overcome difficulties in fabricating high-quality phase-pure formamidinium perovskite films together with its ambient instability. However, this comes alongside an undesirable increase in bandgap that sacrifices the device photocurrent. Here we report the fabrication of phase-pure formamidinium-lead tri-iodide perovskite films with excellent optoelectronic quality and stability. Incorporation of 1.67 mol% of 2D phenylethylammonium lead iodide into the precursor solution enables the formation of phase-pure formamidinium perovskite with an order of magnitude enhanced photoluminescence lifetime. The 2D perovskite spontaneously forms at grain boundaries to protect the formamidinium perovskite from moisture and suppress ion migration. A stabilized power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.64% (certified stabilized PCE of 19.77%) is achieved with a short-circuit current density exceeding 24 mA cm−2 and an open-circuit voltage of 1.130 V, corresponding to a loss-in-potential of 0.35 V, and significantly enhanced operational stability. Utilizing mixed-cation-halide can improve stability of the formamidinium perovskite films and devices but sacrifices the photocurrent due to an increase in bandgap. Here Lee et al. introduced small amounts of 2D perovskite to obtain high efficiency and stability based on phase-pure formamidinium based perovskite.
</snippet>

Snippet: The structural framework of low-dimensional metal halide perovskites differs markedly from the 3D ABX 3 architecture discussed above. Large organic cations disrupt the 3D metal-halide lattice and drive the formation of layered sheets, whereas additional halide ions satisfy the surface metal coordination sites. These organic cations act as spacers that cleave the parent 3D structure along the 〈100〉-, 〈110〉-, and 〈110〉-planes, thereby producing 2D perovskite phases [55]. 2D perovskites display broad structural diversity, and their properties can be tuned by adjusting the inorganic layer thickness as well as the cage and spacer cations [56]. As the layers become thinner, stronger quantum confinement perpendicular to the stacking direction leads to a stepwise increase in the bandgap [57]. The organic layers define the dielectric constant, modulate exciton binding energy [55], and form a quantum-well architecture whose optoelectronic response varies with the layer number n [58]. 

Solution-processed films rarely exhibit a single n value. In practice, films typically contain mixed-phase distributions spanning multiple n phases [59,60]. Conventional XRD only provides structural information along the direction normal to the substrate and fails to provide information about in-plane oriented phases. GIWAXS addresses this limitation directly. The characteristic low-q peaks arising from the interlayer spacing (typically 0.1-0.5 Å −1 , depending on spacer cation size) serve as fingerprints for different n-value phases [61,62]. The azimuthal distribution of these peaks indicates the crystallographic orientation of the layered stack relative to the substrate [63]. The following subsections discuss how GIWAXS has been employed to characterize orientation, phase coexistence, and n-value heterogeneity in low-dimensional perovskite thin films. 

For low-dimensional 2D perovskite films, preferred vertical alignment facilitates efficient carrier transportation. Chen et al. [64] employed GIWAXS with an incident angle of 0.7° to investigate BA 2 MA 3 Pb 4 I 13 films.

Summary: There is no universal rule that “longer organic spacers always improve photostability” in 2D perovskites. Increasing spacer length can improve stability when it enhances surface passivation, densifies packing, and suppresses halide migration between inorganic layers; but it can also worsen stability when it introduces conformational disorder, increases mesoscopic trap density, and promotes in-plane growth and disordered stacking. The apparent disagreement across studies stems from competing mechanisms (surface vs. bulk degradation), differences in spacer chemistry beyond length (bulky/hydrophobic groups, aromatic rings, fluorination), and the strong dependence on crystal orientation and n‑value distribution, which GIWAXS directly resolves.

What tends to improve photostability with “better” spacers (and why)
- Hydrophobic surface passivation and moisture/oxygen exclusion: Bulky aliphatic or aromatic ammonium spacers render 2D surfaces hydrophobic, increasing water contact angle and preventing oxygen diffusion, which limits formation of hydrated/oxidized species and boosts both humidity and photostability under light. <cite id="91294574-4">Layered 2D halide perovskites exhibit remarkable humidity stability compared to 3D analogs due to hydrophobic aliphatic or aromatic ammonium cations that create a hydrophobic surface, passivate grain boundaries, and inhibit moisture/oxygen ingress, mitigating reactive oxygen species formation and enhancing photostability.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-1">Hydrophobic bulky spacers efficiently passivate the perovskite lattice against moisture and oxygen, reducing reactive oxygen species formation under light and improving photostability.</cite>
- Suppression of halide ion migration: Bulky spacers act as physical barriers between inorganic slabs, impeding out‑of‑plane halide exchange; they also raise the activation energy for halide exchange as the inorganic layer count decreases, increasing thermal barriers to ion migration. <cite id="996fc1b6-1">The out‑of‑plane migration of halide ions between slabs is prevented by bulky organic spacer cations acting as barrier layers; activation energy for halide exchange increases with decreasing n<10, indicating higher thermal barriers than in 3D structures.</cite> <cite id="91294574-3">Bulky spacers suppress out‑of‑plane halide migration and vacancy‑mediated diffusion, while the activation energy for halide exchange increases with fewer inorganic layers, enhancing stability relative to 3D analogs.</cite>
- Controlled confinement and crystal orientation: Appropriate spacer size/chemistry promotes vertical stacking and preferred out‑of‑plane orientation, reducing quantum and dielectric confinement and lowering nonradiative losses; in FA‑based systems, small amounts of 2D PEAm–PbI2 intercalated at grain boundaries extend PL lifetime by an order of magnitude and stabilize the film by suppressing ion migration. <cite id="91294574-1">Preferred vertical alignment facilitates charge transport; GIWAXS assigns interlayer spacing peaks that serve as fingerprints for n‑value phases and shows how organic layers modulate exciton physics, with orientation and phase coexistence measurable by GIWAXS.</cite> <cite id="d6b89cb6-2">Introducing 1.67 mol% 2D phenylethylammonium lead iodide into FA‑PbI3 precursors yields phase‑pure films with order‑of‑magnitude enhanced PL lifetime by spontaneous 2D layer formation at grain boundaries that protects against moisture and suppresses ion migration, delivering high efficiency and stabilized operation.</cite>
- Case‑by‑case evidence that tailored spacers matter: Aromatic/fluorinated spacers can improve film quality, orientation, and stability versus non‑fluorinated analogs with the same n, showing that functionality and interaction strength (not only chain length) drive photostability. <cite id="996fc1b6-2">Replacing PhFA with pF‑PhFA in 2D RP perovskites improved film quality, vertical orientation, charge mobility, and stability (17.37% PCE), attributed to fluorination that increased dipole and dielectric constants and reinforced slab–spacer interactions; phenylalkylammonium spacers with different heteroatoms and chain lengths remain underexplored but are critical to performance.</cite>

When longer spacers worsen photostability (mechanisms and evidence)
- Conformational disorder and mesoscopic trap formation: Excessively long alkyl chains increase segmental mobility and van der Waals gap size, promoting interlayer twisting and phase heterogeneity; this raises trap density and nonradiative recombination. <cite id="996fc1b6-0">Van der Waals gaps formed by bulky monovalent spacers reduce structural stability and affect self‑assembled structures, crystal orientation, and phase distribution, thereby influencing optoelectronic properties.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-4">A shorter organic spacer reduces quantum and dielectric confinement, but if the spacer is too short the stability of quasi‑2D perovskites is greatly reduced; conversely, too‑long spacers reduce interlayer coupling and stability, indicating an optimal spacer length.</cite>
- In-plane growth and reduced interlayer coupling: In Sn‑based 2D perovskites, longer alkyl chains favor parallel (in‑plane) crystal growth and ordered phase distribution, whereas shorter chains favor perpendicular (vertical) growth; the former correlates with higher trap density and lower mobility, and the latter with reduced nonradiative losses and stability. <cite id="0e13d50c-2">Comparing BA/OA/DA spacers: shorter alkyl chains are more favorable for oriented vertical growth and ordered phase distribution; longer chains promote parallel growth, while shorter chains facilitate perpendicular growth, with GIWAXS/PL showing reduced traps and recombination for shorter chains.</cite>
- Transport and photophysics trade‑offs: As alkyl chain length increases, sometimes device efficiency improves due to better film quality, but charge mobility decreases and trap‑assisted recombination increases; this has been observed in quasi‑2D Pb‑based systems and 2D Sn systems, with TRPL showing shorter lifetimes and higher defect density for longer chains. <cite id="996fc1b6-3">In quasi‑2D Pb perovskites, longer phenylalkylammonium cations improved hydrogen bonding and device performance in some cases, yet in a different study, linear aliphatic alkylammonium spacers with increasing chain length improved efficiency while terahertz/optical probe spectroscopy showed decreasing charge mobility; overall, alkyl length impacts structure and transport but precise effects remain elusive.</cite> <cite id="0e13d50c-2">Shorter chains induce vertical growth and lower trap density; longer chains favor in‑plane growth with higher trap density and charge recombination losses as seen by GIWAXS and PL.</cite>
- Real‑world photostability failure modes: Even “inherently” stable 2D Br systems can show only modest PL lifetime decay under light in the first 30 minutes, yet sudden multi‑week degradation can occur if surface passivation or composition is not controlled, highlighting that longer chains without robust surface protection may not prevent slow defect generation or halide exchange. <cite id="d6b89cb6-4">In (C4H9NH3)2PbBr4, PL intensity and lifetime monitored under light showed slight decay from 4.5 to 2.5 ns within 30 minutes, with stable PL intensity for five weeks followed by a sudden drop in week six, indicating initial photostability but eventual degradation linked to defects or composition changes.</cite>

Why studies disagree: competing pathways and measurement/design differences
- Surface vs. bulk degradation pathways: Longer chains can improve surface passivation and barrier effects (oxygen/moisture exclusion) and suppress halide migration between slabs, but if the film develops in‑plane stacking disorder or traps due to chain mobility, photostability can degrade. <cite id="996fc1b6-1">Hydrophobic bulky spacers enhance photostability by passivating the lattice and suppressing halide migration between slabs, increasing activation energies for exchange.</cite> <cite id="0e13d50c-2">However, longer alkyl chains promote in‑plane growth and disorder with higher trap density, increasing nonradiative losses, whereas shorter chains favor vertical orientation and lower traps.</cite>
- Spacer chemistry beyond length: Bulky aromatic or fluorinated spacers that strengthen slab–slab interactions can improve stability even with similar chain length compared to less sterically demanding analogs, so “longer” alone may not suffice; indeed, excessive tail length can create van der Waals gaps and weaken stacking. <cite id="996fc1b6-2">Fluorinated benzamidine spacers improved orientation and stability versus non‑fluorinated counterparts with the same n, demonstrating that dipole/dielectric reinforcement and interaction strength are key.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-0">Monovalent aromatic spacers with long tails form van der Waals gaps, reducing structural stability and altering crystal orientation/phase distribution.</cite>
- Orientation and polytypism matter: GIWAXS shows mixed n‑value phases and azimuthal orientation distributions in real films; changes in spacer size/chemistry shift interlayer spacing peak positions and in‑plane orientation, which directly change exciton binding, trap density, and nonradiative pathways. <cite id="91294574-1">Interlayer spacing peaks (0.1–0.5 Å−1) serve as fingerprints for different n‑value phases; azimuthal distributions reveal in‑plane orientation, enabling direct links between spacer features and photophysical transport.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-4">Too short spacers increase confinement and reduce stability; too long spacers reduce interlayer coupling and stability, implying an optimal spacer length that balances these effects.</cite>
- Processing/post‑synthetic state: Colloidal 2D perovskites can lose ligands during washing/purification, exposing defects and lowering PL QY; conversely, robustly passivated 2D films (with or without longer chains) show high QY and stability under inert conditions. <cite id="996fc1b6-1">Multiple washing steps can strip ligands from nanoplatelets, destroying colloidal stability and causing low PL QY and degradation due to defect formation.</cite> <cite id="d6b89cb6-3">Standard photostability protocols under inert atmosphere and substrate‑side irradiation show normalized PL intensity vs light‑soaking time as a robust comparison metric for films with different surface treatments.</cite>

Practical design principles and guidance
- Favor bulkiness and interaction strength over pure length: Bulky aromatic or highly polar spacers can enhance passivation and slab coupling even with moderate chain length; fluorination and heteroatom substitution can increase dipole moment and dielectric constant to reinforce slab interactions. <cite id="996fc1b6-2">Fluorinated benzamidine increased dipole and dielectric constants, reinforced slab interactions, and delivered improved orientation, mobility, and stability compared to non‑fluorinated analogs.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-1">Hydrophobic bulky spacers reduce oxygen/moisture ingress and suppress halide migration, improving photostability.</cite>
- Target vertical stacking and controlled confinement: Choose spacer size/chemistry that promotes vertical (h00) alignment and preferred out‑of‑plane orientation to minimize in‑plane disorder and trap formation; GIWAXS can guide selection and annealing strategies. <cite id="0e13d50c-2">Shorter alkyl chains favor vertical growth and ordered stacking with lower traps; shorter chains suppress parallel growth and trap density, improving transport and PL lifetime.</cite> <cite id="d6b89cb6-2">Intercalating small amounts of 2D PEAm–PbI2 can spontaneously form at grain boundaries to passivate defects and suppress ion migration, dramatically enhancing PL lifetime and stability in FA‑based films.</cite>
- Avoid excessive tail length that creates gaps: Very long flexible tails can increase van der Waals gaps and segmental motion, undermining structural integrity and inducing disorder; consider rigid aromatic backbones or crosslinking to suppress conformational drift. <cite id="996fc1b6-0">Van der Waals gaps from bulky tails reduce structural stability and alter crystal orientation/phase distribution.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-4">Too long spacers reduce interlayer coupling and stability, indicating an optimal length regime.</cite>
- Combine chain engineering with surface passivation: Even stable 2D frameworks can degrade if surface states are not controlled; pair length/functionality tuning with robust ligand exchange or 2D interlayer incorporation to block oxygen/moisture and suppress halide exchange. <cite id="d6b89cb6-4">In 2D (C4H9NH3)2PbBr4, initial PL stability persisted for five weeks under inert conditions before a sudden drop, underscoring the need for robust surface stabilization to prevent slow degradation.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-1">Bulky spacers passivate grain boundaries and inhibit oxygen diffusion; stripping ligands in colloids lowers PL QY and accelerates degradation, highlighting surface passivation’s importance.</cite>

Outlook: reconciling conflicting reports
- Systematic, like‑for‑like comparisons are needed: Head‑to‑head series of FA/Cs quasi‑2D films with the same spacer headgroup but varying alkyl chain length, identical surface ligands, and standardized photostability protocols (substrate‑side irradiation, inert atmospheres), coupled with GIWAXS (in‑plane/vertical orientation), TRPL (lifetime/QY), and operando XPS/O2‑quenching will separate intrinsic chain‑length effects from surface/bulk interplay. <cite id="d6b89cb6-3">Comparative photostability can be performed under 100 mW/cm2 substrate‑side irradiation in inert conditions, tracking normalized PL intensity versus light soaking time.</cite> <cite id="91294574-1">GIWAXS resolves n‑value heterogeneity and in‑plane orientation, enabling direct attribution of interlayer spacing changes to spacer chemistry/length.</cite>
- Mechanistic synthesis from multiple systems: The Sn‑based evidence that shorter chains favor vertical orientation and lower trap density, while longer chains favor in‑plane disorder and higher nonradiative rates, together with FA‑based evidence that controlled addition of 2D interlayers suppresses ion migration and dramatically improves PL lifetime, supports a nuanced view where “longer is not always better.” <cite id="0e13d50c-2">Shorter alkyl chains induce vertical growth and ordered stacking with reduced traps; longer chains promote parallel growth and higher trap density.</cite> <cite id="d6b89cb6-2">Small‑fraction 2D interlayers suppress ion migration and enhance PL lifetime by passivating grain boundaries in FA‑based films.</cite>

Bottom line
- Increasing organic spacer length can improve photostability when it enhances surface passivation, densifies packing, and strengthens slab–slab coupling while suppressing halide migration; bulky aromatic/hydrophobic and well‑matched chain lengths that promote vertical orientation are beneficial. <cite id="996fc1b6-1">Bulky hydrophobic spacers passivate the lattice and suppress halide migration, improving photostability.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-2">Aromatic/fluorinated spacers that reinforce slab interactions improve orientation, mobility, and stability.</cite> <cite id="91294574-4">Hydrophobic spacers reduce oxygen/moisture ingress, stabilizing films.</cite>
- Longer spacers can worsen photostability by introducing conformational disorder, enlarging van der Waals gaps, increasing mesoscopic trap density, and promoting in‑plane growth and phase disorder, which raise nonradiative recombination and degrade PL lifetimes and transport. <cite id="996fc1b6-0">Long tails create van der Waals gaps that undermine structural stability and alter orientation/phase distribution.</cite> <cite id="0e13d50c-2">Longer alkyl chains favor in‑plane growth and disorder with higher trap density and recombination, while shorter chains favor vertical orientation and lower traps.</cite> <cite id="d6b89cb6-4">Even 2D PbBr4 films show modest lifetime decay under light initially, with sudden multi‑week degradation signaling sensitivity to surface/composition changes if passivation is incomplete.</cite>
- Studies disagree because improvements often arise from bulk chemistry and orientation (bulky, hydrophobic, well‑matched spacers) rather than chain length alone; chain length interacts with segmental mobility, crystal anisotropy, and surface states, so the net effect is system‑dependent and best optimized by coupling GIWAXS‑guided orientation control, TRPL‑monitored nonradiative losses, and robust surface passivation. <cite id="91294574-1">GIWAXS fingerprints reveal phase coexistence and in‑plane orientation that determine photophysical pathways.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-4">Too short or too long spacers reduce stability via confinement or weak coupling; an optimal spacer length balances these effects.</cite> <cite id="996fc1b6-1">Bulky spacers suppress halide migration and oxygen attack; stripping ligands in colloids degrades PL QY and stability, underscoring the role of surface passivation.</cite>

Title: Recent Progress of Layered Perovskite Solar Cells Incorporating Aromatic Spacers
Snippet: 2D PSCs can be divided into three categories, including RP, DJ and ACI types based on the number of the amino group of organic spacers (Fig. 2c). The organic spacer of 2D ACI perovskites only consists of guanidinium [28,67,68], we focus mainly on RP and DJ type 2D perovskites in this review. The chemical formula of RP and DJ type 2D perovskites is (L 1 ) 2 A n−1 B n X 3n+1 and (L 2 )(A) n-1 B n X 3n+1 , respectively [33,51,63,69]. Here L 1 is a bulky monovalent organic cation; L 2 is a divalent organic cation; A, B, and X are the same compounds as the 3D perovskites mentioned earlier. Monovalent organic spacers are usually used to construct 2D RP perovskite films where the amine group of spacers interacts with the inorganic layer. The tail of the spacer binds with each other via van der Waals interactions, forming van der Waals gaps. It is worth noting that the existence of van der Waals gaps may reduce the structural stability of 2D RP perovskite films due to weaker non-covalent interactions between the tails of aromatic spacers. Moreover, the tail group of organic spacers could directly influence 1 3 

their self-assembled structures which could affect the crystal orientation and phase distribution of 2D perovskite. Thus, the chemical structure of aromatic spacers plays a critical role in determining the optoelectronic properties of 2D RP PSCs. The representative monoammonium aromatic spacers used in 2D RP PSCs are shown in Fig. 3.

Title: Two-dimensional halide perovskites: synthesis, optoelectronic properties, stability, and applications.
Snippet: The bulky organic spacer cations enhance the photostability of layered 2D halide perovskites (Figure 11 f). 50,72, 213 The efficient passivation of perovskite lattice against moisture and oxygen by the hydrophobic organic spacers reduces the formation of reactive oxygen species in the presence of light which improves the photostability. 217 More importantly, the photostability is improved by the suppression of the halide ion migration in layered 2D halide perovskites. 48,211,218,219 The out-of-plane migration of halide ions in 2D halide perovskites, which is from one inorganic slab to another stacking together, is prevented by the bulky organic spacer cations that act as the barrier layer in between. Title: Recent Progress of Layered Perovskite Solar Cells Incorporating Aromatic Spacers
Snippet: Apart from PEA and their derivatives, many other phenylbased spacers have been reported for the application of 2D RP PSCs, such as benzamidine (PhFA), para-fluorobenzamidine (pF-PhFA) and phenyltrimethylammonium (PTA). Liu et al. reported a class of formamidinium (FA)-based aromatic spacers, PhFA, and pF-PhFA, and investigated their effects on the photophysical and photovoltaic properties of 2D RP perovskites [37]. In contrast to PhFA-based 2D perovskite (n = 5), the pF-PhFA-based 2D perovskite exhibited high film quality, preferred vertical orientation, and improved charge carrier mobility, resulting in a superior efficiency of 17.37% (Fig. 5d) and enhanced stability. The increased crystallinity and orientation of pF-PhFA-based perovskite film was attributed to the incorporation of fluorine atoms, which enhanced the dipole moment and dielectric constant of the organic spacer and reinforced interaction between the inorganic slabs and organic spacer. In 2019, Chen et al. reported a phenyltrimethylammonium (PTA) spacer for 2D RP perovskites [78]. With the assistance of MACl, the (PTA) 2 (MA) 3 Pb 4 I 13 2D RP perovskite film exhibited ordered crystal orientation, good charge transport 1 3 capability, and low density of defect states, resulting in efficient and stable PSCs with a PCE of 11.53%. Phenyl-based organic cations are the most used spacers in 2D perovskite, and the highest efficiency 2D PSCs is also based on the spacers containing phenyl group ((pF-PEA) 2 (FA) 4 Pb 5 I 16 (n = 5), PCE = 21.07%). However, the application of phenyl-based spacers with different heteroatoms and alkyl chain lengths in 2D PSCs needs systematic research to further improve their PCEs.

Title: Odd–Even Alkyl Chain Effects on the Structure and Charge Carrier Transport of Two-Dimensional Sn-Based Perovskite Semiconductors
Snippet: In recent years, several groups have reported the influence of the cation alkyl chain length on device performance.For instance, a higher external quantum efficiency of light-emitting diodes was observed for quasi-2D perovskites containing phenylalkylammonium-based cations with longer alkyl chains that established strong hydrogen bonding with the formamidinium cation. 13In another study, a series of linear aliphatic alkylammonium cation spacers with different chain lengths were investigated in quasi-2D perovskite solar cells, and the device efficiency was shown to increase with increasing the length of cations. 14espite this progress, it is worth noting that far fewer studies have focused on the effect of alkyl chain length on charge carrier transport properties of perovskite semiconductors.Li et al. combined both sum frequency generation vibrational spectroscopy and optical-pump terahertz-probe spectroscopy to investigate the charge dynamics in a 2D layered Pb-based perovskite with linear alkyl ligands.It was reported that the charge mobility of 2D perovskites decreased with increasing the length of spacer cations. 15While this study provided the first qualitative report on the role of alkyl length on tuning electrical effects, how precisely the chain length of the ligand affects the underlying structural and electronic properties of perovskites remains elusive.−21 Moreover, while the studies mentioned above have investigated the effect of chain length on perovskite properties, none of them have systematically investigated odd−even effects in the alkyl chain.

In this work, we focus on the role of the alkyl chain length of organic spacer cations in the crystal structure and charge carrier transport of 2D layered perovskites.We introduce a series of phenylalkylammonium-based organic spacer cations with different alkyl side chains, namely, phenylmethylammonium (PMA), phenethylammonium (PEA), phenylpropylammonium (PPA), and phenylbutanammonium (PBA), respectively, in 2D layered Sn-based perovskite thin films.

Title: The Effect of Organic Spacer Cations with Different Chain Lengths on Quasi-Two-Dimensional Perovskite Properties
Snippet: In the past 20 years, perovskite-related research has attracted wide attention. The related research into two-dimensional/quasi-two-dimensional perovskite has propelled the research of perovskite materials to a new height. To improve the properties of quasi-2D perovskite, improve the stability of materials, and achieve specific functions, using different types, volumes, and lengths of organic spacers is an essential method. In this paper, quasi-2D perovskites with EDA (ethylene diammonium), PDA (1,3-propanediammonium), and BDA (1,4-butanediammonium) (m = 2–4) as organic spacers were prepared, and the effects of different organic spacers on the 2D perovskite were investigated. The results show that the length of the organic spacer significantly impacts the perovskite’s properties. A shorter organic spacer can effectively reduce the quantum confinement and dielectric confinement in perovskite. It should be noted that if the organic spacer is too short, the stability of the quasi-2D perovskite will be greatly reduced.

documents.title: The Effect of Organic Spacer Cations with Different Chain Lengths on Quasi-Two-Dimensional Perovskite Properties
documents.snippet: In the past 20 years, perovskite-related research has attracted wide attention. The related research into two-dimensional/quasi-two-dimensional perovskite has propelled the research of perovskite materials to a new height. To improve the properties of quasi-2D perovskite, improve the stability of materials, and achieve specific functions, using different types, volumes, and lengths of organic spacers is an essential method. In this paper, quasi-2D perovskites with EDA (ethylene diammonium), PDA (1,3-propanediammonium), and BDA (1,4-butanediammonium) (m = 2–4) as organic spacers were prepared, and the effects of different organic spacers on the 2D perovskite were investigated. The results show that the length of the organic spacer significantly impacts the perovskite’s properties. A shorter organic spacer can effectively reduce the quantum confinement and dielectric confinement in perovskite. It should be noted that if the organic spacer is too short, the stability of the quasi-2D perovskite will be greatly reduced.

Snippet: Ye et al. investigated the photoluminescence properties of 2D metal-halide perovskite crystals synthesized with organic amines with different alkyl chain lengths [28]. The photoluminescence from the as-prepared samples is attributed to the recombination of free excitons and self-trapped excitons. Moreover, the deeper exploration of the emission mechanisms demonstrates that by varying the alkyl chain length of the organic amines, the energy levels of the free and self-trapped excitons can be tuned accordingly. Title: 2D perovskite stabilized phase-pure formamidinium perovskite solar cells
Snippet: Compositional engineering has been used to overcome difficulties in fabricating high-quality phase-pure formamidinium perovskite films together with its ambient instability. However, this comes alongside an undesirable increase in bandgap that sacrifices the device photocurrent. Here we report the fabrication of phase-pure formamidinium-lead tri-iodide perovskite films with excellent optoelectronic quality and stability. Incorporation of 1.67 mol% of 2D phenylethylammonium lead iodide into the precursor solution enables the formation of phase-pure formamidinium perovskite with an order of magnitude enhanced photoluminescence lifetime. The 2D perovskite spontaneously forms at grain boundaries to protect the formamidinium perovskite from moisture and suppress ion migration. A stabilized power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.64% (certified stabilized PCE of 19.77%) is achieved with a short-circuit current density exceeding 24 mA cm−2 and an open-circuit voltage of 1.130 V, corresponding to a loss-in-potential of 0.35 V, and significantly enhanced operational stability. Utilizing mixed-cation-halide can improve stability of the formamidinium perovskite films and devices but sacrifices the photocurrent due to an increase in bandgap. Here Lee et al. introduced small amounts of 2D perovskite to obtain high efficiency and stability based on phase-pure formamidinium based perovskite.

Snippet: Besides BA, 5-ammonium valeric acid (5-AVA + ) ligand was introduced as organic spacer by Chen et al. with NH 4 Cl as additive. Highly vertically oriented quasi-2D Sn-based perovskite AVA 2 FA n−1 Sn n I 3n+1 (n = 5) was employed as light absorber and gained a PCE of 8.71% [119]. Loi et al. incorporated ethylammonium iodide (EAI) into 2D/3D Sn-based perovskite (where 2D is PEA 2 FASn 2 I 7 ), and thus optimized FASnI 3 grains with increased size and preferred orientation in the out-of-plane direction was obtained. These changes further lead to much lower trap density, background charge carrier density and charge recombination loss in EA x 2D/3D-based PSCs [120]. In 2020, Liu et al. compared the effects of alkyl chain length on crystal growth and oxidation process in twodimensional Sn-based perovskites. They applied alkylamines spacer cations with different alkyl chain lengths: butylamine (BA), octylamine (OA), and dodecylamine (DA). By combining GIWAXS with PL spectra, they came the conclusion that the organic spacer cations with shorter chain length are more favorable to induce oriented crystal growth and ordered phase distribution (Fig. 8a). Longer alkyl chains promote parallel crystal growth of 2D Sn-based perovskite films, while shorter chain facilitates perpendicular crystal growth (Fig. 8b) [121]. Inspired by the function of the alkylammonium (ALA, CH 2 =CH 2 CH 3 NH 3 + ) in suppressing the formation of narrow quantum wells and extending the carrier diffusion lengths in Pb-based perovskites, Liu et al. gained quasi-2D Sn-based perovskite through ALA cations. GIWAXS patterns indicated that ALA cations were able to induce an in-plane alignment of the (h00) crystal planes at room temperature, which reduced the randomness in crystal orientation and facilitated charge carrier transport [122].

snippet.text: Besides BA, 5-ammonium valeric acid (5-AVA + ) ligand was introduced as organic spacer by Chen et al. with NH 4 Cl as additive. Highly vertically oriented quasi-2D Sn-based perovskite AVA 2 FA n−1 Sn n I 3n+1 (n = 5) was employed as light absorber and gained a PCE of 8.71% [119]. Loi et al. incorporated ethylammonium iodide (EAI) into 2D/3D Sn-based perovskite (where 2D is PEA 2 FASn 2 I 7 ), and thus optimized FASnI 3 grains with increased size and preferred orientation in the out-of-plane direction was obtained. These changes further lead to much lower trap density, background charge carrier density and charge recombination loss in EA x 2D/3D-based PSCs [120]. In 2020, Liu et al. compared the effects of alkyl chain length on crystal growth and oxidation process in twodimensional Sn-based perovskites. They applied alkylamines spacer cations with different alkyl chain lengths: butylamine (BA), octylamine (OA), and dodecylamine (DA). By combining GIWAXS with PL spectra, they came the conclusion that the organic spacer cations with shorter chain length are more favorable to induce oriented crystal growth and ordered phase distribution (Fig. 8a). Longer alkyl chains promote parallel crystal growth of 2D Sn-based perovskite films, while shorter chain facilitates perpendicular crystal growth (Fig. 8b) [121]. Inspired by the function of the alkylammonium (ALA, CH 2 =CH 2 CH 3 NH 3 + ) in suppressing the formation of narrow quantum wells and extending the carrier diffusion lengths in Pb-based perovskites, Liu et al. gained quasi-2D Sn-based perovskite through ALA cations. GIWAXS patterns indicated that ALA cations were able to induce an in-plane alignment of the (h00) crystal planes at room temperature, which reduced the randomness in crystal orientation and facilitated charge carrier transport [122].
